label: Dr. Haitham Nabil
description: Clinical Case Question Bank by an Iraqi Doctor.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old adolescent presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe headaches and exertional chest pain. Physical examination reveals upper-body hypertension and lower-body hypotension. These findings prompt suspicion of coarctation of the aorta. All the following are signs of coarctation of the aorta EXCEPT?

options.label: A
options.text: Femoral pulses are weak or absent

options.label: C
options.text: Femoral pulse occurs slightly before the radial pulse

options.label: D
options.text: Blood pressure in the legs is lower than that in the arms

options.label: E
options.text: Precordial impulse and heart sounds are usually normal

questions.initialExplanation:
Coarctation causes delayed and weak femoral pulses compared with the radial pulse. Normally, the femoral pulse is felt slightly before the radial pulse.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The radial and femoral pulses should always be palpated simultaneously for the presence of a radial-femoral delay. Normally, the femoral pulse occurs slightly before the radial pulse. A radial-femoral delay occurs when blood flow to the descending aorta is dependent on collaterals, in which case the femoral pulse is felt after the radial pulse.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-month history of worsening fatigue and shortness of breath with exertion. She has no primary care physician, stating that she has been healthy all her life. She reports no chronic medical problems, takes no medications, and has never been hospitalized nor had surgery. She originally attributed her symptoms to being "out of shape," but she now finds it difficult to climb stairs and even walk long distances. Her vital signs are unremarkable. Breath sounds are clear bilaterally. Her cardiac examination is significant for a normal S1 with a prominent S2 and a short 1/6 diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. A plain radiograph of her chest shows a prominent main pulmonary artery and increased pulmonary vascularity at the hilum. An echocardiogram demonstrates hypertrophy of the right ventricle (RV), tricuspid and pulmonary insufficiency, and blood shunting from the RV to the left ventricle across a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Of the following, what is the best explanation of these findings for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: This is the natural history of the acyanotic form of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

options.label: B
options.text: Critical pulmonary valve stenosis is responsible for the VSD shunt

options.label: C
options.text: She has primary pulmonary hypertension from a congenital heart defect

options.label: D
options.text: RV hypertrophy developed in response to increasing pulmonary pressures and does not represent HCM

options.label: E
options.text: She has developed pulmonary vascular obstructive disease

questions.initialExplanation:
An unrepaired left-to-right shunt can cause pulmonary vascular disease over time. When pulmonary pressure becomes very high, the shunt reverses to right-to-left, producing Eisenmenger syndrome.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: She has developed pulmonary vascular obstructive disease. Eisenmenger syndrome is the reversal of a left-to-right shunt into a right-to-left shunt due to the development of pulmonary vascular obstructive disease that develops over time due to excessive pulmonary blood flow. It is seen in patients with a communication between the left and right heart, for example, in patients with a VSD, atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, atrioventricular septal defect, and/or aortopulmonary window, that goes unrepaired. In normal infants, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and the RV becomes more compliant in the initial weeks after birth. Excess blood enters the pulmonary circulation and the pulmonary arterioles dilate in order to accommodate the excessive volume. Over years, hypertrophy occurs within the medial and intimal layers of the muscular pulmonary arteries and arterioles, raising the pulmonary vascular resistance. Ultimately, right-sided pressures become greater than those in the left heart, and flow across the VSD reverses, resulting in Eisenmenger syndrome. (A) The patient in the vignette does not have TOF. The murmur is not one of pulmonary stenosis, but of pulmonary insufficiency that has developed due to increased pressure within the pulmonary arteries. Similarly, the RV has hypertrophied in response to increasing pulmonary pressures. The acyanotic form of TOF occurs when the RV outflow tract obstruction is mild and does not severely limit pulmonary blood flow. Affected infants may be asymptomatic and maintain adequate oxygen saturations. Over time, they may present with signs of heart failure due to the left-to-right VSD shunt. Infants with the acyanotic form of TOF eventually become cyanotic as hypertrophy of the RV infundibulum increases as they grow. This typically occurs in the first year of life. (B) A VSD in the setting of critical pulmonary valve stenosis may shunt right-to-left; however, critical PS requires attention in the newborn period. (C) The patient in the vignette does not have primary pulmonary hypertension. Her pulmonary disease progressed over years as a result of excess pulmonary blood flow due to the VSD. If her VSD had been treated early in life, this patient would not have developed Eisenmenger syndrome. (D) As described earlier, the RV hypertrophy developed in response to increasing pulmonary pressures and does not represent HCM.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old female is brought to the pediatrician by her parents due to concerns about recurrent respiratory infections and poor growth. The parents report that the child has had several episodes of cough and wheezing over the past year, which seem to worsen during the winter months. In patients with atrial septal defect, which one of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Primum atrial septal defect is the most common type

options.label: B
options.text: Heart failure is common presentation of patient with atrial secundum septal defect

options.label: C
options.text: Left axis deviation is characteristic ECG finding of atrial primum septal defect

options.label: D
options.text: There is a single second heart sound on auscultation

options.label: E
options.text: Majority of children with ASD develop pulmonary hypertension before school entry

questions.initialExplanation:
Primum ASD is associated with left-axis deviation on ECG. Secundum ASD is the most common type, and a fixed, wide split S2 is a classic examination finding.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: ECG in primum ASD is distinctive and shows left axis deviation. Heart failure is in general a rare complication of ASD unless there is a big left-to-right shunt and even an extremely large ASD rarely produces heart failure in childhood. ASD secundum is the most common type of ASD. On auscultation, there is a wide fixed splitting of S2, and pulmonary hypertension rarely complicates ASD.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is found to be hypertensive on a routine health assessment. She was born at term and has had normal growth and development. Her blood pressure is 130/68 mmHg in the right arm, 100/62 mmHg in the left arm, and 104/66 mmHg in the left leg. There is a systolic ejection click and a 1/VI early systolic murmur at the upper sternal border. The right radial pulse is 3+. Her right femoral pulse is 1+ and is felt after the radial pulse when they are palpated simultaneously. Additional testing to confirm the diagnosis is ordered. Of the following, which findings are most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Electrocardiogram (ECG) demonstrating a sinus rhythm, left axis deviation, and increased voltage in the left lateral leads

options.label: B
options.text: Echocardiogram showing a discrete coarctation of the aorta between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries

options.label: C
options.text: Plain radiography of the chest showing an enlarged cardiac silhouette and notching of the inferior border of the ribs

options.label: D
options.text: Abdominal ultrasound showing stenosis of the right renal artery

options.label: E
options.text: Increased concentration of vanillylmandelic acid in a 24-hour urine collection

questions.initialExplanation:
Coarctation is confirmed by echocardiography and typically causes high arm pressure, lower leg pressure, and weak or delayed femoral pulses.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Echocardiogram showing a discrete coarctation of the aorta between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries. The patient described is characteristic of coarctation of the aorta. Normally, blood pressure in the lower extremities is 10 to 20 mmHg higher than in the upper extremities. In coarctation of the aorta this is reversed. For a discrete juxtaductal coarctation, blood pressure is higher in the right arm than in the left arm and in the right and left legs because of collateral flow from the aortic arch. The murmur and the femoral arteries may be abnormal. While older patients with unrecognized coarctation may have evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG as well as cardiomegaly and rib notching on chest radiography, this is not typically seen in young children with the first decade of life. Rib notching occurs over years due to pressure erosion by enlarged collateral vessels that develop in order to offset diminished blood flow from the descending aorta. The cause of the systolic click in the patient described in the vignette is likely due to a bicuspid aortic valve. Bicuspid aortic valve is associated with coarctation of the aorta in the majority of cases.

questions.stem: A pediatrician is asked to review a heart murmur of a 2-day-old baby born by vaginal delivery following an uneventful period to a primiparous mother, aged 38. The prenatal period was normal and the baby has been feeding well. On examination, he is hypotonic, has single palmar creases and epicanthic folds. What is the most likely heart lesion?
questions.initialExplanation:
AVSD is strongly associated with Down syndrome. Hypotonia, single palmar creases, and epicanthic folds are clues to trisomy 21.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: AVSD is a congenital heart defect in which there are holes between the chambers of the right and left sides of the heart. The valves that control blood flow between these chambers may not be formed correctly. Also known as atrioventricular canal (AV canal) defect or endocardial cushion defect, AVSD is common in babies with Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Approximately 50% of children with Down syndrome have AVSD.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric clinic by concerned parents who report recurrent respiratory infections and difficulty in feeding. Physical examination reveals a harsh, holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border, consistent with a ventricular septal defect (VSD). The child is thriving poorly, and there are signs of increased work of breathing. Indications for surgical closure of a VSD include the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Patients in whom clinical symptoms and failure to thrive cannot be controlled medically

options.label: B
options.text: Infants between 6 and 12 months of age with large defects associated with pulmonary hypertension

options.label: C
options.text: Patients older than 24 months with a Qp:Qs ratio greater than 2:1

options.label: D
options.text: Patients with a supracristal VSD of any size

options.label: E
options.text: Severe pulmonary vascular disease nonresponsive to pulmonary vasodilators

questions.initialExplanation:
Advanced pulmonary vascular disease that does not respond to treatment can make VSD closure unsafe, so it is an exception to usual indications for surgery.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Severe pulmonary vascular disease that is nonresponsive to pulmonary vasodilators (Option E) may preclude surgical intervention due to the increased risk associated with the existing pulmonary hypertension. In such cases, the focus may shift towards managing the pulmonary vascular disease and optimizing the patient’s condition medically rather than pursuing surgical closure.

questions.stem: Careful evaluation of the character of the pulses is an important early step in the physical diagnosis of congenital heart disease. A wide pulse pressure with bounding pulses may suggest the following EXCEPT?
questions.initialExplanation:
Wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses are associated with high-output states or aortic runoff. Cardiomyopathy is not the typical cause among the listed options.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The presence of diminished pulses in all extremities is associated with pericardial tamponade, left ventricular outflow obstruction, or cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old primigravida who is at 36 weeks’ gestation presents for her scheduled gynecology visit. She is concerned that the fetus will have birth defects because she had a viral infection early during the pregnancy. She tested positive for rubella during the first trimester, and she was counseled that the baby might have multiple problems, including congenital heart disease. Of the following, which heart defect is her baby most likely to have?

options.label: E
options.text: There is no increased risk unless the infection occurred in the third trimester

questions.initialExplanation:
Congenital rubella syndrome classically causes PDA and pulmonary artery stenosis, together with cataracts and hearing impairment.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The triad of congenital cataracts, deafness, and congenital heart defects characterizes congenital rubella syndrome. Infection during the first trimester is the most damaging for the fetus. Additional manifestations include microcephaly, microphthalmia, thrombocytopenia, and purpura. The most common heart defects include patent ductus arteriosus and stenosis of the pulmonary arteries. (A) An increased incidence of coarctation of the aorta along with bicuspid aortic valve is associated with Turner syndrome. (B) Williams syndrome is associated with supravalvar aortic stenosis. (C) Kartagener syndrome is associated with dextrocardia and situs inversus.

questions.stem: In the outpatient setting, a 2-month-old infant was brought in for a routine checkup. The child’s parents, attentive to their baby’s well-being, mentioned mild concerns about feeding difficulties and occasional breathlessness. A careful examination by the pediatrician revealed a continuous machinery-like murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border. Further diagnostic evaluation, including echocardiography, confirmed the presence of a small patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Patients with a small PDA have the following criteria EXCEPT?

options.label: A
options.text: Continuous murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border

options.label: C
options.text: Normal pulmonary artery pressure by echocardiography

options.label: D
options.text: Asymptomatic and live a normal life expectancy

options.label: E
options.text: Risk for endocarditis is extremely low

questions.initialExplanation:
A small PDA usually causes a continuous machinery murmur and may leave chamber size and pulmonary pressure normal. The source notes that endocarditis risk is not extremely low.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: A silent PDA is a tiny defect that cannot be heard by auscultation and is detected by other nonclinical means such as echocardiography. Life expectancy is always normal in this population and the risk for endocarditis is extremely low. Patients with a small PDA have an audible continuous or machinery murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border. In addition, they have normal peripheral pulses. Because there is negligible left-to-right shunting, these patients have normal left atrial (LA) and left ventricular (LV) size and normal pulmonary artery pressure by echocardiography and chest X-ray. These patients are asymptomatic and live a normal life expectancy. They have a higher risk for endocarditis.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician by her parents due to concerns about poor feeding and excessive sweating during feeds. The parents report that the infant appears to become tired easily and has episodes of rapid breathing. The doctor diagnosed her with PDA after the examination and investigations. Regarding PDA all true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: LV enlargement causing cardiomegaly with pulmonary hyperemia is seen on CXR film

options.label: B
options.text: Collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure and machinery murmur are the hallmarks of diagnosis

options.label: C
options.text: Large PDAs only need closure, because small ones can close spontaneously even in older children

options.label: D
options.text: It is more common in females and in a newborn delivered to mother in acquiring Rubella infection in pregnancy

options.label: E
options.text: It is a remnant of an embryonic channel connecting the pulmonary artery with the aorta near its isthmus

questions.initialExplanation:
PDA closure is considered based on the shunt and clinical risk; the source says the statement that only large PDAs need closure is the exception.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: All PDAs require closure, as there is a significant risk of infective endocarditis. While small PDAs may have the potential to close spontaneously, especially in premature infants, older children with symptomatic PDAs or evidence of left ventricular volume overload may still require closure to prevent complications such as heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is referred to pediatric cardiology for a murmur and cardiomegaly. Referral had been made for the same murmur after her 6-month and 12-month well-child evaluations, but the family did not follow up until now. At her 2-year evaluation, the murmur was noted again and she was tachypneic, but in no apparent distress. A chest radiograph demonstrated cardiomegaly. At the cardiologist’s office, she is shy, but playful. She is slightly tachypneic and tachycardic. Her systolic blood pressure is normal, while her diastolic pressure is lower than expected. She has a 2/6 harsh, continuous murmur at the upper left sternal border and the left infraclavicular area. The cardiologist also notes an apical diastolic rumble and bounding peripheral pulses. Her ECG is indicative of biventricular hypertrophy. Of the following, which is her echocardiogram most likely to reveal as the etiology of these findings?
questions.initialExplanation:
A PDA causes continuous left-to-right flow, a machinery murmur, bounding pulses, and widened pulse pressure; a large shunt can cause heart failure.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The tachycardia, tachypnea, and cardiomegaly described in the vignette are indicative of congestive heart failure (CHF). That, along with the wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses, and the description of the murmur point toward a PDA as the etiology. With a large PDA, there is a large continuous left-to-right shunt that reduces systemic blood pressure due to flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery during diastole. Because systolic blood pressure is not affected, the pulse pressure widens and bounding pulses may be present. The continuous shunt is also the cause of the continuous murmur, which may be described as harsh or machinery sounding. The apical diastolic murmur is due to relative mitral stenosis from increased flow from increased pulmonary venous return. The murmur of peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis may be best heard transmitting to the back and/or axillae, and signs of CHF are not typical. The pulmonary valve murmur is a systolic murmur, not a continuous murmur. An isolated PFO would not be responsible for the signs and symptoms of CHF described.

questions.stem: In the pediatric cardiology clinic, a 4-year-old child presented with a ventricular septal defect (VSD), a congenital heart anomaly discovered during examination. The child’s parents express concerns about recurrent respiratory infections and slowed growth. A thorough examination revealed a palpable thrill and a harsh holosystolic murmur over the lower left sternal border. Regarding the treatment, Surgical repair of VSD at the time of diagnosis should be considered in?
questions.initialExplanation:
Small supracristal or perimembranous VSDs can damage the aortic valve when a cusp prolapses into the defect. Early repair may prevent progressive aortic regurgitation.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The renal issue? (Source text:) The risk to these patients with small supracristal or perimembranous VSD with associated prolapse of the aortic cusp into the defect resulting in progressive aortic regurgitation. These patients should be considered for surgical repair at the time of diagnosis to prevent progressive aortic valve damage.

questions.stem: During a regular checkup of an 8-year-old child, you note a loud first heart sound with a fixed and widely split second heart sound at the upper left sternal border that does not change with respirations. The patient is otherwise active and healthy. Which of the following heart lesions most likely explains these findings?
questions.initialExplanation:
A fixed, widely split S2 that does not vary with respiration is a classic auscultatory feature of ASD.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Most children with an ASD are asymptomatic. The lesion is found during a routine examination. In older children, exercise intolerance can be noted if the lesion is of significant size. On examination, the pulses are normal, a right ventricular systolic lift at the left sternal border is palpable, and a fixed splitting of the second heart sound is audible. For lesser degrees of ASD, surgical treatment is more controversial. VSD commonly presents as a harsh or blowing holosystolic murmur best heard along the left lower sternal border and may radiate to the precordium. Tricuspid regurgitation is a mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal border; a history of birth asphyxia or findings of other cardiac lesions often is present. Tetralogy of Fallot is a common form of congenital heart disease. The four abnormalities include right ventricular outflow obstruction, VSD, dextroposition of the aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy; the cyanosis presents in infants and in young children. Mitral valve prolapse occurs with the billowing into the atria of one or both mitral valve leaflets at the end of systole. It is a congenital abnormality that frequently manifests only during adolescence or later.

questions.stem: A 2-week-old newborn is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination. He was born at term and the pregnancy was uncomplicated. His mother says he has been feeding well and passing adequate amounts of urine. He appears healthy. He is at the 60th percentile for length and 40th percentile for weight. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse is 130/min, respirations are 49/min and blood pressure is 62/40 mm Hg. A thrill is present over the third intercostal space. A 5/6 holosystolic murmur is heard over the left lower sternal border. An echocardiography shows a 3-mm membranous ventricular septal defect. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation:
A small VSD in a thriving, asymptomatic infant without heart failure or chamber enlargement can be monitored with outpatient follow-up rather than closed immediately.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The most appropriate next step in management for this newborn with a 3-mm membranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) is outpatient follow-up. The newborn appears healthy and is feeding well, with no signs or symptoms of heart failure or other complications related to the VSD. This indicates that the defect is likely small and not causing significant hemodynamic compromise. The echocardiogram reveals a 3-mm membranous VSD, which is relatively small. Small VSDs are less likely to cause symptoms or complications compared to larger defects. There are no indications for immediate intervention such as heart failure, cyanosis, or evidence of left ventricular volume overload. Therefore, the newborn can be safely managed with outpatient follow-up to monitor for any changes in symptoms or progression of the defect.

questions.stem: A newborn infant with has facial features suggestive of Down syndrome. Echo study demonstrates small ASD. What is the characteristic physical finding during auscultation of this infant?

options.label: B
options.text: A fixed split second heart sound

questions.initialExplanation:
ASD classically causes a wide, fixed split S2 because increased right-sided flow delays pulmonary valve closure.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In most patients with an ASD, the characteristic finding is that the second heart sound is widely split and fixed in its splitting during all phases of respiration.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician for a routine check-up. The parents report that the infant has been feeding well and appears to be gaining weight appropriately. However, they express concern about a bluish discoloration noticed around the lips during feeding. On examination, the infant appears well-nourished and active. There are no signs of respiratory distress, and the infant’s oxygen saturation is within the normal range. Which of the following statements is true about a ventricular septal defect (VSD)?

options.label: A
options.text: A murmur may not be present at birth

options.label: C
options.text: A continuous machinery-like murmur is characteristic

options.label: D
options.text: A larger defect will have a louder murmur than a small defect

options.label: E
options.text: A normal ECG excludes the presence of a VSD

questions.initialExplanation:
A VSD can be present even when no murmur is heard, especially early in life or when associated pulmonary pressure is high.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: While many infants with VSDs present with a characteristic holosystolic murmur, the absence of a murmur does not rule out the presence of VSD. In some cases, particularly if the defect is small or if there is associated pulmonary hypertension, the murmur may not be audible.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl with short stature, neck webbing, and sexual infantilism is found to have coarctation of the aorta. A chromosomal analysis likely would demonstrate which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation:
Turner syndrome (45,X or XO) causes short stature, webbed neck, sexual infantilism, and is associated with coarctation of the aorta.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Short stature, neck webbing, sexual infantilism, and a shieldlike chest with widely spaced nipples are signs of Turner syndrome, which is usually associated with an XO karyotype. Aortic coarctation occurs in about 15% to 20% of those with this disorder. Down syndrome is most commonly associated with endocardial cushion defects or VSD. Marfan syndrome (mutation 15q21.1) is associated with dilatation of the aorta and mitral and aortic regurgitation. Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (defect 4p16) is associated with ASD.

questions.stem: 14-year-old girl complaining of amenorrhea. General look of the patient demonstrates webbing of the neck and wide chest. You want to perform cardiovascular examination. What clinical sign is MOST indicative of coarctation of the aorta?

options.label: B
options.text: Notching of the inferior border of the ribs

options.label: C
options.text: A systolic ejection click or thrill in the suprasternal notch

options.label: E
options.text: Diminished or absent femoral or lower-extremity pulses

questions.initialExplanation:
Coarctation obstructs blood flow to the lower body, producing higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The most common clinical sign of coarctation of the aorta in older children is differential blood pressure: arms > legs (100%).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her parents for a routine check-up. She has no significant past medical history and is generally healthy. Upon auscultation of her heart, the pediatrician hears a murmur. The child is asymptomatic and has no complaints of chest pain, shortness of breath, or exercise intolerance. She has normal growth and development for her age. A small ventricular septal defect is associated with:

options.label: A
options.text: Pansystolic murmur at the sternal edge

options.label: C
options.text: Fixed splitting of the second heart sound

questions.initialExplanation:
A small VSD classically causes a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border. Fixed split S2 is associated with ASD, not VSD.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: A small ventricular septal defect (VSD) typically presents with a pansystolic murmur, which is caused by the flow of blood from the left ventricle to the right ventricle through the defect throughout the systole. The murmur is best heard at the left sternal border due to the location of the VSD. Small VSDs are generally considered benign and have a low risk of complications. They often present asymptomatically, as seen in this case scenario. Low risk of infective endocarditis is also associated with small VSDs, as they are less likely to disrupt normal cardiac function or cause turbulent blood flow that predisposes to bacterial adherence and colonization. Fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2) is characteristic of atrial septal defects (ASDs) due to delayed closure of the pulmonary valve, not typically seen in VSDs. Cyanosis on exertion is not typically associated with small VSDs. Cyanosis may occur in larger VSDs with significant left-to-right shunting, leading to increased pulmonary blood flow and potential development of Eisenmenger syndrome over time. Mid-diastolic murmurs at the apex are associated with mitral stenosis, not VSDs.

questions.stem: A mother presents for prenatal care with a complicated medical history as listed in the following choices. Which of the conditions most predisposes her fetus to congenital heart disease?
questions.initialExplanation:
Poorly controlled maternal diabetes during early embryonic heart development increases the risk of congenital cardiac malformations.

---

## Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease
questions.detailedExplanation: Maternal diabetes mellitus during cardiogenesis results in an approximately threefold increased risk of congenital anomalies. This includes cardiac malformations and lumbosacral agenesis. The increased risk is associated with poor maternal glucose control during embryogenesis. In late gestation, poor maternal glucose control predisposes the infant to asymmetric septal hypertrophy which can lead to aortic outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A 15-hour-old neonate appears dusky. He is tachycardic and tachypneic but the lung fields are clear to auscultation and he has no murmur. His oxygen saturation is 82% and does not improve with administration of 90% oxygen via oxyhood. A chest radiograph shows slightly increased pulmonary vascularity and a narrow mediastinum. Initial management of this infant’s condition should include which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Perform electrocardiogram and increase the administered oxygen concentration to 100%

options.label: B
options.text: Perform echocardiogram and begin prostaglandin E1 infusion

options.label: C
options.text: Administer furosemide and repeat the chest radiograph

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a karyotype and begin dopamine infusion

options.label: E
options.text: Perform electrocardiogram and administer packed red blood cells

questions.initialExplanation:
A duct-dependent lesion can deteriorate when the ductus arteriosus closes. Prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open while echocardiography and definitive management are arranged.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: This presentation is suggestive of a duct-dependent congenital heart lesion, where the ductus arteriosus plays a critical role in maintaining systemic perfusion. PGE1 maintains ductal patency, allowing blood to flow from the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta. It is crucial to prevent ductal closure until definitive management (e.g., surgery or catheter-based intervention) can be performed. PGE1 infusion should be initiated promptly to improve oxygenation and stabilize the neonate.

questions.stem: A newborn infant presents with cyanosis and mild tachypnea at about 6 hours of life. The infant is placed in 95% oxyhood and saturations normalize. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this infant?
questions.initialExplanation:
Cyanosis that improves with high-concentration oxygen, especially with tachypnea, is more consistent with respiratory or lung disease than a fixed cyanotic cardiac lesion.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Cyanosis in the newborn can be due to many causes, but by far the most common cause is respiratory disease. If cyanosis is present without respiratory symptoms, such as tachypnea, one must classically consider congenital heart disease or the less commonly identified methemoglobinemia. Cyanosis typically will not normalize in the case of congenital heart disease or methemoglobinemia. Central nervous system disease could also cause cyanosis, but this is typically due to hypoventilation.

questions.stem: A full-term newborn male is born via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Shortly after birth, the attending pediatrician notices that the infant has central cyanosis. The infant is breathing rapidly, with a respiratory rate of 80 breaths per minute, and has a heart rate of 160 beats per minute. Cyanosis in the first few days of life is likely related to one of the following:
questions.initialExplanation:
Transposition of the great arteries creates parallel circulations, so oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood do not mix adequately. Severe central cyanosis therefore appears soon after birth unless there is mixing through another connection.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Cyanosis in the first few days of life is a classic presentation of transposition of the great vessels (TGV). In TGV, the aorta arises from the right ventricle, while the pulmonary arteries arise from the left ventricle, leading to parallel circulations. As a result, oxygenated blood from the lungs returns to the lungs via the pulmonary artery instead of being pumped to the systemic circulation, resulting in central cyanosis. Signs of CHF in the first hours to weeks in young infants with TGV are seen if significant interatrial communication is present, and a single loud second heart sound (S2) is characteristic for TGV due to the presence of two separate semilunar valves producing two distinct sounds. The "egg on a string" appearance on chest X-ray results from the narrow mediastinum caused by the abnormal positioning of the great vessels.

questions.stem: A term newborn in the nursery is noted to be tachypneic. Pregnancy, labor, and vaginal delivery were unremarkable. Vital signs are pulse 180 beats/min, respirations 60 breaths/min, right arm blood pressure 72/30 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air. There is a somewhat dusky appearance of the lips and tongue, along with a bluish coloration of the hands and feet. Auscultation reveals tachycardia with a regular rhythm. S1 is normal, and S2 is prominent and single. Brachial and femoral pulses are normal. The abdomen is soft. The liver is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen is not palpable. The infant is given 100% FiO2 by nasal cannula for 15 minutes. Vital signs, including oxygen saturation, remain unchanged. A chest radiograph shows an enlarged cardiothymic silhouette with a slender anterior mediastinum and hyperemic lung fields. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.text: Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)

questions.initialExplanation:
Central cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen, a single loud S2, increased pulmonary vascularity, and an egg-on-a-string chest film suggest D-TGA.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: D-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA). The patient in the case has D-TGA. This newborn has central cyanosis with signs of congestive heart failure (CHF). The bluish color of the hands and feet, or acrocyanosis, is not abnormal and can be found in most newborns. However, a blue or dusky coloration of the lips, gingiva, or tongue may be due to central cyanosis and is indicative of hypoxia. Signs of CHF in the infant include tachycardia, tachypnea, cardiomegaly, and hepatomegaly. It is not unusual to feel the liver edge in newborns, but 4 cm below the costal margin is excessive. This infant also failed to respond to supplemental oxygen given by nasal cannula. The findings with auscultation are due to the abnormal positioning of the semilunar valves in D-TGA. The chest radiograph shows a "egg on side" appearance of the cardiac silhouette on the chest film, demonstrating an egg on a string. The mediastinum is narrowed due to the abnormal position of the great vessels. The lung fields are hyperemic, with increased pulmonary vascular markings due to excessive pulmonary blood flow into the main pulmonary artery from the left ventricle.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is admitted to the hospital. His parents report that he was fussy and difficult to console earlier in the day. In the emergency department, he is irritable and crying after his blood is drawn. While crying, he becomes blue and efforts to calm him are unsuccessful. As he continues crying, he becomes progressively more cyanotic. Which of the following, which of these interventions is the best choice for treating acute hypoxic spells associated with TOF?

options.label: E
options.text: Bringing the knees to the chest

questions.initialExplanation:
Knee-to-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting during a Tet spell. Oxygen and sedation may also be used, but the posture is the key immediate maneuver.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Bringing the knees to the chest. Hypoxic spells (also known as "tet spells") are the result of a cycle that involves crying and hyperpnea that increases systemic venous return. Due to the fixed obstruction or spasms of the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT), increased systemic venous return increases the amount of deoxygenated blood that shunts right-to-left through the ventricular septal defect and makes the infant more cyanotic and hypoxic. Hypoxia and acidosis cause hyperpnea, creating the cycle. Treatments are directed at breaking the cycle. (E) The best choice is to place the infant in the knee-chest position. This will increase the systemic vascular resistance and promote blood flow into the pulmonary circulation. Supplemental oxygen is often given; however, it has a limited role because the main problem is decreased pulmonary blood flow, not oxygenation. (A) Similarly, inhaled nitric oxide will not reverse the fixed obstruction at the RVOT and is less useful. (B) Enalaprilat is an intravenous angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor that causes vasodilation by inhibiting conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Systemic vasodilation is counterproductive during a hypoxic spell, as it would lower systemic vascular resistance and further increase the right-to-left shunt, worsening the hypoxia. (C) Furosemide is a loop diuretic commonly used in the treatment of congestive heart failure. In contrast to diuresis, volume expansion is sometimes helpful during a hypoxic spell by increasing preload. (D) Urgent surgery is required when all medical efforts have failed. Additional medical treatments for patients with a tet spell include subcutaneous or intramuscular morphine sulfate (for respiratory suppression and sedation), sodium bicarbonate (as acidosis stimulates the respiratory center), ketamine (for respiratory suppression and sedation), intravenous propranolol (for negative chronotropic), and phenylephrine (to increase systemic vascular resistance and promote pulmonary blood flow).

questions.stem: In the pediatric cardiology ward, a previously diagnosed 2-year-old child with Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) experienced a sudden hypercyanotic spell. The child’s parents, familiar with the underlying condition, brought the distressed child to the emergency department. Clinical assessment revealed profound cyanosis, and the child became increasingly agitated. Depending on the frequency and severity of hypercyanotic attacks in tetralogy of Fallot, all the following procedures are true EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: Placement of the infant in the knee-chest position

options.label: D
options.text: Rapid correction with intravenous sodium bicarbonate irrespective of the spell severity

questions.initialExplanation:
Sodium bicarbonate is not given automatically for every Tet spell. It is reserved for severe spells with significant metabolic acidosis or inadequate response to initial measures.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Because metabolic acidosis develops when arterial PO2 is <40 mmHg. Rapid correction (within several minutes) with intravenous administration of sodium bicarbonate is necessary if the spell is unusually severe and the child shows a lack of response to the foregoing therapy.

questions.stem: A newborn exhibits cyanosis without respiratory distress. Which congenital heart disease is NOT associated with this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation:
Aortic stenosis usually causes left-sided pressure overload and may cause heart failure. The listed cyanotic lesions reduce pulmonary blood flow and can present with cyanosis without prominent respiratory distress.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In aortic stenosis, there is an obstruction of blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta. This typically leads to increased left ventricular pressure, and the newborn would present with signs of left heart failure, such as respiratory distress, rather than isolated cyanosis. On the other hand, conditions like Tetralogy of Fallot (Option E), Tricuspid Atresia (Option A), Ebstein Anomaly (Option C), and Pulmonary Atresia (Option D) can cause decreased pulmonary blood flow, leading to cyanosis without significant respiratory distress. Therefore, Aortic Stenosis does not fit the pattern described in the question.

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a distressed 18-month-old child was rushed in by anxious parents due to sudden-onset severe cyanosis. The child, known to have a diagnosis of Tetralogy of Fallot, was experiencing a hypercyanotic spell. The medical team quickly initiated measures to alleviate the cyanosis, including placing the child in a knee-chest position to enhance venous return and administering supplemental oxygen. Paroxysmal hypercyanotic attacks (hypoxic, "blue," or "tet" spells) are a particular problem during the 1st or 2nd year of life. They are characterized by

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in intensity of the systolic murmur

options.label: E
options.text: More frequent spells in patients with marked cyanosis at rest

questions.initialExplanation:
Tet spells can occur suddenly and unpredictably, often after crying or waking. They result from worsening right-to-left shunting and reduced pulmonary blood flow.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The spells occur most frequently in the morning on initially awakening or after episodes of vigorous crying. Temporary disappearance of a decrease in intensity of the systolic murmur is usual as flow across the right ventricular outflow tract diminishes. The onset is usually unpredictable. Spells are associated with reduction in afterload and increased pulmonary blood flow, which, when developed, results in severe systemic hypoxia and metabolic acidosis. Infants who are only mildly cyanotic at rest are often more prone to development of hypoxic spells because they have not acquired the homeostatic mechanisms to tolerate rapid lowering of arterial oxygen saturation, such as polycythemia.

questions.stem: A previously normal newborn infant in a community hospital nursery is noted to be cyanotic at 14 hours of life. She is placed on a face mask with oxygen flowing at 10 L/min. She remains cyanotic, and her pulse oximetry reading does not change. An arterial blood gas shows her PaO2 to be 23 mm Hg. Bilateral breath sounds are present, and she has no murmur. She is breathing deeply and quickly, but she is not retracting. While you are waiting for the transport team from the nearby children’s hospital, you should initiate which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation:
In a cyanotic newborn with suspected duct-dependent pulmonary blood flow, start PGE1 promptly to maintain ductal patency while arranging urgent specialist care.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The vignette describes an infant with a ductal-dependent cyanotic congenital heart lesion. The child had pulmonary atresia without a VSD, another example of a ductal-dependent cyanotic lesion. Without a patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary blood flow may be critically compromised. The ductus arteriosus is kept open by prostaglandin E1 (PGE1), which allows blood flow to continue until definitive management can be performed. PGE1 does not correct the underlying defect, but maintains blood flow and oxygenation while transfer and evaluation are arranged.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old male infant is brought to the pediatric emergency department due to concerns about bluish discoloration noticed around the lips and poor feeding. Upon examination, the infant appears cyanotic, particularly evident in the lips and nail beds. Auscultation reveals a single loud second heart sound (S2) with no audible murmurs appreciated. A chest X-ray is performed, which shows a characteristic "egg on side" appearance. Egg on side appearance is seen in which of the following conditions:
questions.initialExplanation:
The classic egg-on-a-string or egg-on-side chest radiograph is associated with transposition of the great arteries because the great vessels are abnormally positioned.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The "egg on side" appearance of chest X-ray refers to the abnormal cardiac silhouette seen in TGA. It appears as an egg-shaped heart with a narrow superior mediastinum due to the abnormal positioning of the great vessels. Ebstein anomaly is characterized by downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, resulting in atrialization of the right ventricle. Fallot tetralogy is characterized by pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Chest X-ray findings may show a boot-shaped heart due to right ventricular hypertrophy. Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a complex congenital heart defect characterized by underdevelopment of the left side of the heart. It does not typically present with the egg on side appearance on chest X-ray. Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing of the aorta, which may result in differential blood pressure between the upper and lower extremities.

questions.stem: A 4-day-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of poorly feeding and fussiness. She is afebrile, tachycardic, tachypneic, and cyanotic. Examination reveals a normal S1 and a single loud S2 with no murmur. A plain radiograph of the chest shows well-expanded lungs, increased pulmonary vascular markings, and a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette with a narrow mediastinum. The infant is intubated and supplemental oxygen is given, but fails to improve oxygen saturations. Of the following, what is the next best step in management of this patient?
questions.initialExplanation:
When a newborn has cyanosis that does not respond to oxygen and a duct-dependent lesion is suspected, PGE1 should be started immediately; do not delay for imaging.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1). The age at presentation, cyanosis, and inability of supplemental oxygen to improve oxygenation are indicative of a ductal-dependent congenital heart defect. The presence of a single S2 and the description of the chest radiograph are suggestive of D-transposition of the great arteries. The most important step is to reopen the ductus arteriosus with intravenous PGE1. (A) While echocardiography is integral in the ongoing management and surgical planning, treatment with PGE1 will be lifesaving and should not be delayed. (D) In infants with a restrictive foramen ovale, severe hypoxemia and elevated left atrial pressure may require balloon atrial septostomy. (B, C) Adenosine and cardioversion will not reestablish mixing between the desaturated blood recirculating through the pulmonary circulation and the saturated blood recirculating through the systemic circulation.

questions.stem: 3-day-old infant with a single second heart sound has had progressively deepening cyanosis since birth but no respiratory distress. Chest radiography demonstrates no cardiomegaly and normal pulmonary vasculature. An ECG shows an axis of 120° and right ventricular prominence. Which of the following congenital cardiac malformations is most likely responsible for the cyanosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

options.label: E
options.text: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return below the diaphragm

questions.initialExplanation:
Early cyanosis, a single S2, and an egg-on-a-string/normal-sized cardiac silhouette favor transposition of the great arteries.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Transposition of the great vessels with an intact ventricular septum presents with early cyanosis, a normal-sized heart (classic "egg on a string" radiographic pattern), and often slightly increased pulmonary vascular markings. An ECG showing right-axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy is characteristic. In tetralogy of Fallot, cyanosis is often not seen in the first few days of life. Tricuspid atresia, a cause of early cyanosis, causes diminished pulmonary arterial blood flow; the pulmonary fields on X-ray demonstrate a diminution of pulmonary vascularity. Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum and total anomalous pulmonary venous return are also in the differential, but the combination of early cyanosis, single S2, and normal-sized heart supports TGA.

questions.stem: A newborn is observed to have difficulty breathing, with cyanosis. Further evaluation reveals a heart defect. What is the MOST common cyanotic cardiac lesion in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: Dextroposed transposition of the great arteries

questions.initialExplanation:
The source identifies dextroposed transposition of the great arteries as the most common cyanotic lesion to present in the newborn period.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Although dextroposed transposition of the great arteries represents only about 5% of congenital heart defects, it is the most common cyanotic lesion to present in the newborn period.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with a known diagnosis of unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot becomes severely cyanotic while crying. Which of the following is not indicated for acute management of this situation?

options.label: B
options.text: Placing the child in the knee-chest position

questions.initialExplanation:
Acute Tet spells are treated with oxygen, knee-chest positioning, beta-blockade, and sometimes phenylephrine. Digoxin is not an acute treatment for the spell.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Digoxin is not indicated for acute management during a cyanotic episode. Administering oxygen: providing supplemental oxygen is essential during a cyanotic episode. Placing the child in the knee-chest position: this increases systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting. Propranolol is a beta-blocker that can help manage hypercyanotic episodes. It reduces the severity of spells by decreasing heart rate and contractility, thus reducing the right-to-left shunt. Administration of phenylephrine: phenylephrine is a vasoconstrictor that increases systemic vascular resistance.

questions.stem: You are seeing a 2-year-old boy for the first time. His father denies any past medical or surgical history, but does note that the child’s day care recently sent a note home asking about several episodes, usually after the child does not get what he wants, when he “breathes funny” and sits in a corner with his knees under his chin for a few minutes. The day-care staffers think this “self-imposed time-out” is a good thing, but they worry about the breathing. On examination, you identify a right ventricular impulse, a systolic thrill along the left sternal border, and a harsh systolic murmur (loudest at the left sternal border but radiating through the lung fields). Which of the following congenital cardiac lesions would you expect to find in this child?
questions.initialExplanation:
The knee-chest posture and episodic breathing/cyanosis are characteristic of Tet spells in tetralogy of Fallot, which includes right ventricular outflow obstruction.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: This child has tetralogy of Fallot, which consists of right ventricular outflow obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), VSD, dextroposition of the aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Children with tetralogy of Fallot may have cyanotic episodes ("Tet spells") associated with acute reduction in pulmonary blood flow. Typically, these spells are self-limited, lasting no more than 30 minutes. Assuming the knee-chest position is thought to increase peripheral resistance, decreasing the amount of right-to-left shunting and thus increasing pulmonary blood flow. Alternative therapies include morphine sulfate and propranolol. Prolonged hypoxia can lead to acidosis; correction may require infusion of sodium bicarbonate. Patent ductus arteriosus is likely to present in this age child with a constant machine-like murmur and, if the flow is big enough, with evidence of progressive congestive heart failure. An ASD will have a fixed split-second heart sound and a pulmonic stenosis murmur; it can also present with progressive evidence of heart failure if the atrial septal defect is large enough. Transposition of the great vessels with a patent foramen ovale and hypoplastic left heart syndrome are neonatal conditions; presentations are in the newborn period.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old male child is brought to the pediatrician’s office by his parents due to concerns about his bluish discoloration of the lips and fingertips, particularly during episodes of crying or exertion. The parents report that the child has had these episodes since birth, but they have become more noticeable recently. The child has a history of poor weight gain and frequent episodes of squatting during play. On examination, the child appears cyanotic, with oxygen saturation measured at 85% by pulse oximetry. Children with fallot tetralogy, one of the following is FALSE:

options.label: A
options.text: Cyanosis presents few weeks after birth

options.label: B
options.text: Heart failure is a common complication

options.label: C
options.text: Auscultation reveals a systolic ejection murmur in the pulmonary area

options.label: E
options.text: Functional anemia may be present in spite of a normal hemoglobin concentration

questions.initialExplanation:
Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanosis and hypercyanotic spells. Squatting reduces right-to-left shunting. Heart failure is not a common complication in typical childhood TOF.

---

## Arrhythmias and Tachycardia
questions.detailedExplanation: This statement is false because heart failure is not a common complication of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) in children. TOF is characterized by four main features: pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect (VSD), overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Cyanosis typically presents in the first few months of life, often within the first few weeks after birth, due to the degree of pulmonary stenosis and right-to-left shunting of blood. Auscultation in TOF typically reveals a systolic ejection murmur in the pulmonary area due to the stenosis of the pulmonary valve. Squatting is a classic maneuver observed in children with TOF. Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, which reduces the degree of right-to-left shunting and improves oxygenation, resulting in temporary relief of cyanosis. Functional anemia may be present in children with TOF despite having a normal hemoglobin concentration. Chronic hypoxemia can lead to increased erythropoiesis as a compensatory mechanism, resulting in a relative polycythemia. However, the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood may still be inadequate, leading to functional anemia.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought to your office for pallor and listlessness. Your physical examination reveals tachycardia that is constant and does not vary with crying. He has no hepatomegaly and the lungs are clear. His ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this patient?
questions.initialExplanation:
In a stable infant with SVT, first try a vagal maneuver such as carotid massage or facial immersion in cold water. Adenosine is used if vagal maneuvers fail; unstable patients need synchronized cardioversion.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Supraventricular tachycardia, as shown on the ECG, is characterized by rapid heart rate (in this case about 250 beats per minute), little rate variability, and a consistent P wave for each QRS complex. Prolonged SVT can lead to heart failure with hepatomegaly and respiratory compromise. Fetal SVT can lead to hydrops fetalis. The first-line treatment is to stimulate the vagus nerve using techniques such as carotid massage, immersion of the face in cold water, or voluntary straining. Rapid infusion of IV adenosine can affect resolution if the maneuvers are not successful. Verapamil is contraindicated in this age group, as it may cause acute hypotension and cardiac arrest. Synchronized DC cardioversion may be performed in patients in shock or with heart failure; it must, however, be synchronized to the QRS complex. Transthoracic pacing is typically useful in bradyarrhythmias. A precordial thump might help individuals with an acute arrest from ventricular fibrillation, but does not resolve SVT.

questions.stem: You are called to the nursery to evaluate a newborn. The mother has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus and gestational diabetes. The nurses are concerned because the baby has developed petechiae and bruising after his birth. Vital signs have been stable, with a heart rate in the 60 beats per minute range and a respiratory rate in the 40 breaths per minute range. You note a large liver, scattered petechiae, and an erythematous rash on the cheeks and on the bridge of the nose. Choose the most likely diagnosis based on the patient’s presentation:
questions.initialExplanation:
Maternal lupus antibodies can cross the placenta and damage the fetal conduction system, causing congenital heart block and marked neonatal bradycardia.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Neonatal lupus is a rare manifestation of transferred maternal IgG autoantibodies. Infants can have thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, rash, liver dysfunction, and a congenital heart block. Most manifestations are self-resolved; however, the congenital heart block is permanent and frequently requires pacing.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric emergency department by his parents due to episodes of sudden, rapid heartbeat associated with palpitations. The child has experienced intermittent episodes lasting for a few minutes, often triggered by excitement or stress. On examination, the pediatrician notes an irregular heart rate exceeding 180 beats per minute. The following procedures may abort an attack of SVT EXCEPT?

options.label: A
options.text: Placing of the face in ice water

questions.initialExplanation:
Vagal maneuvers can sometimes terminate SVT, but ocular pressure is unsafe and should not be performed.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Ocular pressure must never be performed, and carotid sinus massage is very rarely effective.

questions.stem: 14-year-old adolescent with a known history of Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome presented to the pediatric emergency department with acute-onset palpitations, chest pain, and profound dyspnea. The electrocardiogram confirmed a regular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Despite initial attempts at vagal maneuvers and administration of intravenous adenosine, the SVT persisted. The patient rapidly developed symptoms of severe heart failure, including respiratory distress and hypotension. In urgent situations of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) when symptoms of severe heart failure have already occurred. Of the following, the initial management is?
questions.initialExplanation:
Persistent SVT with hypotension or severe heart failure is unstable and requires synchronized electrical cardioversion.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: DC cardioversion (0.5-2 J/kg). In urgent situations when symptoms of severe heart failure have already occurred, synchronized DC cardioversion (0.5-2 J/kg) is recommended as the initial management.

questions.stem: A newborn infant has mild cyanosis, diaphoresis, poor peripheral pulses, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly. Respiratory rate is 60 breaths per minute, and heart rate is 250 beats per minute. The child most likely has congestive heart failure caused by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Large ASD and valvular pulmonic stenosis

options.label: B
options.text: VSD and transposition of the great vessels

questions.initialExplanation:
A heart rate around 250 beats/min in a newborn strongly suggests a tachyarrhythmia such as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, which can cause heart failure.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Congestive heart failure from any cause can result in mild cyanosis, even in the absence of a right-to-left shunt, and in poor peripheral pulses when cardiac output is low. Congestive heart failure from many causes can be associated with a rapid pulse rate (up to 200 beats per minute). A pulse rate near 250 beats per minute in a newborn would suggest the presence of a tachyarrhythmia. Common causes for supraventricular tachycardia include Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, congenital heart disease, and symptomatic drug use. In this patient, evaluation for WPW syndrome and cardiac abnormalities must be performed to determine the cause of the tachyarrhythmia. Once the arrhythmia is controlled, the heart failure can be treated.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child with a history of symptomatic ventricular tachycardia was prescribed propranolol for rhythm control. After several weeks of treatment, the child’s parents reported some symptoms. The pediatric cardiologist recognized these symptoms as potential side effects of propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker. The medication was tapered off, and the child’s symptoms gradually improved. Side effects of propranolol may include which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation:
Propranolol can cause fatigue or reduced exercise tolerance and may affect concentration or school performance. Hypothyroidism, liver toxicity, and pulmonary fibrosis are classically associated with amiodarone, not propranolol.

---

## Heart Failure
questions.detailedExplanation: The source indicates that the other options are side effects of amiodarone.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old male child was brought to the pediatric emergency department by his parents due to complaints of difficulty in feeding for the past week. On examination, the child appears pale and lethargic. He has tachypnea with a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute. The child was diagnosed with heart failure after further evaluation. All of the following are identified causes of heart failure in childhood EXCEPT:
questions.initialExplanation:
Nephrotic syndrome primarily causes protein loss and edema; it is not usually a direct cause of childhood heart failure, unlike anemia, myocarditis, glomerulonephritis, or valve damage.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Some identified causes of heart failure in childhood include: (1) Sickle cell anemia: Children with sickle cell disease can develop cardiomyopathy due to chronic anemia, hypoxia, and increased cardiac output, leading to heart failure. (2) Kawasaki disease: Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness that can lead to coronary artery aneurysms and myocarditis, resulting in heart failure in severe cases. (3) Glomerulonephritis: Acute glomerulonephritis, particularly in the context of post-streptococcal infection, can lead to fluid overload and hypertension, contributing to heart failure. (4) Infective endocarditis: Infective endocarditis can cause valvular damage and heart failure, especially if the infection involves the mitral or aortic valve. Nephrotic syndrome, characterized by proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia, typically does not directly lead to heart failure. However, severe fluid overload and hypertension associated with nephrotic syndrome may contribute to cardiovascular complications over time.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatric clinic by her parents due to concerns of heart failure. One of the following is FALSE regarding cardiac failure during the neonatal period:

options.label: E
options.text: Raised pulse rate and respiratory rate

questions.initialExplanation:
Infants with heart failure often feed poorly, breathe rapidly, and fail to gain weight. Peripheral edema is not a typical neonatal finding.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: This statement is false because peripheral edema is not typically seen in neonates with cardiac failure. Neonatal cardiac failure often presents with symptoms such as failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, episodes of apnea or respiratory distress, and tachycardia/tachypnea.

questions.stem: An infant previously diagnosed with a large muscular VSD comes to the office with complaints from the mother of fatigue and poor feeding over the past month. You note the child has not gained weight since the previous visit 2 months ago. The child is apathetic, tachypneic, and has wheezes and crackles on lung auscultation. Choose the most likely diagnosis based on the patient’s presentation:
questions.initialExplanation:
A large VSD can cause pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure, presenting with poor feeding, poor weight gain, tachypnea, and crackles or wheezes.

---

## Cardiomyopathy and Myocarditis
questions.detailedExplanation: Congestive heart failure can result from a number of causes, including congenital heart disease, Kawasaki disease, metabolic cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias, and viral myocarditis. The case presented is typical of an infant with heart failure. Such infants are weak, diaphoretic, have poor weight gain, and may be tachypneic with retractions. Lung findings can include crackles, wheezes, or both. Prompt evaluation by a pediatric cardiologist is imperative.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old full-term girl is brought to the pediatrician by her parents with a 2-day history of poor feeding and fevers to 38.6°C. She has had an uncomplicated pregnancy and routine pediatric care. Newborn metabolic screening was normal. She is not febrile in the office and minimally reactive during the examination. Her heart rate is 180 beats/min and respiratory rate is 68 breaths/min. She has distant heart sounds, but no murmur. Her breath sounds are clear with shallow respirations and subcostal and intercostal retractions. Peripheral pulses are diminished, and the capillary refill time is 5 seconds. The infant is stabilized after intubation and mechanical ventilation. Echocardiography demonstrates a structurally normal heart with normal coronary arteries and severely depressed function of both ventricles. Of the following, what is the most common causative agent for this infant’s condition?
questions.initialExplanation:
Coxsackievirus B is a common viral cause of myocarditis in infants. Severe ventricular dysfunction with a structurally normal heart and poor perfusion supports myocarditis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Coxsackievirus B. The infant described in the vignette is quite ill with signs of impending respiratory failure and shock. While fever and dehydration from poor feeding may cause tachycardia, the infant is afebrile in the office. Her tachycardia is out of proportion to her temperature. This along with prolonged capillary refill time, diminished pulses, and lethargy are signs of poor or insufficient cardiac output. Poor ventricular function in the absence of congenital heart disease or anomalous coronary arteries may be evidence of myocarditis. Viral myocarditis is more common than other infectious causes. (C, D) Adenovirus and coxsackievirus B are more common than rubella or Epstein-Barr virus. (A) The early form of neonatal listeriosis presents in the first few days of life with septicemia. The late-onset form occurs after the first week of life, typically as a form of meningitis. Beyond the neonatal period, listeriosis is rare in the absence of immunosuppression or malignancy. Again, central nervous system involvement is the typical presentation. (B) Bacterial myocarditis is less common than viral myocarditis, and a-hemolytic Streptococcus such as S. viridans is the most common cause of endocarditis, not myocarditis.

questions.stem: An ill-appearing 2-week-old baby girl is brought to the emergency room. She is pale and dyspneic with a respiratory rate of 80 breaths per minute. Heart rate is 195 beats per minute, heart sounds are distant, a gallop is heard, and she has cardiomegaly on X-ray. An echocardiogram demonstrates poor ventricular function, dilated ventricles, and dilation of the left atrium. An ECG shows ventricular depolarization complexes that have low voltage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on this clinical picture?

options.label: D
options.text: Aberrant left coronary artery arising from pulmonary artery

options.label: E
options.text: Glycogen storage disease of the heart

questions.initialExplanation:
An infant with acute heart failure, dilated chambers, poor ventricular function, and low-voltage ECG complexes is most consistent with myocarditis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The findings of pallor, dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, and cardiomegaly are common in congestive heart failure regardless of the cause. The most common causes of myocarditis include adenovirus and coxsackievirus B, although many other viruses can cause this condition. The constellation of findings in the question point to myocarditis as the etiology of this patient’s condition. The echocardiogram in the question shows ventricular and left atrial dilatation as well as poor ventricular function. With glycogen storage disease of the heart muscle, thickening would be expected, and pericardial effusion would be seen with pericarditis. The ECG findings in this case are not consistent with aberrant origin of the left coronary artery, although the origin of the coronary arteries can be difficult to visualize. On ECG, the voltages of the ventricular complexes seen with aberrant origin of the left coronary artery are not diminished, and a pattern of myocardial infarction can be seen. Voltages from the left ventricle are usually high in endocardial fibroelastosis, and both right and left ventricular forces are high in glycogen storage disease of the heart.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old adolescent male presents to the office for a sports physical. In his screening questionnaire, he notes that he occasionally gets short of breath and dizzy during exercise, with occasional chest pain. He lost consciousness once last summer during football practice, but attributed it to the heat. His grandfather died suddenly at the age of 35 of unknown etiology, but otherwise the family is healthy. Choose the most likely diagnosis based on the patient’s presentation:
questions.initialExplanation:
Exertional chest pain, dizziness or syncope, and a family history of sudden death are warning signs for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in an adolescent athlete.

---

## Heart Murmurs and Examination
questions.detailedExplanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), also called idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis, is often inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion with variable penetrance. Many children are completely asymptomatic, while others may have complaints of weakness, fatigue, chest pain, and syncope. A midsystolic ejection murmur and a left ventricular lift sometimes can be appreciated on physical examination. The diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography. HCM can be a cause of arrhythmia and death in young athletes.

questions.stem: One of the following leads you to consider a murmur to be innocent in a 4.5-year-old child:

options.label: C
options.text: Marked variation of loudness with change in posture

options.label: E
options.text: Association with fixed splitting of the second heart sound

questions.initialExplanation:
An innocent murmur is usually soft, systolic, short, and changes with posture. A thrill, wide radiation, or abnormal associated findings suggest structural disease.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Innocent murmurs are common in children and are often referred to as functional or harmless murmurs. They result from normal blood flow patterns and do not indicate structural heart abnormalities. Innocent murmurs are typically benign and do not require specific treatment or follow-up. Characteristics of innocent murmurs: systolic timing (innocent murmurs are usually systolic, occurring during ventricular contraction); soft sound (typically no more than grade I or II); short duration (brief and do not persist throughout the entire cardiac cycle); musical or low pitch; variation with posture (inconspicuous murmurs may become louder or softer with changes in the child’s position, e.g., supine vs. sitting); limited radiation (innocent murmurs are usually localized to specific areas on the chest and do not radiate widely); no associated thrill; and no other abnormal findings. Innocent murmurs occur in otherwise healthy children without concerning symptoms or abnormal physical examination findings.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old presents for a well-child evaluation. He has no significant past medical or surgical history, and neither he nor his parents have any complaints. He is afebrile with a heart rate of 100 beats/min and respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min. He remains at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Upon auscultation, he has a 2/6 nonradiating, crescendo-decrescendo, midsystolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border. The murmur does not change with a Valsalva maneuver, but increases in intensity when the patient is supine. Records indicate that he had no murmur at any previous evaluation. The remainder of his examination is unremarkable. Of the following, which best explains this child’s cardiac findings?
questions.initialExplanation:
Still murmur is a common innocent systolic murmur in children aged about 3-7 years. It is vibratory, nonradiating, and changes with position.

---

## Cardiac Tumors
questions.detailedExplanation: Still murmur. The murmur described in the vignette is consistent with a Still murmur. Still vibratory murmur is an innocent murmur most commonly heard in toddlers and young school-aged children, typically between 3 and 7 years of age. Its intensity often changes with respiration and position, and there is often no radiation of the murmur. (A) A venous hum is also a common innocent murmur of childhood caused by turbulent flow in the jugular veins. However, venous hum is a low-pitched, continuous murmur and best heard at the lower portion of the neck or in the infraclavicular region. (C) The murmur of peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis is also known as a pulmonary flow murmur of infancy. It is an innocent systolic ejection murmur often heard at the left upper sternal border that radiates to the axillae and back. It is typically noted during the newborn period, more common in preterm infants, and should disappear by 6 months of age. (D) Children with mild forms of aortic stenosis may be asymptomatic and have normal development. Examination findings of mild aortic stenosis include an early systolic ejection click that is often absent in severe obstruction. Severe obstruction generates a more intense and longer murmur, heard at the right upper sternal border and radiating to the neck. (E) Children with significant mitral regurgitation often exhibit symptoms of congestive heart failure such as tachypnea, tachycardia, failure to thrive, and exercise intolerance far earlier than adults with the same degree of regurgitation. The murmur of mitral regurgitation varies with severity and is often described as a harsh holosystolic murmur at the apex that radiates to the axillae and back.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant was brought to the pediatric cardiology clinic for evaluation due to an incidental finding of a heart murmur during a routine check-up. Echocardiography revealed the presence of benign tumor. The vast majority of tumors originating from the heart are benign. Of the following, the MOST common pediatric cardiac tumors are?
questions.initialExplanation:
Rhabdomyoma is the most common cardiac tumor in children and has a strong association with tuberous sclerosis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Rhabdomyomas are the most common pediatric cardiac tumors and are associated with tuberous sclerosis in 70-95% of cases.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents to the emergency unit with seizure, high-grade fever, and bloody diarrhea. What is the FIRST line antibiotic therapy for this child?
questions.initialExplanation:
Seizures, high fever, and bloody diarrhea suggest severe invasive bacterial gastroenteritis. The source identifies ciprofloxacin as the first-line choice in this severe presentation, while noting its pediatric safety caution.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In the case of a child presenting with seizures and bloody diarrhea, a bacterial cause such as Shigella or Salmonella may be suspected. Ciprofloxacin is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that can cover these pathogens and is often used as first-line therapy for severe cases. It is important to note that the use of ciprofloxacin in children is generally advised against unless the benefits outweigh the risks due to the potential for adverse effects on cartilage and bone growth.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl was recently discharged from the hospital after a 1-week stay for bacterial pneumonia. She received antibiotic therapy with a third-generation cephalosporin for a total of 10 days. For the past 2 days, she has been experiencing profuse, foul-smelling diarrhea. Today her mother reports she has been to the bathroom 10 times and noted streaks of blood in the stool. Of the following options, which is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?
questions.initialExplanation:
