Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics followed by frequent foul-smelling diarrhea suggest C. difficile colitis. The source recommends oral metronidazole as initial treatment and reserves oral vancomycin for selected cases.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Oral metronidazole. Given the history and clinical presentation, Clostridium difficile infection is the most likely cause of this patient’s diarrhea. Although classically considered a hospital-acquired infection, there are now increasing numbers of patients experiencing community-acquired infection as well. Antibiotic treatment within the last 6 months places a patient at increased risk for developing C. difficile colitis. First-line treatment is oral metronidazole for 10 to 14 days. (B) Oral vancomycin should be reserved for those who fail or cannot tolerate metronidazole or have recurrent disease. (E) The preferred treatment route is oral, and intravenous treatment should be reserved only for those who are unable to tolerate enteral medication. (A, C) Ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin are not appropriate choices to treat a C. difficile infection.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with a 3-day history of watery diarrhea. The mother reports that the infant was recently diagnosed with rotavirus infection. The infant is alert, has a moist mouth, is teary, and is producing wet diapers regularly. The pediatrician discusses the role of oral rehydration solution (ORS) with the mother. In which of the following scenarios would oral rehydration solution (ORS) or food-based oral rehydration therapy NOT be suitable?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintenance therapy for an infant with Rotavirus diarrhea

options.label: B
options.text: Rehydration of a child with cholera and moderate dehydration

options.label: C
options.text: Maintenance therapy of an exclusively breastfed infant with diarrhea

options.label: D
options.text: Non-dehydrated infant with frequent loose bowel motions

options.label: E
options.text: Rehydration of a child with diarrhea and paralytic ileus

questions.initialExplanation:
ORS works when the intestine can absorb fluid. Paralytic ileus prevents normal intestinal movement and absorption, so intravenous fluids are required.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: ORS is effective for rehydration and maintenance therapy in a variety of diarrheal illnesses, including rotavirus and cholera, as long as the gut is functional. In the case of paralytic ileus, where the intestinal motility is impaired, oral rehydration therapy is not effective because the intestine cannot adequately absorb the fluids and electrolytes. In such cases, intravenous therapy is typically required.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl presents to the clinic with a 48-hour history of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. She reports no recent travel or antibiotic use. On physical examination, her vital signs are within normal limits, but she appears to be in moderate distress due to abdominal cramping. Which of the following organisms is NOT a cause of bloody diarrhea?
questions.initialExplanation:
EPEC usually causes non-bloody diarrhea. The other listed organisms can cause bloody or dysenteric diarrhea.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) is typically associated with non-bloody diarrhea and is a common cause of diarrhea in children, especially in developing countries. It does not usually cause bloody diarrhea as the other pathogens listed, which are well-known causes of dysentery or bloody diarrhea. E. histolytica is known to cause amoebic dysentery, which is bloody diarrhea with mucous and abdominal pain. Campylobacter jejuni is one of the most common bacterial causes of gastroenteritis and can lead to bloody diarrhea. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), particularly the O157:H7 strain, is notorious for causing bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. Shigella species are a common cause of bacillary dysentery, characterized by bloody and mucoid stools.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is referred to the gastrointestinal (GI) clinic for complaints of chronic diarrhea. She has four to five loose stools each day, which occasionally contain pieces of undigested food. There is no blood or mucus in the stool. She is growing well and denies abdominal pain, nausea, or other complaints. Her diet consists of a variety of table foods. Her mother reports that the girl does not like milk and drinks mostly apple juice instead. Her pediatrician has sent two sets of stool cultures for bacteria, viruses, and parasites, which have yielded negative results. Of the following, which is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Schedule a colonoscopy and endoscopy to look for underlying inflammation

options.label: B
options.text: Prescribe a course of antibiotics for empiric treatment of bacterial overgrowth syndrome

options.label: C
options.text: Instruct the mother to limit fruit juice to 4 oz or less per day

options.label: D
options.text: Order testing for Clostridium difficile infection

options.label: E
options.text: [The option is cut off in the screenshot; the explanation’s labelled (E) rationale states: “Normal stooling patterns can vary greatly from one child to the next, with stooling every other day to two to three times per day as normal.”]

questions.initialExplanation:
Toddler’s diarrhea is often related to excessive fruit juice intake in a thriving child. Limit juice and increase dietary fat and fiber rather than starting invasive tests or antibiotics.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Instruct the mother to limit fruit juice to 4 oz or less per day. The patient in the vignette has symptoms consistent with toddler’s diarrhea, an osmotic diarrhea caused by excessive intake of fruit juices. The child will have multiple watery stools per day, and the parents often describe that there are chunks of undigested food in the stools. Toddler’s diarrhea occurs in an otherwise healthy child, who is growing and gaining weight normally. There is no blood or inflammatory cells in the stool and this condition can be resolved by changes in the diet. The treatment involves removing fruit juice from the diet and increasing the fat and fiber content. (A) Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy are invasive procedures requiring the child to undergo anesthesia. Although these tests are invaluable in the evaluation of some serious conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and celiac disease, this procedure is not indicated in an otherwise healthy child with isolated diarrhea. (B) Bacterial overgrowth can cause malabsorptive diarrhea. However, the patient in the vignette does not have any risk factors, such as a chronic condition or prematurity. C. difficile is becoming an increasingly important cause of disease in childhood. (D) C. difficile infection typically causes bloody, foul-smelling diarrhea and is often associated with other symptoms such as fever, abdominal pain, and cramping. (E) Normal stooling patterns can vary greatly from one child to the next with stooling every other day to two to three times per day as normal.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for poor growth, dental enamel defects, and a rash suspected to be dermatitis herpetiformis. She has a history of abdominal distension and chronic diarrhea. A diagnosis of celiac disease is being considered. What is the MOST common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease?
questions.initialExplanation:
Celiac disease damages the small-intestinal mucosa and reduces iron absorption. Iron-deficiency anemia is therefore a common extraintestinal manifestation.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease. It can occur due to malabsorption of iron in the small intestine, which is damaged by the immune response to gluten in individuals with celiac disease. This malabsorption can lead to a range of symptoms, including fatigue and pallor, and is more common than other extraintestinal manifestations like short stature, dental enamel defects, aphthous stomatitis, and peripheral neuropathies.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has been experiencing gas, bloating, and watery diarrhea for several months. There is no weight loss, and physical examination is unremarkable except for a distended abdomen with active bowel sounds. His stool pH is acidic. Based on these findings, which test would you MOST likely recommend to investigate the cause of his symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation:
Acidic stool and gas with bloating suggest carbohydrate malabsorption. A hydrogen breath test can help identify carbohydrate malabsorption.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: An acidic stool pH and symptoms of gas, bloating, and diarrhea suggest a condition like carbohydrate malabsorption, which can be assessed with a hydrogen breath test. This test measures the amount of hydrogen in the breath after the patient consumes a sugar solution, which can indicate malabsorption. A sweat test would be used to diagnose conditions such as cystic fibrosis, which does not align with the current presentation, and the other tests listed do not specifically address the concern of carbohydrate malabsorption.

questions.stem: At 1 year of age, a boy was at the 50th percentile for height and weight. At 2 years of age, he is at the 25th and 10th percentiles respectively. His mother mentions that after she stopped breastfeeding and introduced table foods, he developed fussiness, loose stools, and occasional stomach aches. The mother has been consuming milk products her entire life without issue, and her son does not drink cow’s milk. Which is the most likely cause of these symptoms in the boy?
questions.initialExplanation:
Symptoms and falling growth percentiles after gluten-containing foods are introduced point toward celiac disease.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Celiac disease is a possible cause of growth faltering and gastrointestinal symptoms that started after the introduction of table foods, which likely contain gluten. The absence of exposure to cow’s milk makes cow milk protein allergy less likely, and the symptoms are more persistent and systemic than what would typically be seen with toddler’s diarrhea or lactose intolerance. Chronic giardiasis could cause similar symptoms but is less likely without a history of exposure to contaminated water or chronic infections.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. The child has a fever and appears lethargic. The medical team is considering antibiotic therapy. Antibiotics to control diarrhea should NOT be given in which of the following situations?

options.label: A
options.text: Bloody diarrhea with fever for 2 days

options.label: B
options.text: Diarrhea associated with signs of sepsis and disseminated intravascular coagulation

options.label: C
options.text: Diarrhea in children with sickle cell disease

options.label: D
options.text: Diarrhea in children with cancer on chemotherapy

options.label: E
options.text: Acute watery diarrhea with moderate dehydration

questions.initialExplanation:
Uncomplicated acute watery diarrhea is often viral and does not routinely need antibiotics. Antibiotics are reserved for selected invasive bacterial infections or high-risk patients.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Antibiotics are generally not indicated for acute watery diarrhea unless there is evidence of bacterial infection. Most cases of acute watery diarrhea are viral in origin, and antibiotics would not be effective. In cases of bloody diarrhea, fever, sepsis, and specific conditions like sickle cell disease or chemotherapy, antibiotics may be necessary due to the increased risk of bacterial infections and complications. Antibiotic use should be guided by clinical judgment and, when possible, stool culture results.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital with a 6-kg weight loss, bloody diarrhea, and fever that have occurred intermittently over the previous 6 months. She reports cramping abdominal pain with bowel movements. She also reports secondary amenorrhea during this time. Stool cultures in her physician’s office have shown only normal intestinal flora. A urine pregnancy test was negative, while an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was elevated. Her examination is significant for the lack of oral mucosal ulcerations and a normal perianal examination. Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA) are negative, while anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (p-ANCA) are positive. You confirm your presumptive diagnosis with a rectal biopsy. In counseling her about her disease, which of the following statements would be true?

options.label: B
options.text: Her risk of colon cancer is minimally elevated over the general population

options.label: D
options.text: The most serious complication of her disease is toxic megacolon

options.label: E
options.text: [Option E is not visible in the supplied PDF image]

questions.initialExplanation:
The findings support ulcerative colitis. Its dangerous acute complication is toxic megacolon, which can lead to perforation; colorectal cancer risk also rises with long-standing disease.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The most serious complication of her disease is toxic megacolon. The patient in the vignette has ulcerative colitis, a chronic inflammatory condition usually involving the entire colon. While there does seem to be some genetic predisposition (twin concordance is 16%, while twin concordance for Crohn disease is 36%), inheritance is not clearly dominant or recessive. Patients usually have intermittent symptoms of bloody diarrhea, and can have abdominal pain and growth failure. Perianal disease is uncommon, as are mouth ulcerations. So-called skip areas, portions of the intestine free of disease, are common in Crohn disease, but are not seen in ulcerative colitis. ASCA is positive in about 55% of those with Crohn disease, but are uncommon in ulcerative colitis; conversely, p-ANCA is positive in about 70% of patients with ulcerative colitis, but in less than 20% of patients with Crohn disease. The most serious complication of ulcerative colitis is toxic megacolon, a medical and surgical emergency in which patients develop fever, tachycardia, dehydration, leukocytosis, and electrolyte abnormalities associated with a markedly dilated colon. This complication comes with a high risk of intestinal perforation. Patients with ulcerative colitis have a markedly elevated risk of colon cancer; after 10 years of disease, the annual cumulative risk is 0.5% to 1% a year. Strictures are more common in Crohn disease and are unusual in ulcerative colitis.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old male infant is brought to the pediatric clinic with suspected anorectal malformation (ARM). The parents report that the baby has not passed meconium since birth and has a visible abnormality in the perianal area. Upon examination, the pediatrician observes an imperforate anus with a fistula. There are many anomalies associated with anorectal malformations. Of the following, the MOST common are
questions.initialExplanation:
Renal and urinary tract abnormalities are common associated findings in infants with anorectal malformations, often alongside sacral abnormalities.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: There are many anomalies associated with anorectal malformations. The most common are anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract in conjunction with abnormalities of the sacrum. This complex is often referred to as the caudal regression syndrome.

questions.stem: You are admitting to the hospital a 5-month-old infant who has been having poor feeding, emesis, and diarrhea for 3 days. In the emergency center, her electrolytes were found to be: sodium 157 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, chloride 120 mEq/L, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 68 mEq/L, and glucose 195 mg/dL. She was given a fluid bolus in the emergency center and has subsequently produced urine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.label: A
options.text: Slow rehydration with 1/3 glucose saline over 48 hours

options.label: B
options.text: Continued rapid volume expansion with 1/4 normal saline

questions.initialExplanation:
After initial isotonic resuscitation, hypernatremia must be corrected slowly over about 24–48 hours to avoid dangerous fluid shifts and cerebral edema.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Initial bolus therapy in the emergency center should have been with isotonic fluid such as normal saline or lactated Ringer solution. Slow correction of this hypernatremia (more than 24–48 hours) with 1/3 glucose saline prevents significant fluid shifts and increased intracranial pressure. Hyperglycemia may be seen in hypernatremic dehydration because of decreased insulin secretion and cell sensitivity to insulin; this is particularly important to recognize because increased serum glucose can cause the serum sodium to be falsely decreased. Blood products such as fresh-frozen plasma are not indicated, and rapid infusion of hypotonic solutions such as D10W and 1/4 normal saline could cause rapid fluid shifts resulting in cerebral edema and death. Hypertonic (3%) saline is used only in the event of seizures caused by rapid rehydration (or in children with hyponatremic dehydration and associated central nervous system symptoms), along with other emergent measures typically used to reduce cerebral edema.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician’s office by his parents because of diarrhea. He first started having loose stools 3 days ago, which were watery and green. This continued until this morning, when he noticed that there was blood in his stool. He is having four to five episodes of diarrhea daily with some cramping abdominal pain. He is afebrile and has been eating and drinking enough to stay adequately hydrated. Of the following, which test is most likely to help identify the cause of his illness?

options.label: A
options.text: Stool test for ova and parasites

options.label: B
options.text: Stool test for Clostridium difficile toxin

questions.initialExplanation:
Acute bloody diarrhea suggests bacterial infection. Stool culture can identify the pathogen, including E. coli O157:H7, which is important because of its association with HUS.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Bloody diarrhea in a previously healthy child is most commonly secondary to an infectious cause. It is important to obtain stool cultures early in the course of the illness. Many bacterial pathogens can cause bloody diarrhea, including enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, Shigella, Salmonella enteritidis, Campylobacter jejuni, and Yersinia enterocolitica. Identification of the specific pathogen is important, as treatment varies. It is critically important to identify those who may have disease caused by E. coli O157:H7 strain, as these patients are at risk for developing hemolytic uremic syndrome (A). Testing for ova and parasites in those with prolonged diarrhea may be helpful in certain circumstances, particularly if there are other factors in the history that suggest a parasite infection, such as recent camping, swimming in fresh water, and an immunocompromised status. However, most diarrheal disease in children is nonbloody. (B) Infection caused by C. difficile is becoming more prevalent. Exposure to antibiotics in the past 6 months or recent hospitalization are important risk factors. (E) A complete blood cell count should be considered for any child with prolonged bloody diarrhea. Although this is an important part of the evaluation, it does not help to determine which infectious agent is the cause. (D) Viral agents frequently cause diarrheal illness in children. However, most virus-mediated diarrhea is non-bloody. Common viral causes include rotavirus, norovirus, and adenovirus.

questions.stem: A community health worker is providing education to a group of parents in a rural clinic about preventing diarrhea in children. She discusses various strategies to reduce the incidence and severity of diarrhea among the young population. All of the following factors can reduce the incidence and severity of diarrhea in young children, EXCEPT:

options.label: D
options.text: Introducing foods after 6 months of age

options.label: E
options.text: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 4–6 months of life

questions.initialExplanation:
DPT vaccine prevents diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus, not diarrheal disease. Rotavirus immunization, measles immunization, breastfeeding, and safe complementary-feeding practices can reduce diarrheal illness. The source selects DPT immunization as the exception.

---

## Liver and Biliary Disorders
questions.detailedExplanation: DPT immunization, which protects against diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), and tetanus, does not directly reduce the incidence or severity of diarrhea. However, immunizations like the rotavirus vaccine can reduce the incidence of diarrhea. Measles immunization can indirectly reduce the severity of diarrhea because measles can lead to complications that include diarrhea. Avoiding unnecessary antibiotics can prevent diarrhea by preserving normal gut flora. Introducing foods after 6 months of age, while continuing breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond, is recommended for nutritional reasons but also helps to prevent diarrhea by avoiding early introduction of potentially contaminated foods. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 4–6 months of life protects infants against various infections, including diarrheal diseases.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child presented with progressive jaundice, ascites, and signs of liver failure. Despite previous surgical interventions, the child’s liver function continues to deteriorate. Comprehensive assessments, including liver function tests, imaging studies, and biopsy, confirmed advanced cirrhosis and portal hypertension. The medical team initiated the child’s evaluation for liver transplantation. The MOST common indication for liver transplantation in children is?
questions.initialExplanation:
In children, biliary atresia is the leading indication for liver transplantation, ahead of metabolic, autoimmune, and other cholestatic conditions.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Biliary atresia is the most common indication for liver transplantation in children, followed by metabolic and inborn disorders, autoimmune and familial cholestatic disorders, and acute hepatic necrosis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presented with nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, abdominal pain, and mild jaundice. Initial blood tests revealed elevated liver enzymes and hypergammaglobulinemia, prompting further investigations. Serological markers indicated the presence of autoantibodies associated with autoimmune hepatitis (AIH). Autoimmune hepatitis is a clinical diagnosis based on certain diagnostic criteria; no single test will make this diagnosis. Important positive features include the following EXCEPT
questions.initialExplanation:
Autoimmune hepatitis usually produces a hepatocellular pattern with raised ALT and AST. A primary alkaline-phosphatase elevation is more typical of cholestatic or bile-duct disease.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), the liver inflammation is characterized by a primary elevation in transaminases, specifically alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). These enzymes are increased in the bloodstream when liver cells are damaged. Unlike some other liver conditions, AIH typically does not cause a significant increase in alkaline phosphatase (ALP), which is an enzyme associated with bile duct function. This pattern of liver enzyme elevation, with a predominant increase in transaminases and a less prominent rise in ALP, can help differentiate AIH from other liver disorders, such as primary biliary cholangitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis, where ALP is often more prominently elevated.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman, during her routine prenatal check-up, was informed about the importance of hepatitis screening during pregnancy. As part of standard prenatal care, she underwent blood tests that included screening for Hepatitis B. Routine screening for HBV infection requires an assay of multiple serologic markers, all the following are true EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: HBsAg is the first serologic marker of infection to appear

options.label: B
options.text: Anti-HBc is a valuable serologic marker of acute HBV infection

options.label: C
options.text: Anti-HBs and anti-HBc are detected in persons immunized with hepatitis B vaccine

options.label: D
options.text: HBeAg is a marker of infectivity

options.label: E
options.text: HBsAg levels fall before symptoms wane

questions.initialExplanation:
Hepatitis B vaccination produces anti-HBs, not anti-HBc. Anti-HBc indicates natural exposure to the virus, so the statement in option C is the exception.

---

## Celiac Disease and Malabsorption
questions.detailedExplanation: Only anti-HBs is present in persons immunized with hepatitis B vaccine, whereas both anti-HBs and anti-HBc are detected in persons with resolved infection.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents, who are concerned about his chronic diarrhea, poor growth, and the fact that he seems to avoid food. His parents describe the stools as frequent and voluminous. Initial laboratory tests are ordered to evaluate for malabsorption. Which of the following findings is NOT suggestive of carbohydrate malabsorption?

options.label: B
options.text: Perianal excoriation and gaseous abdominal distention

options.label: C
options.text: The patient may present with food avoidance more than being anorexic

options.label: E
options.text: Pasty, bulky and yellowish offensive stool

questions.initialExplanation:
Bulky, pale, foul-smelling stools point more toward fat malabsorption. Carbohydrate malabsorption more often causes acidic stools, gas, and positive reducing substances.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Pasty, bulky, and yellowish offensive stools are more typically associated with fat malabsorption rather than carbohydrate malabsorption. In carbohydrate malabsorption, symptoms such as acidic stool pH, increased gas, and perianal excoriation can occur due to the fermentation of undigested carbohydrates, leading to a lower pH. Positive reducing substances in the stool are also indicative of the presence of undigested carbohydrates. Perianal excoriation can occur due to the irritating nature of the stools, and gaseous distention may be present due to fermentation gases. Food avoidance can be a behavioral response to the discomfort associated with eating foods that are not well-absorbed.

questions.stem: The boy diagnosed with celiac disease is starting a gluten-free diet. His parents are being educated about which foods he should avoid to prevent symptoms and promote intestinal healing. Patients with celiac disease should avoid consuming which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation:
Celiac disease requires lifelong avoidance of gluten-containing grains, including rye, wheat, and barley. Rice, corn, and legumes are naturally gluten-free.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Patients with celiac disease must avoid all sources of gluten, which is found in wheat, barley, and rye. While pure, uncontaminated oats may be tolerated by most individuals with celiac disease, caution is advised due to the potential for cross-contamination with wheat during processing. Corn, rice, and legumes are naturally gluten-free and can be included in a gluten-free diet.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is being evaluated for short stature. The physical examination reveals pallor, abnormal teething, and wasting of the thigh and buttock. The complete blood count shows anemia with a hemoglobin level of 7 g/dL, and serum ferritin is low at 9 mg/dL. Screening for celiac disease reveals positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies at 90 U/mL, but endomysial antibodies (EMA) and HLA DQ8/DQ2 genotyping are not available. Given this clinical picture, what is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.text: Continue normal diet with follow-up serological testing

questions.initialExplanation:
Positive screening antibodies and compatible symptoms require confirmation with duodenal biopsy before starting a gluten-free diet, because dietary treatment can alter biopsy findings.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Given the positive anti-tTG antibodies and symptoms consistent with celiac disease, the next appropriate step is to confirm the diagnosis with duodenal biopsies. This procedure will look for the characteristic histopathological changes of celiac disease, such as villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia. Starting a gluten-free diet before confirmation can interfere with the biopsy results, and other diagnoses should not be considered until celiac disease has been ruled out or confirmed.

questions.stem: At 1 year of age, a boy was at the 50th percentile for height and weight. At 2 years of age, he is at the 25th and 10th percentiles respectively. Review of systems reveals fussiness, loose stools, and possibly stomach aches all beginning soon after the mother stopped breastfeeding and introduced table foods. The mother has consumed milk products lifelong, but her son does not drink cow milk. The most definitive test to diagnose this child’s condition is which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation:
Serologic tests help screen for celiac disease, but the source identifies small-bowel biopsy as the definitive diagnostic test.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation suggests a possible malabsorption issue, and celiac disease is the most likely diagnosis based on the timing of the issue (immediately after weaning). The most definitive test for diagnosing celiac disease is a small bowel biopsy. Therefore, in this case, the appropriate choice would be a small bowel biopsy to assess the intestinal lining and confirm the diagnosis of celiac disease. Serum anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are used as the initial tests but they are not definitive, and a small bowel biopsy is usually needed to confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with large, foul-smelling stools and poor weight gain. A sweat chloride test reveals a level of 68 mmol/L, suggesting a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis, which is associated with pancreatic insufficiency. What are the appropriate nutritional recommendations for this infant?
questions.initialExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis may cause pancreatic enzyme deficiency and poor fat absorption. Pancreatic enzyme replacement helps digest and absorb nutrients; fat-soluble vitamins may also be needed.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy is essential in the management of pancreatic insufficiency due to cystic fibrosis. It helps with the digestion and absorption of nutrients, particularly fats, which are commonly malabsorbed in these patients. This therapy often needs to be accompanied by fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K) due to poor absorption of these vitamins.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant, previously healthy, presents with a 2-month history of chronic diarrhea. The diarrhea persists despite dietary changes. The infant was treated for a suspected viral gastroenteritis at 4 months of age but has had persistent diarrhea since. The infant’s growth has started to falter, and the parents are concerned. Which of the following is a common cause of chronic diarrhea in infancy?
questions.initialExplanation:
Gastroenteritis can temporarily damage the intestinal lining and reduce lactase activity. Diarrhea may continue after the infection when lactose is consumed, but usually improves as the mucosa heals.

---

## Intestinal Disorders and GI Bleeding
questions.detailedExplanation: Post-infectious secondary lactase deficiency is commonly observed after an episode of gastroenteritis in infants. This condition results from damage to the intestinal villi, where lactase is produced, leading to a temporary decrease in lactase enzyme activity. This can result in chronic diarrhea when lactose-containing foods are ingested, as lactose is not adequately digested and absorbed. The condition is usually self-limiting and improves as the intestinal mucosa heals.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old baby boy, recently adopted from Guyana, has a 5-hour history of crying, with intermittent drawing up of his knees to his chest. On the way to the emergency room he passes a loose, bloody stool. He has had no vomiting and has refused his bottle since the crying began. Physical examination is noteworthy for an irritable infant whose abdomen is very difficult to examine because of constant crying. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). The rectal ampulla is empty, but there is some gross blood on the examining finger. Which of the following studies would be most helpful in the immediate management of this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: Examination of the stool for ova and parasites

questions.initialExplanation:
Intermittent colicky pain, drawing up the legs, and bloody mucus stool suggest intussusception. An air-contrast enema can diagnose and often reduce it, with surgical backup available.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The usual presentation of intussusception is that of an infant between 4 and 10 months of age who has a sudden onset of intermittent colicky abdominal pain. The child can appear normal when the pain abates, but as it recurs with increasing frequency, the child can begin to vomit and become progressively more obtunded. The passage of stool containing blood and mucus, frequently described as resembling currant jelly, is often observed. Early examination of the abdomen can be unremarkable, but as the problem persists, a sausagelike mass in the right upper quadrant is frequently palpated. An air, barium, or saline enema examination under fluoroscopic or ultrasound control can be therapeutic as well as diagnostic when the hydrostatic effects of the contrast serve to reduce the intussusception, but should be performed with surgical backup, as a complication of attempted reduction is intestinal perforation. Rates of intestinal perforation are lowest with air reduction. Early diagnosis prevents bowel ischemia. The cause of most intussusceptions is unknown, but a Meckel diverticulum or polyp can serve as a lead point. None of the other choices would result in a correct diagnosis (and potential therapy) for the child with a classic presentation for intussusception.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old presents to the emergency center with several days of rectal bleeding. The mother first noticed reddish-colored stools 2 days prior to arrival and has since changed several diapers with just blood. The child is afebrile, alert, and playful, and is eating well without emesis. He is slightly tachycardic, and his abdominal examination is normal. Which of the following is the best diagnostic study to order to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Meckel diverticulum can contain ectopic gastric mucosa and cause painless rectal bleeding in young children. A technetium radionuclide scan detects the gastric mucosa.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The child described has a typical presentation for Meckel diverticulum. The embryonic duct connecting the yolk sac to the intestine can fail to regress completely and persist as a diverticulum attached to the ileum. It is common, occurring in 1.5% of the population; however, it rarely causes symptoms. Children symptomatic with this condition usually present with painless rectal bleeding in the first 2 years of life but can have symptoms throughout the first decade. The lining of the Meckel diverticulum usually contains acid-secreting gastric mucosa that can produce ulcerations of the diverticulum or of the adjacent ileum. In children with painless rectal bleeding, the diverticulum can be explored surgically. More commonly, the diverticulum can lead to volvulus of itself and of the small intestine, and it can also undergo eversion and intussusception. Diagnosis can be made by technetium scan that labels gastric mucosa, and treatment is surgical excision. Barium studies do not readily reveal the diverticulum, nor do plain films.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old toddler presents to the pediatric clinic with a history of chronic diarrhea, abdominal distension, and occasional vomiting. The mother reports that the symptoms seem to worsen after the toddler drinks cow’s milk or eats dairy products. The physical exam is notable for mild abdominal distension, but no tenderness. Stool examination does not reveal any infectious cause. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of cow milk protein intolerance?

options.label: B
options.text: Streaks of bloody mucus in stools

questions.initialExplanation:
Cow-milk protein intolerance can cause immune-mediated intestinal inflammation, sometimes producing blood and mucus in the stool. Distension, vomiting, and eosinophilia may also occur.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Cow milk protein intolerance can present with a range of gastrointestinal symptoms due to the immune system’s reaction to the proteins present in cow’s milk. This can lead to inflammation of the intestinal tract, resulting in symptoms such as blood and mucus in the stools. Abdominal distension and vomiting are also common symptoms, and peripheral eosinophilia can occur due to the allergic component of the intolerance.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old female presents with a history of recurrent, painless rectal bleeding. She has a past medical history significant for intussusception at the age of 9 months, which was treated non-operatively. Her clotting profile is normal, but she has mild anemia. Based on the clinical history, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Recurrent painless bleeding is a classic presentation of Meckel diverticulum because ectopic gastric mucosa can ulcerate nearby bowel.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Recurrent painless rectal bleeding in a child with a history of intussusception is suggestive of Meckel diverticulum. Meckel diverticulum can cause bleeding due to ectopic gastric mucosa leading to ulceration. While intussusception can recur, it usually presents with abdominal pain, a palpable sausage-shaped mass, and sometimes bilious vomiting, not isolated rectal bleeding. Amoebic dysentery, fissure, and polyps are less likely given the presentation and history provided.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old female presents with recurrent attacks of painless rectal bleeding; she had previous history of intussusception at age of 9 month treated by pneumatic reduction; clotting profile and blood film are normal apart from mild anemia. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Meckel diverticulum can cause painless rectal bleeding and can also act as a lead point for intussusception. A technetium Meckel scan can detect ectopic gastric mucosa.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: One of the most common presentations of Meckel diverticulum in children is painless rectal bleeding due to the presence of ectopic gastric mucosa. Meckel diverticulum is the most common gastrointestinal tract anomaly, occurring in 2% of the population. It can also present as intussusception which happened to this child when he was younger. Meckel diverticulum scan (Meckel scan) is a noninvasive nuclear medicine imaging technique using radiolabeled technetium (99mTc), which is preferentially absorbed by the gastric mucosa and can identify ectopic gastric mucosa and is appropriate for this patient to confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the office with complaints of bleeding while stooling. He was seen for this same complaint about 2 months ago. At that time, he was placed on stool-softening medications for constipation. His mother reports that he is taking the medication every day. He stools daily and denies any hard stools or pain with stooling. However, he has had three more episodes of bleeding. The patient reports a significant amount of bright red blood in the toilet following defecation. He denies any abdominal pain associated with these episodes. Of the following options, which is the most likely cause of this patient’s bleeding?
questions.initialExplanation:
Juvenile polyps commonly cause recurrent, painless bright-red rectal bleeding in children. Colonoscopy identifies them and allows removal.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Intermittent painless bleeding associated with defecation should raise the suspicion for colonic polyps. Juvenile polyps typically present in children aged 2 to 10 years old. The diagnosis is made by colonoscopy. The treatment is removal at the time of colonoscopy. (B, E) There are several inherited polyposis syndromes, which can also present similarly but are much less likely than juvenile polyps. These include FAP, which is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a mutation in the APC gene. Typically 5 or more polyps are seen at the time of diagnosis and will progress to 100 or more by early adulthood. Patients will ultimately require surgical colectomy, as the risk of colon cancer is extremely high if left untreated. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is another autosomal dominant polyposis syndrome, which can present with rectal bleeding. Children with Peutz–Jeghers typically have freckling of the lips and gingiva. These patients have polyps that are benign hamartomas. Patients with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome have an increased risk of breast, colon, and gynecologic cancers. (C) Constipation is unlikely for the patient in the vignette given his current stooling pattern and medication compliance. (D) Intussusception generally presents with intermittent episodes of colicky abdominal pain and eventually bloody stools.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy, recently adopted through an international adoption service, is noted to have intermittent watery diarrhea, nausea, belching, and abdominal pain. His weight is less than the fifth percentile for his age. Which of the following studies would be most helpful in making the diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.text: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites

questions.initialExplanation:
Chronic diarrhea and poor growth after international adoption raise concern for Giardia. Stool microscopy can identify Giardia cysts or trophozoites.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Parasites are a common medical problem, found in about 60% of international adoptees, in most cases related to tainted water ingestion; Giardia is the most frequent isolate. Patients with Giardia infection complain of recurrent abdominal pain, cramping, intermittent diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss. Although many cases are self-limited, symptoms can recur or become chronic. Identifying the Giardia cysts or trophozoites makes the diagnosis. Upper endoscopy and microscopic examination of duodenal biopsies can also be diagnostic. Although international adoptees may also have hepatitis, it is much less common than parasitic infection. Most patients with Giardia infection have normal CBCs. An upper GI series may reveal nonspecific changes associated with Giardia infection, but an ultrasound would not be helpful. An ESR is merely a nonspecific marker for inflammation, and would not help make the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child was brought to the pediatrician with a sudden onset of abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. The parents reported that the symptoms began shortly after the child consumed a meal at a local restaurant. Physical examination revealed signs of dehydration, and the child appeared lethargic. Regarding foodborne bacterial illness, antibiotics are not indicated in the following foodborne bacterial illness:
questions.initialExplanation:
EHEC O157:H7 can cause HUS. The source recommends supportive care and avoiding antibiotics and antimotility agents because they may increase HUS risk.

---

## Dehydration, Rehydration, and Electrolytes
questions.detailedExplanation: Treatment of Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) O157:H7 include supportive care, monitor renal function, hemoglobin, and platelets closely. E. coli O157:H7 infection is also associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), which can cause life-threatening complications. Studies indicate that antibiotics might promote the development of HUS. Antidiarrheal agents like loperamide also increase the risk of developing HUS.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with lethargy and fatigue. Her mother states she has not been eating or drinking well the past few days and has had multiple episodes of vomiting and diarrhea. In the last 24 hours, the patient has not had any urine output. On examination, the patient’s pulse is 164 beats/min and her blood pressure is 81/64 mmHg. She is anxious with cold, sweaty skin. Her pulses are diminished and her mucous membranes are very dry. Of the following, which is the next best step in the management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: 20 mL/kg bolus of D5 half-normal saline over 20 minutes

options.label: B
options.text: 20 mL/kg bolus of lactated Ringer’s solution over 2 hours

options.label: C
options.text: 20 mL/kg bolus of normal saline over 20 minutes

options.label: D
options.text: D5 half-normal saline with 20 mEq/L of potassium chloride maintenance rate

questions.initialExplanation:
Shock from severe dehydration requires rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation, usually 20 mL/kg of normal saline or lactated Ringer’s solution, followed by reassessment. Do not add potassium until urine output/renal function is established.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The patient in the vignette has symptoms consistent with severe dehydration and requires immediate intervention to restore adequate tissue perfusion. (A, B, D, E) The best initial option to restore intravascular volume is aggressive fluid therapy with a bolus of 20 mL/kg of an isotonic solution, either normal saline or lactated Ringer’s solution. The bolus should be given quickly, ideally within 20 minutes. Once the initial fluid bolus is administered, the patient should be reassessed for clinical improvement and additional fluid boluses given as necessary. Once resuscitation is complete, an appropriate fluid plan can be determined to include maintenance fluid therapy needs and replacement of any ongoing losses. Severely dehydrated patients may have acute renal failure; thus, potassium is initially withheld from resuscitation fluids until adequate renal function is established.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old adolescent was admitted with symptoms suggestive of acute hepatitis B infection, displaying fatigue, dark urine, and jaundice. Laboratory tests indicated elevated liver enzymes and positive serological markers for Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and IgM antibodies against Hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc IgM), confirming recent infection, regarding risk factors for HBV infection in children and adolescents include acquisition by the following EXCEPT
questions.initialExplanation:
Hepatitis B spreads through infected blood and certain body fluids, not casual contact or sharing ordinary toys.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is primarily transmitted through direct contact with infected blood or other body fluids, such as semen and vaginal secretions. Unlike some other viruses, HBV is not considered to be transmitted through indirect exposure, such as sharing toys. The virus does not survive well outside the human body, and its transmission typically requires direct contact with infected blood or body fluids. While HBV is highly contagious, precautions like avoiding sharing personal items, such as toothbrushes or razors, can minimize the risk of transmission. However, casual contact or sharing items like toys does not pose a significant risk for the spread of Hepatitis B.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old male presents with moderate dehydration. After initial assessment and a fluid bolus, his lab studies show a serum sodium of 165 mEq/L, indicative of hypernatremia, but with a normal serum potassium level. What is the most appropriate plan for rehydration in this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Correct the hypernatremia over 12 hours with 5% D/W and 0.45% NS with maintenance potassium

options.label: B
options.text: Correct the hypernatremia over 24–48 hours with D10W without maintenance potassium

options.label: C
options.text: Correct the hypernatremia over 8 hours with 5% D/W with maintenance potassium

options.label: D
options.text: Correct the hypernatremia over 24–48 hours with dextrose 2.5 g, 0.45% NS with maintenance potassium

options.label: E
options.text: Correct the hypernatremia over 8 hours with 0.45% NS without maintenance potassium

questions.initialExplanation:
High sodium must be lowered gradually over 24–48 hours to reduce cerebral-edema risk. The source selects a dextrose-containing hypotonic saline solution with maintenance potassium.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The correction of hypernatremia should be done slowly to avoid the risk of cerebral edema. A plan over 24–48 hours is considered safer than an 8-hour correction. Dextrose and sodium chloride (0.45% NS) provide rehydration without contributing to the hypernatremia. Maintenance potassium is important as potassium can decrease once fluid levels normalize and the body redistributes potassium intracellularly.

questions.stem: A six-month-old child weighing 8 kg presents to the emergency department with dehydration. A fluid bolus (20 ml/kg) has been prescribed to be administered over one hour. To administer the prescribed bolus over one hour to a six-month-old child weighing 8 kg, how many macro-drops per minute should be delivered?
questions.initialExplanation:
An 8-kg child needs 160 mL at 20 mL/kg. With a 15-drop/mL set over 60 minutes, the rate is 40 drops/minute.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: To administer a bolus of 20 ml/kg over one hour to an 8 kg child, the total volume is 160 ml. Using a standard macrodrip set where 1 ml is 15 drops, the calculation is 160 ml multiplied by 15 drops/ml, equaling 2400 drops. This is then divided by 60 minutes to get 40 drops per minute.

questions.stem: You are determining the daily maintenance fluid requirements for a 16-kg afebrile toddler. What is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a 16-kg afebrile toddler?
questions.initialExplanation:
Using the 100–50–20 rule: 1000 mL for the first 10 kg, 250 mL for the next 5 kg, and 20 mL for the final kilogram gives 1270 mL, approximately 1300 mL/day.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The daily fluid requirement for children is calculated using the 100-50-20 rule: 100 ml/kg for the first 10 kg, 50 ml/kg for the next 5 kg, and 20 ml/kg for each kilogram for 10 to 20 kg. For a 16-kg toddler, the first 10 kg require 1000 ml, the next 5 kg require 250 ml, and the last 1 kg requires 20 ml, totaling 1270 ml, which can be approximated to 1300 ml.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child from a low-income community was brought to a local health clinic with a history of persistent diarrhea and signs of malnutrition. The child appeared emaciated, had a distended abdomen, and exhibited generalized weakness. The parents reported a limited diet due to financial constraints. Laboratory tests confirmed severe malnutrition with deficiencies in essential nutrients. Management of the diarrhea in chronically malnourished children is based on:
questions.initialExplanation:
For malnourished children with diarrhea, the source emphasizes oral rehydration, early feeding, and treatment of the cause; the selected solution is reduced-osmolarity ORS.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Management of the diarrhea in chronically malnourished children is based on 3 principles: oral rehydration to correct dehydration, rapid resumption of feeds with avoidance of periods of nothing by mouth, and treating the etiology of the diarrhea.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a history of prolonged vomiting and diarrhea. The parents report that the child has been unable to keep fluids down and has been passing very little urine. On examination, the child is lethargic, has a rapid pulse, sunken eyes, and the mucous membranes are very dry. A child with severe dehydration may present with any of the following complications Except:
questions.initialExplanation:
Severe diarrhea-related dehydration usually causes metabolic acidosis. Metabolic alkalosis is the exception among the listed complications, although vomiting can contribute to alkalosis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Severe dehydration typically leads to metabolic acidosis due to the loss of bicarbonate with diarrhea and the accumulation of lactic acid from poor tissue perfusion. Metabolic alkalosis is less common and not typically associated with dehydration without additional contributing factors, such as vomiting, which can lead to the loss of gastric acid.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old is brought to the emergency center by ambulance. The child had been having emesis and diarrhea with decreased urine output for several days, and the parents noted that she was hard to wake up this morning. Her weight is 9 kg, down from 11 kg the prior week at her 9-month checkup. You note her heart rate and blood pressure to be normal. She is lethargic, and her skin is noted to be “doughy.” After confirming that her respiratory status is stable, you send electrolytes, which you expect to be abnormal. You start an IV. Which of the following is the best solution for an initial IV bolus?
questions.initialExplanation:
Hypernatremic dehydration can cause significant intravascular depletion despite less obvious physical signs. The source recommends isotonic normal saline for the initial bolus.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The description is that of a child with hypernatremia (in this case, the child’s sodium was 170 mEq/L); the “doughy” skin is often seen in this type of dehydration. The extracellular fluid and intracellular fluid volumes tend to be preserved with hypernatremic dehydration at the expense of the intravascular volume. Therefore, hypernatremic dehydration may not be observed, nor may the signs of circulatory inadequacy be typical of isotonic or hypotonic dehydration. Signs suggesting involvement of the central nervous system (such as irritability or lethargy) are characteristic of both hypertonic and hypotonic dehydration. Isotonic saline is the best fluid for an initial bolus in a patient such as the one described in the question. Use of 1/4 normal saline (38.5 mEq sodium/L) or D10 water (100 g glucose/L) in this dehydrated child would not expand the intravascular space and its hyponatremic nature might lead to cerebral edema. The child in the question is not severely hypernatremic, so 3% saline (513 mEq sodium/L) would only exacerbate the problem; its use in dehydration might be considered for some patients with severe hyponatremia. Fresh-frozen plasma can be used in the setting of decreased albumin, but is generally not rapidly available, is more expensive, can be associated with infectious agents, and offers no advantage to saline.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with gastroenteritis is being treated with oral rehydration therapy (ORT). She is mildly dehydrated but is able to drink fluids and has no signs of shock. The mother inquires about the properties of the ORT solution being used and its preparation. Regarding standard oral rehydration solution (ORS), which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Works by passive absorption of glucose

options.label: B
options.text: Is not given for mildly dehydrated infants

options.label: C
options.text: Should not be used for a child with hypertonic dehydration

options.label: E
options.text: Can be made safely at home using salt and sugar

questions.initialExplanation:
Standard ORS contains about 20 mmol/L of potassium and uses sodium–glucose cotransport for absorption. Correct preparation is essential.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Standard ORS indeed contains a specific amount of potassium; 20 mmol/L is a typical concentration. This potassium content helps replace losses due to diarrhea and vomiting. The other statements about ORS are incorrect or incomplete regarding its use and mechanism of action. ORS is a cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration in children, even those with hypertonic dehydration, as it provides fluids and electrolytes in a ratio that helps to replenish what the body has lost and promotes rehydration. It also functions through active transport of glucose and sodium across the intestinal wall, not by passive absorption of glucose. Lastly, while ORS can be made at home, specific proportions must be followed carefully to ensure safety and effectiveness.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old male infant presents with persistent diaper rash, intermittent diarrhea, and a reluctance to eat solid foods. His mother is vegetarian, and the child has been predominantly breastfed. The child has dry, plaque-like skin lesions and a scanty, coarse hair. Which nutrient deficiency should be considered in this child’s condition?
questions.initialExplanation:
Dermatitis, diarrhea, and hair loss are characteristic clues to zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis enteropathica).

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation of dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia can be indicative of zinc deficiency, which is known as acrodermatitis enteropathica. This condition is often genetic or can also occur due to dietary insufficiency. Zinc is vital for immune function, skin health, and growth, and deficiencies can result from a low intake in animal proteins, which are a primary source of zinc, especially if the breastfeeding mother has a low zinc intake as well.

questions.stem: An infant with a history of diarrhea has been assessed as being 10% dehydrated. Prior to the onset of illness, the infant weighed 5 kg, and the surface area was 0.3 m². With a normal serum sodium concentration, the caregiver is inquiring prior to the onset of illness, the infant weighed 5 kg, and the surface area was 0.3 m². A parent is inquiring about the amount of fluid required to correct the dehydration. What is the approximate total amount of fluid you should deliver to meet maintenance needs and restore the child to a state of normal hydration in the first 24 hours?
questions.initialExplanation:
For a 5-kg infant, maintenance is about 500 mL/day. A 10% deficit is another 500 mL, giving approximately 1000 mL for the first 24 hours.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: To calculate the fluid needs for a dehydrated child, you need to consider both the maintenance fluid requirements and the deficit due to dehydration. For an infant, the maintenance fluid requirement is approximately 100 ml/kg/day. His weight is 5 kg and that gives us a total of 500 ml of fluids. This child is 10% dehydrated, which corresponds to a 500 ml deficit (10% of 5 kg is 500 ml). Therefore, the total fluid requirement is the sum of the maintenance need (500 ml for maintenance) and the deficit (500 ml for dehydration), totaling 1000 ml for the first 24 hours.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child was admitted to the pediatric ward with a 2-day history of acute diarrhea. The child appeared dehydrated, with increased frequency of watery stools and mild abdominal cramps. During the management, continued enteral feeding in diarrhea aids in recovery from the episode, but the following should be avoided
questions.initialExplanation:
High-sugar juices can worsen osmotic diarrhea. Continue feeding with suitable foods, but avoid fruit juices and other concentrated sugary drinks.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The child should avoid fruit juices, especially those high in simple sugars, as they may exacerbate diarrhea. Instead, the enteral feeding plan should include easily digestible components such as rice-based cereal, lean meats, and carefully selected fruits, while avoiding high-sugar fruit juices. Regular assessments and adjustments to the enteral feeding plan were planned to ensure the child’s nutritional needs were met during the recovery from diarrhea. Fatty foods or foods high in simple sugars (carbonated sodas) should be avoided.

questions.stem: You are presented with a 2-year-old child in the emergency department. The child has severe dehydration and diarrhea, with the mother reporting no urine output for the past 12 hours. The child appears lethargic and in need of urgent rehydration. What is your plan of management for this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately introduce a bolus of one third glucose saline

options.label: B
options.text: Administer furosemide before giving fluid to ensure urine output

options.label: C
options.text: Sodium bicarbonate should be given to correct acidosis (if present) before intravenous fluid administration

options.label: D
options.text: Add potassium chloride infusion after patient voids

options.label: E
options.text: Start ORS in a dose of 75 ml/kg over 4 hours

questions.initialExplanation:
Do not add potassium while the child is anuric or oliguric. Begin potassium replacement only after urine output has returned.

---

## Congenital and Surgical GI Disorders
questions.detailedExplanation: In cases of severe dehydration where there is no urine output, it is crucial to reestablish fluid balance cautiously. Potassium should not be added to the initial rehydration fluids because hyperkalemia can be exacerbated if the patient is anuric or oliguric. Once urine output is established, potassium can be added to fluids to address any deficits.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant was recently hospitalized for dehydration secondary to a rotavirus diarrheal illness. He was discharged home once rehydrated and demonstrating adequate oral intake. However, 1 day after discharge, the mother reports that since he started drinking normal amounts of his formula, she is seeing a dramatic increase in the amount of diarrhea. He had five loose stools today and she is worried that he is going to end up back in the hospital. A temporary switch to a soy-based formula is suggested. Of the following, which is the underlying mechanism for this patient’s current diarrhea?
questions.initialExplanation:
Rotavirus enteritis can temporarily damage the intestinal brush border and reduce lactase. Formula lactose then causes recurrent watery diarrhea until the mucosa heals.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Transient lactase deficiency. Postinfectious transient lactase deficiency is common among pediatric patients. The inflammation caused by the infection of the lumen causes damage to the brush border, and subsequent enzyme production is decreased. As such, as the child improves after a diarrheal illness and resumes intake of lactose-containing products, such as milk or formula, malabsorption occurs secondary to a temporary inability to break down the sugars. This will result in watery diarrhea and increased gas. If the symptoms are reasonable and the child is maintaining adequate hydration, this condition is self-limited and will resolve. If the diarrhea is profuse, a reasonable alternative is to switch to a soy-based formula for a few weeks, as is commercially available for most infants. True congenital lactase deficiency is extremely rare at infancy. A secondary infection such as C. difficile should be considered, but patients with this infection typically have bloody diarrhea. (C) Allergy to milk protein generally presents earlier than 9 months of age, usually within the first 3 months of life. There is not an indication for bowel rest in a stable child with uncomplicated viral-induced diarrhea. (A) Rather than a recurrence of his infectious diarrhea or infection with a new virus, it is more likely the patient in the vignette has developed a known complication of gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old boy presents with a 10-day history of vomiting that has increased in frequency and forcefulness. The vomitus is not bile stained. The child feeds avidly and looks well, but he has been losing weight. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Upper GI with small-bowel follow through

options.label: C
options.text: Intravenous (IV) fluids alone to maintain hydration

questions.initialExplanation:
Progressive, forceful, nonbilious vomiting in a young infant with persistent hunger and weight loss suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The source recommends surgical consultation for pyloromyotomy.

---

## Inflammatory Bowel Disease
questions.detailedExplanation: A history of nonbilious vomiting for 10 days in a child of this age who does not look ill points to infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis as the likely diagnosis; surgical consultation for pyloromyotomy is indicated. The ultrasound in the question demonstrates the thickened pylorus. The incidence of this condition in infants is between 1:2000 and 1:500, with males affected more often than females. Although there is no specific pattern of inheritance, a familial incidence has been observed in about 15%. Information about potassium and chloride levels is important, as are data concerning the assertion of a firstborn male. Metabolic alkalosis with low serum potassium and chloride levels is frequently seen in pyloric stenosis as a result of loss of gastric contents from vomiting. A child with a small-bowel obstruction (who may require an upper GI with small-bowel follow through to help diagnose the point of obstruction) should develop bilious emesis and should not look well 10 days into the illness, similarly, a child with intussusception (who requires an air contrast enema) does not have a 10-day history of vomiting and should show other symptoms such as irritability and somnolence.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy under evaluation for growth failure and delayed sexual development. Past history reveals recurrent attacks of abdominal pain, diarrhea, mouth ulcer, malaise, and weight loss; examination shows pallor, height and weight below 3rd centile, small testicular size, digital clubbing, and purulent drainage from anus. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnostic tool is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Perianal drainage, mouth ulcers, growth failure, and chronic diarrhea suggest Crohn disease. Colonoscopy with biopsy can visualize and confirm intestinal inflammation.

---

## Source integrity note
- No missing question numbers or unseen option text have been invented. The missing option in Question 10 is explicitly identified. The two Meckel-diverticulum entries (Questions 31 and 32) are kept separate as they appear in the source.
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation described, including recurrent abdominal pain, diarrhea, mouth ulcer, malaise, weight loss, poor stature and digital clubbing, and purulent drainage from the anus, is suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), specifically Crohn’s disease. The most appropriate diagnostic tool in this case would be colonoscopy with biopsy. Colonoscopy allows for direct visualization of the colon and terminal ileum, where Crohn’s disease commonly affects, and biopsies can confirm the characteristic inflammatory changes associated with the condition.

topics.name: Maternal Diabetes and Neonatal Metabolic Problems

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is seen in the pre-conception clinic. She reports sporadic adherence to her insulin regimen and glucose monitoring. She expresses her desire to conceive within the next year. The physician uses this opportunity to emphasize the importance of tight glycemic control prior to and during pregnancy. She explains that infants of diabetic mothers are at increased risk for various complications. Which of the following is the most common problem seen in infants of diabetic mothers?
questions.initialExplanation:
The fetus is exposed to high maternal glucose and produces extra insulin. After birth, the maternal glucose supply stops but the infant's insulin remains high, so blood glucose can fall.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Hypoglycemia is the most common neonatal complication in infants born to mothers with diabetes, due to the high levels of insulin in the baby's bloodstream following separation from the maternal glucose supply at birth. The physician emphasizes the importance of blood sugar regulation to reduce the risk of neonatal hypoglycemia and other complications associated with diabetic pregnancies.

questions.stem: You are counseling a diabetic teenager who states she is trying to get pregnant. She has not been compliant with her diabetes management over the past few years. You are trying to stress the importance of glucose control prior to conception and during pregnancy by explaining the possible complications associated with infants born to diabetic mothers. Which of the following is the most common problem in infants of diabetic mothers?
questions.initialExplanation:
High fetal insulin causes neonatal hypoglycemia when the placental glucose supply is interrupted at delivery.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Infants of diabetic mothers present with a variety of problems. The most common is hypoglycemia resulting from hyperinsulinism. Hypoglycemia develops in 25%–50% of infants of diabetic mothers. The probability of hypoglycemia after delivery increases when maternal fasting glucose is high. There is a threefold increase in the incidence of congenital anomalies in these infants, including sacral agenesis, congenital cardiac malformations, and intestinal atresias. Large birth weights are common among infants of diabetic mothers, predisposing the babies to birth trauma and asphyxia. Cardiomegaly is common in 30% of these infants; asymmetric septal hypertrophy may occur and can resemble idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis. This septal hypertrophy typically resolves with time. Hypocalcemia and associated hypomagnesemia are seen frequently, but infants do not typically develop hyponatremia beyond what is normally seen in newborn infants.

questions.stem: As a medical student in the neonatal intensive care unit, you report a calcium level in a 1-day-old term newborn that was flagged as abnormal by the laboratory. Which of the following is true of serum calcium levels in the newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: High parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels suppress the serum calcium.

options.label: B
options.text: The serum calcium promptly decreases after delivery.

options.label: C
options.text: The serum calcium remains essentially unchanged over the first 3 days.

options.label: D
options.text: The serum calcium is usually higher on day 2 than day 1.

options.label: E
options.text: Infants of diabetic mothers have an accentuated PTH response resulting in hypercalcemia.

questions.initialExplanation:
Calcium falls after birth because placental calcium transfer stops; PTH normally helps restore the level over the next days.

> **Source note:** The stem includes the source book number “66”; the gray question marker on the PDF is 16.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: After delivery, the infant is cut off from its continuous calcium supply, prompting a precipitous fall in serum calcium over the first 1–2 days. In normal circumstances, this stimulates PTH, causing a gradual return to higher serum calcium levels. PTH secretion is inhibited in infants of diabetic mothers. Therefore, hypocalcemia is a common problem in infants of diabetic mothers.

questions.stem: A normal newborn is screened for hypoglycemia after birth as per the normal nursery protocol at your hospital. In the asymptomatic term neonate, evaluation and treatment of hypoglycemia should be initiated when the glucose level is at or below which of the following levels?
questions.initialExplanation:
The key in the source selects 40 mg/dL, while the explanation says that many authorities recommend evaluation and treatment below 50 mg/dL.

> **Source note:** The keyed option and the explanation threshold do not match exactly: the answer list marks 40 mg/dL, while the text panel cites <50 mg/dL.

---

## Birth Trauma and Newborn Examination
questions.detailedExplanation: There is not always a correlation between blood glucose levels and classic clinical manifestations of hypoglycemia in the neonate. The lack of symptoms does not indicate that the glucose level is adequate for brain metabolism. Although a clear lower limit glucose level in newborn infants has not been determined, many authorities are recommending that any blood glucose value less than 50 mg/dL in the neonate be evaluated and treated.

questions.stem: The father of a 1-week-old infant comes to the office in a panic. He has just noticed on his child a right anterior shoulder mass that seems tender. The father is an osteosarcoma survivor and fears the child has the same malignancy. In reviewing the baby's discharge papers, you note the child was a term, appropriate-for-gestational-age vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3200 g (7 lb, 1 oz). Apgar scores were 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. Your examination is significant for a large firm mass on the right clavicle; the rest of the examination is normal. Management of this problem should include which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder

options.label: C
options.text: A biopsy of the mass for culture and cytology

options.label: E
options.text: Skin biopsy to test for osteogenesis imperfecta

questions.initialExplanation:
A clavicle fracture can become noticeable when a firm callus forms several days after birth. Most uncomplicated neonatal clavicle fractures heal with supportive care.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clavicle is the most commonly fractured bone in the delivery process. While some fractures are identified at birth, others may not be identified until callus formation is noted at about a week of age. Clavicular fracture may happen in any delivery, although there is higher risk with large-for-gestational-age infants. Initial presentation may include a pseudoparalysis, in which the infant refuses to move the ipsilateral arm, mimicking an Erb-Duchenne palsy.

questions.stem: A 40 weeks' gestation infant is born by forceps-assisted vaginal delivery to a diabetic mother following a prolonged course of active labor. The infant is appropriately resuscitated and transferred to the nursery without issue. The nursery course over the next 2 days is uneventful; however, the baby develops diffuse bruising and petechiae on the scalp and lateral face. There is a large midline area on his scalp of soft edema that completely obscures the posterior fontanelle. Of the following, what is the best explanation for this baby's scalp edema?
questions.initialExplanation:
Caput is a diffuse superficial scalp swelling that crosses suture lines. A cephalohematoma stays within one skull bone; subgaleal bleeding can cause shock.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Caput succedaneum is edema and ecchymotic swelling of the soft tissues of the head that results from birth trauma sustained during the birthing process. It presents as a diffuse swelling and fluid collection located superficial to the periosteum and characteristically crosses suture lines. Caput succedaneum usually resolves in the first 2 weeks of life. Infants are at increased risk for elevated bilirubin levels secondary to increased hemolysis. (A) In contrast, a cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal hemorrhage that is limited to one cranial bone and therefore does not cross the suture lines. (B) Subgaleal hemorrhage is a life-threatening hemorrhage in infants that occurs beneath the aponeurosis and may be associated with significant blood loss and shock. (C) Extradural hemorrhage is usually the result of a skull fracture with a resultant bleed between the dura and skull and is often associated with trauma in children and adolescents. (E) Intraventricular hemorrhage is seen mostly in premature infants from bleeding of the germinal matrix secondary to immaturity of the vasculature.

questions.stem: A 1-day-old male newborn is brought to the pediatric clinic for his first wellness check-up. Upon examination, the pediatrician notes that the infant has a robust cry, reactive pupils, and a healthy skin color. The baby's Apgar scores were 8 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes post-delivery. While discussing the assessment findings with the medical students, the pediatrician questions which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: The Apgar score at 5 minutes is more predictive of later neurodevelopmental prognosis than the Apgar score at 1 minute.

options.label: B
options.text: Anemia may be caused by a cephalhematoma.

options.label: C
options.text: It may be normal to find palpable kidneys in a newborn due to their abdominal size.

options.label: D
options.text: The presence of bilateral single palmar creases may suggest chromosomal abnormalities and could warrant a chromosome analysis.

questions.initialExplanation:
Apgar scores describe immediate adaptation and resuscitation needs; they are not reliable standalone predictors of long-term neurodevelopment.

> **Source note:** The fifth option is below the cropped lower edge of the supplied page image and is not reproduced.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The false statement is that the Apgar score at 5 minutes is more predictive of later neurodevelopmental prognosis than the Apgar score at 1 minute. While the Apgar score at 5 minutes can give an indication of the newborn's immediate health post-delivery and the need for further resuscitative measures, it does not provide a definitive long-term neurodevelopmental prognosis. Anemia due to a cephalhematoma is unlikely since a cephalhematoma is a collection of blood between the skull bone and its covering, not within the blood circulation. Palpable kidneys can indeed be normal due to the proportionally larger abdominal organs in newborns. Bilateral single palmar creases can be associated with chromosomal abnormalities, but not all cases warrant a chromosome analysis. Edema of the feet and hands could be a sign of various conditions, including Turner syndrome, which is not present in males, and this discrepancy can be a teaching point about sex-linked genetic conditions.

questions.stem: A newborn delivered vaginally after a prolonged labor is noted to have a significant swelling on the head. The parents are concerned and inquire about the nature of the swelling and its implications. Which of the following statements is true regarding Caput succedaneum in this infant?

options.label: C
options.text: It is subcutaneous extra-periosteal fluid collection.

options.label: D
options.text: It is confined to suture lines.

questions.initialExplanation:
Caput is superficial edema that crosses sutures and resolves over days; cephalohematoma is subperiosteal and stays over one bone.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Caput succedaneum is an edema of the scalp at the neonate's presenting part caused by pressure during delivery.
