It is characterized by extra-periosteal fluid collection, which is not confined to suture lines, allowing it to cross them, distinguishing it from cephalohematoma, which is sub-periosteal. Caput succedaneum typically resolves over the first several days of life, does not cause anemia, and is not a hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 1-day-old infant who was born by a difficult forceps delivery is alert and active. She does not move her left arm spontaneously or during a Moro reflex. Rather, she prefers to maintain it internally rotated by her side with the forearm extended and pronated. The rest of her physical examination is normal. This clinical scenario most likely indicates which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation:
The classic internally rotated shoulder with an extended, pronated forearm is Erb-Duchenne palsy, usually involving C5–C6 roots.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In a difficult delivery in which traction is applied to the head and neck, several injuries, including all those listed in the question, may occur. Erb-Duchenne paralysis affects the fifth and sixth cervical nerves; the affected arm cannot be abducted or externally rotated at the shoulder, and the forearm cannot be supinated. Injury to the seventh and eighth cervical and first thoracic nerves (Klumpke paralysis) results in palsy of the hand and also can produce Horner syndrome. Fractures in the upper limb are not associated with a characteristic posture, and passive movement usually elicits pain. Spinal injuries cause complete paralysis below the level of injury. When paralysis of an upper extremity from injury to the brachial plexus is found in a neonate, injury to the phrenic nerve should also be suspected because the nerve roots are close together and can be injured concurrently. The paralyzed diaphragm can be noted to remain elevated on a chest x-ray taken during deep inspiration when it will contrast with the opposite normal diaphragm in its normal position; on expiration, this asymmetry cannot be seen. On inspiration, not only is breathing impaired since the paralyzed diaphragm does not contract, but also the negative pressure generated by the intact diaphragm pulls the mediastinum toward the normal side, impairing ventilation further. The diagnosis can easily be made by fluoroscopy, where these characteristic movements on inspiration and expiration can be seen. Rarely, both diaphragms can be paralyzed, producing much more severe ventilatory impairment. Fortunately, these injuries frequently improve spontaneously.

questions.stem: A newborn is noted to have a characteristic arm posture immediately after birth. The pediatrician observes the arm to be adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder, with the forearm extended and pronated. In discussing this condition with the parents, which of the following statements about this newborn's condition is NOT TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: If paralysis persists without improvement for 3–6 months, surgery is needed.

options.label: B
options.text: The cause is difficult labor that stretched the nerves which result in either edema, hemorrhage, & rarely laceration.

options.label: C
options.text: Gentle massage and range of motion exercises are started 7–10 days after delivery.

options.label: D
options.text: It is not a serious problem and prognosis depends on the cause.

options.label: E
options.text: The affected nerve roots are C7 and C8.

questions.initialExplanation:
Erb palsy classically affects C5–C6, so the statement that the roots are C7–C8 is false.

---

## Congenital Anomalies and Potter Sequence
questions.detailedExplanation: The condition shown in the image is consistent with a brachial plexus injury, specifically Erb's palsy, which involves nerve roots C5 and C6 more commonly than C7 and C8.

questions.stem: A newborn infant is noted to have a peculiar face with low-set ears and widely spaced eyes with epicanthic folds. The chin is receding, and the nose is broad and flat. Oligohydramnios was noted prior to delivery. Examination of the placental membranes reveals amnion nodosum. Which of the following diagnoses should be suspected?
questions.initialExplanation:
Severe oligohydramnios with Potter facies points to absent fetal kidneys, which reduce fetal urine production.

---

## Neonatal Seizures and Neurologic Conditions
questions.detailedExplanation: Amnion nodosum (granules on the amnion) suggests oligohydramnios, which, in conjunction with the “Potter facies” described, is characteristic of bilateral renal agenesis. Esophageal atresia often is associated with polyhydramnios, not oligohydramnios. None of the features of this case are suggestive of congenital heart disease or infection.

questions.stem: A newborn baby girl, just 36 hours old, is observed by the nursing staff in the neonatal unit to have recurrent episodes of twitching movements in her right arm and leg. These episodes last for about 1–2 minutes each and occur several times over a few hours. The baby was born at 38 weeks via emergency cesarean section due to fetal distress and had a low Apgar score at birth, which required brief resuscitation. Regarding neonatal seizures, one of the following seizure types is frequently not associated with electrographic discharges?
questions.initialExplanation:
Subtle neonatal seizure-like movements often do not have a matching EEG discharge, unlike the more clearly epileptic seizure types listed.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Spasms, focal clonic, focal tonic, and generalized myoclonic seizures are, as a rule, associated with electrographic discharges (epileptic seizures), whereas motor automatisms, the subtle, generalized tonic, and multifocal myoclonic episodes are frequently not associated with discharges and thus are thought to often represent release phenomena with abnormal movements secondary to brain injury rather than true epileptic seizures.

questions.stem: A consultant in the neonatal intensive care unit is recommending a trial of pyridoxine for a patient. Which of the following problems in a newborn infant might respond to a pharmacologic dose of pyridoxine?
questions.initialExplanation:
Rare pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy causes seizures that may respond to high-dose vitamin B6.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: So-called pyridoxine dependency is a group of rare, inborn metabolic errors that cause severe neonatal seizures that respond to pharmacologic (as opposed to physiologic) doses of pyridoxine. Although the disorder is extremely rare, it has given rise to the practice of sometimes empirically administering an intravenous dose of pyridoxine to infants with unexplained and otherwise uncontrollable seizures.

questions.stem: A full-term newborn is admitted to the neonatal ICU with recurrent seizures. The medical team is preparing to administer medication to control the acute seizure activity. Based on standard neonatal care, which medication is typically used first-line in this situation?
questions.initialExplanation:
Phenobarbital is the usual first-line medication for acute neonatal seizures in the source's teaching context.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Phenobarbital is often the initial drug of choice for the control of acute neonatal seizures. It is a long-acting barbiturate with anticonvulsant properties. Its efficacy, long half-life, and extensive experience with use in the neonatal population make it the preferred initial treatment for seizures in newborns. Other anticonvulsants like diazepam, midazolam, lorazepam, and phenytoin are also used in neonates, but they are not typically the first line of treatment for acute seizure control.

questions.stem: A term infant is now 10 hours of age and has a seizure. Which of the following diagnoses is more common among term rather than premature infants?
questions.initialExplanation:
Birth-related subdural bleeding is more characteristic of term infants, whereas intraventricular hemorrhage is classically associated with prematurity.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Clinically significant subdural hemorrhage in the neonatal period is typically a traumatic lesion. The majority of cases have involved full-term infants. Intraventricular hemorrhages occur primarily in premature infants. Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn can occur in either premature or term infants who do not receive vitamin K prophylaxis, but is more common in term infants. Both congenital infection and neonatal sepsis are more common in premature than term infants.

questions.stem: During a teaching round in the neonatal unit, a neonatologist discusses seizure presentations in neonates. The team is asked about the signs of subtle seizures. Which of the following is NOT typically associated with subtle neonatal seizures?
questions.initialExplanation:
Subtle neonatal seizures can produce eye, mouth, and autonomic changes; hypotension is not a typical listed feature.

---

## Newborn Skin Conditions
questions.detailedExplanation: Subtle seizures in neonates may not include the convulsive movements commonly associated with seizures in older children and adults. Instead, they can present with specific signs such as blinking, mouthing, eye deviation, and sometimes alterations in heart rate. Hypotension is not a typical sign of a subtle seizure and may indicate other serious conditions such as sepsis or cardiovascular compromise.

questions.stem: A healthy newborn is noted to have numerous 3 mm vesicles on the chest and neck, along with several similar-sized hyperpigmented macules in the same distribution. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Transient neonatal pustular melanosis causes small pustules that leave temporary dark macules and is usually harmless.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is a benign lesion. It initially appears as pustules without erythema and evolves into ruptured pustules with scale surrounding a hyperpigmented macule. The hyperpigmented macules can last up to 3 months. They typically cluster under the chin, forehead, neck, or lower back. Pustules may have already ruptured at the time of birth. They are somewhat more common in infants with greater amounts of skin pigment.

questions.stem: A full-term newborn has a diffuse rash on the day of anticipated discharge. You diagnose erythema toxicum and must discuss this finding with the parents. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: More common among term than premature infants

options.label: B
options.text: Usually associated with fever and a general toxic state

options.label: C
options.text: Uncommon before the fifth day of life

options.label: D
options.text: Usually associated with an elevated peripheral white blood cell count

options.label: E
options.text: Manifested in less than 10% of newborns

questions.initialExplanation:
Erythema toxicum is a common, harmless rash of healthy term newborns, usually appearing in the first few days.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Erythema toxicum is a benign condition seen in 30%–70% of normal, term infants. It is much less common among premature infants, particularly those weighing less than 2500 g. The skin lesions usually appear within the first 3 days of life and are not associated with any systemic signs or symptoms. They typically last less than 7 days. Infants are afebrile, and the peripheral white blood cell counts are normal. The rash presents with one or more of three types of skin lesions including erythematous macules, wheals, and vesiculopustules on an erythematous base.

questions.stem: A healthy 2-day-old female infant is undergoing a routine physical examination before discharge from the hospital. The examining pediatrician notes the presence of fine hair on the baby's back, a faint pink rash on the cheeks, a small bluish area on the sacrum, petechial spots on the trunk and a birthmark resembling a strawberry on the back of the neck. Which of the following findings in this baby is worrisome?

options.label: A
options.text: The fine hair on her back

options.label: B
options.text: The pink rash on her cheeks

options.label: D
options.text: The petechial spots on her trunk

options.label: E
options.text: The bluish area on the sacrum

questions.initialExplanation:
Lanugo, erythema toxicum, strawberry hemangiomas, and Mongolian spots can be normal; petechiae need evaluation.

---

## Neonatal Brain Injury and Imaging
questions.detailedExplanation: Lanugo hair, erythema toxicum, strawberry nevi, and Mongolian blue spots are all common and typically benign findings on a newborn's skin. A petechial rash, however, is not a normal finding and may indicate a more serious condition such as an infection, coagulation disorder, or other medical issues that warrant further investigation.

questions.stem: A 30-day-old, former 24-weeks gestation, 600 g neonate had a difficult initial respiratory course complicated by a tension pneumothorax. She had serial head ultrasound evaluations during the first weeks of life. All previous studies revealed a normal immature brain. Now, the head ultrasound reveals an abnormality. Among the following, which is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation:
PVL is white-matter injury around the ventricles, especially in very premature infants, and may become visible on ultrasound weeks after birth.

---

## Neonatal Resuscitation and Drug Effects
questions.detailedExplanation: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) is characterized by focal necrotic lesions in the periventricular white matter. Cranial ultrasound can detect focal echo densities and/or cystic lesions surrounding the lateral ventricles that are diagnostic of PVL. Other imaging techniques may be needed to detect more diffuse injury. These lesions are rarely found in infants greater than 32 weeks gestation. Premature infants are predisposed to the development of PVL due to the complex interaction between the cerebral vasculature and regulation of cerebral blood flow that is gestational age dependent. Actively differentiating or myelinating periventricular glial cells are also vulnerable to injury. The findings of PVL may not be evident until 1 month of age or later. Congenital anomalies of the brain and intraventricular hemorrhage usually are readily apparent on imaging in the first days of life.

questions.stem: An infant who appears to be of normal size is noted to be lethargic and somewhat limp after birth. The mother is 28 years old, and this is her fourth delivery. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, with normal fetal monitoring prior to delivery. Labor was rapid, with local anesthesia and intravenous meperidine (Demerol) administered for maternal pain control. Which of the following therapeutic maneuvers is likely to improve this infant's condition most rapidly?

options.label: A
options.text: Intravenous infusion of 10% dextrose in water

options.label: D
options.text: Measurement of electrolytes and magnesium levels

questions.initialExplanation:
Meperidine crosses the placenta and can depress the newborn's breathing and alertness. Naloxone reverses opioid effects after initial resuscitation steps.

---

## Neonatal Sepsis and Infection
questions.detailedExplanation: In the description provided, the most likely cause of the neonatal depression is maternal analgesic narcotic drug administration. While controlling the pain of delivery in the mother, use of narcotics can result in depression of the newborn via crossing the placenta. The appropriate first step in the management of this infant (after managing the ABCs of airway, breathing, and circulation) is the administration of naloxone, 0.1 mg/kg, IM, IV, or endotracheal. The other possibilities are unlikely, given the clinical information provided.

questions.stem: A mother brings her 2-week-old newborn to the emergency department for fever, fussiness, and poor feeding. The infant is febrile and irritable and has a cluster of vesicles with an erythematous base at the site of an intrauterine scalp probe. In addition to admission and an appropriate diagnostic workup, what is the best option for the initial empiric intravenous antibiotic regimen?
questions.initialExplanation:
A febrile 2-week-old infant with vesicles needs coverage for neonatal bacteria and HSV, so the source regimen combines ampicillin, cefotaxime, and acyclovir.

> **Source note:** The option list is cropped in the source page image; the correct combination and letter B are clearly shown in the green answer panel.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: A febrile infant less than 2 months of age is at increased risk for life-threatening conditions, including urinary tract infections, sepsis, and meningitis. The baby described in the vignette is fussy, feeding poorly, febrile, and has a vesicular rash. A complete workup should be done including analysis and culture of blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A polymerase chain reaction assay for herpes simplex virus (HSV) should also be performed on the CSF. Group B Streptococcus remains the major bacterial cause of sepsis and meningitis in neonates. Early-onset disease occurs in the first 6 days of life, while late-onset disease can present between 7 and 90 days of life. Listeria monocytogenes is an additional pathogen that can infect children during the first month of life. HSV is a concern for the baby in the vignette who is irritable and has vesicular lesions. HSV is typically passed to infants at the time of delivery and becomes symptomatic within the first 2 weeks of life. Neonatal HSV can present in three different forms: disseminated disease; localized central nervous system disease; or localized to skin, eyes, and mucosa. The optimal empiric antibiotic regimen should cover the most likely etiologies for the patient's presentation. Cefotaxime covers GBS and provides additional coverage for gram-negative pathogens. Ampicillin adds additional GBS coverage as well as specific activity against Listeria. Acyclovir is included for the specific concern of HSV infection and prevention of disseminated disease. (A) Vancomycin offers broad-spectrum activity against gram-positive organisms, but does not cover gram-negative organisms, such as Escherichia coli. (C) Ampicillin and gentamicin together are an effective and traditional antibiotic regimen for neonatal sepsis, but does not provide any coverage for HSV. (D) Gentamicin and metronidazole together is a reasonable regimen for abdominal infections in older children. (E) There is no need to add fluconazole, as the baby in the vignette does not have any signs or symptoms suggesting a fungal etiology.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman, G2P1, at 37 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in active labor. Her previous pregnancy was complicated by an infection with Group B Streptococcus (GBS), leading to neonatal sepsis. She has received routine prenatal care but has not been tested for GBS colonization during this pregnancy. She is now experiencing regular contractions, and the fetal heart rate is stable. Given her medical history and current presentation, what is the most appropriate management to prevent GBS infection in the newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Obtain a vaginal swab for GBS culture.

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain a vaginal swab for GBS culture and administer intrapartum intravenous ampicillin.

questions.initialExplanation:
A previous infant with GBS disease is an indication for antibiotics during labor, even without a current culture result.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: For a woman with a history of GBS bacteriuria or a previous infant with GBS disease, the CDC recommends intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent early-onset GBS disease in the newborn, regardless of the current GBS colonization status. Administering intravenous ampicillin during labor is the standard approach to reduce the risk of transmitting GBS to the baby.

questions.stem: A term infant is delivered vaginally to an 18-year-old primigravida after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Mother presented with rupture of membranes and a low-grade fever. Labor and delivery proceeded rapidly, maternal antibiotics were not administered prior to delivery, and maternal screening during pregnancy for group B streptococcus was negative. At 30 hours of age the infant is mottled, not feeding well, and cries when handled. A lumbar puncture is performed and the spinal fluid reveals 660 WBC/mm3 and a CSF protein of 290 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely agent causing this infant's infection?
questions.initialExplanation:
GBS is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis; a negative prenatal screen does not eliminate risk if maternal risk factors develop.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The most common cause of neonatal meningitis is group B streptococcus (GBS). Escherichia coli generally is the second leading cause. Listeria is less frequent but not uncommon. Haemophilus influenzae and S. pneumoniae are uncommon causes of meningitis during the first month of life. GBS is usually vertically transmitted from the mother either at delivery or from ascending transmission after rupture of membranes. The risk for neonatal infection increases in the presence of prematurity, prolonged rupture of membranes, intrapartum fever, chorioamnionitis, and maternal GBS bacteriuria. Vaginal colonization of GBS (or absence of colonization) may be transient, so screening cultures are not 100% predictive of status at delivery.

questions.stem: An 8-day-old, 2200 g male neonate is brought to the physician due to poor feeding and irritability. Born at 36 weeks' gestation following premature rupture of membranes, he had Apgar scores of 5 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The baby now appears lethargic, with a temperature of 38.5°C, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Examination reveals scleral icterus and nasal flaring, with prolonged capillary refill time. Pending laboratory tests and chest X-ray, the clinical picture raises a high suspicion for neonatal sepsis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation:
A sick neonate with fever, poor feeding, lethargy, and poor perfusion needs prompt empiric IV antibiotics; the source regimen is ampicillin plus gentamicin.

---

## Respiratory Distress and RDS
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical signs suggest the possibility of neonatal sepsis, which requires prompt empirical antibiotic therapy while awaiting culture results. Ampicillin and gentamicin are commonly used together as initial therapy for neonatal sepsis due to their broad coverage of bacteria typically responsible for this condition. Surfactant therapy is indicated for respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant deficiency, phototherapy for neonatal jaundice, and metalloporphyrins are not standard treatment for sepsis. Endotracheal intubation may be necessary if the infant's respiratory status worsens, but the immediate priority is to address the potential infection.

questions.stem: You are formulating a differential diagnosis for a newborn infant with respiratory distress. Which of the following is most closely associated with the development of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease)?
questions.initialExplanation:
The less mature the lungs, the greater the risk of surfactant deficiency and neonatal RDS.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Prematurity is the strongest predisposing factor for surfactant deficiency disease or respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). While low birth weight infants are also at risk, the risk is more related to the gestational age of the infant. Maternal diabetes can predispose newborns to RDS by causing delayed surfactant release compared with infants of comparable gestational age, but it is not as strong a risk as prematurity itself. Cesarean delivery predisposes more to transient tachypnea of the newborn, related to excessive fluid retention within the lungs. Meconium in the amniotic fluid may cause respiratory disease if aspirated into the infant's lungs, but the pathophysiology differs from RDS.

questions.stem: A full-term newborn male presents with grunting, nasal flaring, and cyanosis shortly after birth. His prenatal history is significant for a mother with diabetes. An X-ray of the chest suggests the presence of a reticulogranular pattern with air bronchograms. Regarding hyaline membrane disease, the risk increases with all of the following, Except:
questions.initialExplanation:
RDS is mainly related to immature surfactant production. Infection is not listed as a primary risk factor in this source.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Hyaline membrane disease, also known as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), is primarily a disease of preterm infants. The risk is increased by factors associated with surfactant deficiency like prematurity, diabetic birth, or a history of previously affected infants. Multiple births and cesarean section delivery without labor are also risk factors as they may lead to reduced stress-induced surfactant release. Cold stress and asphyxia can exacerbate respiratory distress, but they are not primary causes of RDS. Congenital infection is not directly associated with an increased risk of developing hyaline membrane disease, which is why it is the correct answer in this scenario.

questions.stem: A premature infant is now 4 hours old and you suspect respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease). Which of the following is the least likely first clinical presentation of respiratory distress syndrome?
questions.initialExplanation:
RDS is characterized by grunting, retractions, cyanosis, and rapid breathing; wheezing is not a typical first finding.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Tachypnea, retractions, cyanosis, and grunting are common findings in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). Pallor and poor perfusion may also be present but are not the most common initial manifestation. Wheezing is not a feature of RDS. The clinical findings relate to the pathogenesis of the disease, which primarily is atelectasis due to collapse of the terminal airways caused by surfactant deficiency.

questions.stem: A term, 4200-g (9-lb, 4-oz) female infant is delivered via cesarean section because of cephalopelvic disproportion. The amniotic fluid was clear, and the infant cried almost immediately after birth. Within the first 15 minutes of life, however, the infant's respiratory rate increased to 80 breaths per minute, and she began to have intermittent grunting respirations. The infant was transferred to the level 2 nursery and was noted to have an oxygen saturation of 94%. The chest radiograph revealed fluid in the fissures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
A term infant after cesarean delivery with fluid in the fissures on chest X-ray most likely has transient tachypnea from retained fetal lung fluid.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Transient tachypnea of the newborn is usually seen after a normal vaginal or, especially, after a cesarean delivery. The condition is a result of retained fetal lung fluid. These patients have tachypnea, retractions, grunting, and sometimes cyanosis. The chest examination is usually normal; the chest radiograph demonstrates prominent pulmonary vascular markings with fluid in the fissures and hyperexpansion (flat diaphragms). Therapy is supportive, with maintenance of normal oxygen saturation. Resolution usually occurs in the first 3 days of life. Diaphragmatic hernia would demonstrate intestinal contents located in the chest on plain radiograph. Meconium aspiration would present in a patient who was born with meconium at delivery and the radiograph would have patchy infiltrates. Pneumonia in a patient of this age is more likely to have diffuse infiltrates on radiography and clinical findings of temperature instability. Idiopathic respiratory distress syndrome occurs in premature infants whose radiographs demonstrate a “ground glass” appearance.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after a cesarean delivery at term, a 4630-gram male neonate is noted to have signs of respiratory distress. The pregnancy was complicated by gestational diabetes, which was managed with diet and insulin. The baby's Apgar scores were 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The baby exhibits grunting and moderate intercostal retractions, and oxygen saturation is 88% in room air. A chest X-ray suggests showed increased lung volume and fluid in the interlobar fissures. The team is considering the best initial management for this baby. What should be the most appropriate next step?
questions.initialExplanation:
TTN usually improves with observation and oxygen support; more invasive respiratory support is reserved for worsening or persistent distress.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The neonate's presentation is consistent with transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), which is common in infants of diabetic mothers and those delivered by cesarean section without labor. The initial management of TTN typically includes supportive care such as supplemental oxygen and observation. The use of CPAP or endotracheal intubation is reserved for infants who do not respond to initial supportive measures or who have worsening respiratory function.

questions.stem: You are examining the chest X-ray of a 4-hour-old infant born at 30 weeks gestation. The infant is breathing 100 times per minute while breathing 100% oxygen and intubation is imminent. You suspect respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is the characteristic roentgenographic finding of the infant with respiratory distress syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: Diffuse reticulogranular changes and air bronchograms

questions.initialExplanation:
RDS produces low-volume lungs with a diffuse ground-glass/reticulogranular pattern and visible air bronchograms.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The characteristic chest x-ray findings in infants with respiratory distress syndrome include reduced lung volumes, air bronchograms, reticulogranularity, and lung opacification. The x-ray appearance is frequently characterized as a homogeneous ground glass appearance. These changes are presumed to represent diffuse alveolar atelectasis which increases lung density. Air-filled bronchi (ie, air bronchograms) then stand out against the opaque lung tissue. Lobular densities are infrequent. Pneumothorax does occur as a complication of the disease or its treatment, but not in association with patchy densities.

questions.stem: A 770-gram female infant is born prematurely at 28 weeks' gestation via emergency cesarean section. She presents with respiratory distress characterized by rapid breathing, grunting, cyanosis, and subcostal retractions shortly after birth. Her mother did not receive any prenatal care. On auscultation, breath sounds are decreased, and a chest X-ray reveals diffuse fine reticular densities bilaterally. To the team discussing the case, the pediatrician asks which antenatal intervention could have most likely prevented this infant's current respiratory condition.
questions.initialExplanation:
Antenatal betamethasone accelerates fetal lung maturation and lowers the risk and severity of RDS in an anticipated preterm delivery.

---

## Respiratory Distress and Apnea
questions.detailedExplanation: Betamethasone is a corticosteroid given antenatally to mothers at risk of preterm birth to accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). It is indicated when preterm birth is anticipated between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old infant, born at 32 weeks' gestation and weighing 1700 g (3 lb, 12 oz), has three episodes of apnea, each lasting 10 to 25 seconds and occurring after a feeding. During these episodes, the heart rate drops from 140 to 100 beats per minute, and the child remains motionless; between episodes, however, the child displays normal activity. Blood sugar is 50 mg/dL and serum calcium is normal. Which of the following is most likely true regarding the child's apneic periods?

options.label: A
options.text: They are due to an immature respiratory center.

options.label: B
options.text: They are a part of periodic breathing.

options.label: E
options.text: They are evidence of underlying pulmonary disease.

questions.initialExplanation:
Apnea of prematurity occurs because the respiratory control center is immature. The brief 3–10-second pauses of periodic breathing are different from the longer events in the question.

> **Source note:** The same question and explanation are repeated across PDF pages 26–27; it is included once.

---

## Neonatal Oral Infection
questions.detailedExplanation: Apneic episodes are characterized by an absence of respirations for more than 20 seconds and may be accompanied by bradycardia and cyanosis. A large number of conditions can cause apnea. Periods of apnea are generally thought to be secondary to an incompletely developed respiratory center, particularly when they are seen, as is common, associated with prematurity. Although seizures, hypoglycemia, and pulmonary disease accompanied by hypoxia can lead to apnea, these causes are less likely in the infant described, given that no unusual movements occur during the apneic spells, the blood sugar level is more than 40 mg/dL, and the child appears well between episodes. Other, less common, explanations for central apnea include congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (formerly known as Ondine's curse), Arnold-Chiari malformations, and congenital infections. Periodic breathing, a common pattern of respiration in low-birth-weight babies, is characterized by recurrent breathing pauses of 3 to 10 seconds.

questions.stem: A 7-day-old infant develops white, cheesy patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa with mild inflammation of the mucosa. Which of the following organisms is most likely the cause of these oral lesions?
questions.initialExplanation:
White curd-like plaques on the tongue and cheeks of a young infant are typical of oral candidiasis (thrush).

---

## Prematurity and Neonatal Complications
questions.detailedExplanation: The findings described are typical of thrush (oral infection with C. albicans), which is common in young infants. Although E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and group B streptococcus are all important pathogens in the neonatal period, they typically are not associated with pharyngeal infection or oral exudate. Group A streptococcus is a common cause of exudative tonsillitis in the older child but is an extremely rare pathogen in the newborn infant likely due to maternally acquired antibody. Additionally, the exudate noted with group A streptococcal infection would be in the area of the tonsils rather than on the buccal mucosa.

questions.stem: In the neonatal intensive care unit, a prematurely born infant is being managed for various health issues. The neonatologist explains to the parents the common complications that premature infants might experience. Which of the following is NOT typically a complication of prematurity?
questions.initialExplanation:
Premature infants are prone to temperature instability, lung complications, NEC, and hypoglycemia; polycythemia is the exception in this question.

---

## Respiratory Distress and ROP
questions.detailedExplanation: Polycythemia is not a common complication of prematurity. It is characterized by an increased number of red blood cells and can occur in various conditions but is not typically associated with prematurity. Complications of prematurity include hypothermia due to a lack of adequate fat stores and the inability to regulate body temperature; pneumothorax due to the fragility of the lung tissue; necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious intestinal disease; and hypoglycemia due to immature stores and regulation of glucose.

questions.stem: A 30-week-gestation infant with respiratory distress syndrome is weaning from the ventilator. He currently has an oxygen saturation of 100% while breathing 50% oxygen on minimal ventilator settings. In a premature infant with respiratory distress syndrome, which of the following may be an adverse effect of supplemental oxygen therapy?
questions.initialExplanation:
Excess oxygen exposure in premature infants can contribute to abnormal retinal vessel development and retinopathy of prematurity.

---

## Congenital Infections
questions.detailedExplanation: Although the pathophysiologic process in the development of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is not completely understood, several factors have been associated with this disease. Although hypoxia may increase the risk and severity of ROP, hyperoxia and oxygen radicals also have an association with increased risk of this disease. Arterial oxygenation should be closely monitored in the premature infant. Oxygen alone is not the only predisposing factor; acidosis, apnea of prematurity, anemia, nutritional status, and alterations in cerebral perfusion are other associated factors.

questions.stem: A newborn is brought to the pediatric clinic with multiple concerning symptoms. The infant has bilateral cataracts and microphthalmia (abnormally small eyes), intrauterine growth retardation, and hemorrhagic skin lesions scattered throughout the body. Additionally, a harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, which radiates to the lung fields. Given these findings, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Cataracts plus growth restriction, blueberry-muffin rash, and congenital heart disease strongly suggest congenital rubella.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Congenital rubella infection affects all organ systems. Infants will be small, with intrauterine growth retardation. They may also manifest cataracts, microphthalmia, myocarditis, and a red or purple macular rash (“blueberry muffin” rash). Structural heart defects (such as a patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary artery stenosis, and septal defects) are typical of congenital rubella, not the other TORCH infections. Laboratory abnormalities may include a hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia, elevated liver functions, and pleocytosis in the spinal fluid. Affected children do not have a good prognosis. Congenital rubella is not commonly seen in developed countries with high immunization rates.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old newborn boy was born full term by normal, spontaneous vaginal delivery. His parents have no concerns since birth and are getting ready for discharge from the nursery. The results from his screening otoacoustic emissions test show that he did not pass. Of the following, what is the most likely infectious cause for acquired sensorineural hearing loss?
questions.initialExplanation:
CMV is the leading infectious cause of acquired sensorineural hearing loss in children.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: CMV is the most common infectious cause of acquired sensorineural hearing loss. A significant number of children are born in the United States with CMV infection; most have no obvious sequelae. Those with sequelae may present with microcephaly, intracerebral calcifications, intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, petechiae or purpura, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and seizures. Toxoplasma gondii is a bacterial infection transmitted through cat feces. Symptomatic infants may have microcephaly, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, and seizures. Treponema pallidum is the causative agent of syphilis and transmission may occur at any time throughout pregnancy. Infants may have mucocutaneous lesions, eczema-like rash, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, osteochondritis, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia. Congenitally transmitted rubella can result in congenital sensorineural hearing loss; however, CMV remains the most common infectious cause for acquired sensorineural hearing loss. Other symptoms of congenital rubella include cataracts, retinitis pigmentosa, glaucoma, microcephaly, and congenital heart disease such as persistent ductus arteriosus and pulmonary artery stenosis. Herpes simplex virus is most often transmitted during vaginal delivery. Symptoms include meningitis, lung and liver involvement, seizures, and vesicular skin lesions; however, hearing loss is not a commonly associated finding.

questions.stem: An infant delivered precipitously to a mother who had not received prenatal care. The infant has findings suggestive of congenital syphilis. Maternal and infant testing confirm this diagnosis. Which of the following is most suggestive of early congenital syphilis?

options.label: B
options.text: Bullous lesions of the palms and soles

questions.initialExplanation:
Bullous lesions involving the palms and soles are a characteristic clue to early congenital syphilis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Neither DIC nor dermal erythropoiesis are recognized manifestations of congenital syphilis. There are a variety of highly characteristic skin manifestations including bullous lesions on the palms and soles. Cutaneous findings of syphilis classically involve the palmar/plantar, perioral and anogenital regions. Mucous membrane involvement may present as mucous patches and snuffles. Pneumonia and hepatitis may occur but also are seen in many other neonatal infections.

questions.stem: A newborn is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with multiple concerning symptoms. The infant has been diagnosed with hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis (inflammation of the choroid and retina of the eye), intracranial calcifications, and anemia. Given these clinical findings, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications are the classic congenital toxoplasmosis triad.

---

## Congenital Airway Anomalies
questions.detailedExplanation: Toxoplasmosis can cause symptoms similar to other congenital infections, but the combination of hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications are considered the “classic triad” of toxoplasma infection in a neonate. Infection usually occurs during primary infection of the mother or as a reactivation of infection in an immune-compromised host. These infants may also display symptoms similar to other congenital infections, such as anemia, a petechial rash, organomegaly, jaundice, and seizures.

questions.stem: A 2-hour-old full-term newborn infant is noted by the nursing staff to be having episodes of cyanosis and apnea. Per nursery protocol they place an oxygen saturation monitor on him. When they attempted to feed him, his oxygen levels drop into the 60s. When he is stimulated and cries, his oxygen levels increase into the 90s. Which of the following is the most important next step to quickly establish the diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.text: Bronchoscopic evaluation of palate and larynx

questions.initialExplanation:
Choanal atresia causes nasal obstruction: cyanosis worsens during feeding and improves when the infant cries. A nasal catheter cannot pass through the blocked choana.

---

## Neonatal Visceral Trauma
questions.detailedExplanation: It is important to make the diagnosis of choanal atresia quickly because it responds to treatment but can be lethal if unrecognized and untreated. Most neonates are obligate nose breathers and cannot breathe adequately through their mouths. Infants with choanal atresia have increased breathing difficulty during feeding and sleeping and improved respirations when crying. A variety of temporizing measures to maintain an open airway have been used, including oropharyngeal airways, positioning, tongue fixation, and endotracheal intubation, but surgical correction with placement of nasal tubes is most effective. The diagnosis can be made by failure to pass a catheter through the nose to the pharynx or by checking for fog developing on a cold metal instrument placed under each nares. Bronchoscopy would help diagnose lower airway anomalies. A ventilation-perfusion scan would be appropriate if pulmonary embolism were suspected. A newborn with a hemoglobinopathy would not present as this infant did, so electrophoresis would not be helpful. An echocardiogram would be useful if cyanotic heart disease were suspected.

questions.stem: A neonate is being evaluated for abdominal distension and anemia. There is a history of difficult delivery, which raises concerns about potential visceral injury. What is the most accurate statement regarding neonatal visceral trauma?

options.label: A
options.text: They are usually seen after 10 days of birth.

options.label: B
options.text: They usually follow normal vaginal deliveries.

options.label: D
options.text: Sub-capsular hematoma of the liver is the most common.

options.label: E
options.text: They are usually diagnosed by laparotomy.

questions.initialExplanation:
Visceral injuries are uncommon but can follow difficult delivery; the liver is the most commonly injured organ, often with subcapsular hematoma.

---

## Growth and Gestational Age
questions.detailedExplanation: Neonatal visceral trauma is relatively rare and can result from a difficult delivery, especially with instrumental assistance. The most common form of visceral trauma is subcapsular hematoma of the liver. While laparotomy can be a diagnostic step, non-invasive imaging modalities like ultrasound are often used first. These types of trauma do not usually follow normal vaginal deliveries, nor are they commonly seen after 10 days of birth; they typically present earlier.

questions.stem: You are evaluating an infant born at 39 weeks gestation weighing 2000 g. Which of the following would be the appropriate classification of this infant?

options.label: D
options.text: Low birth weight and small for gestational age

options.label: E
options.text: Premature and small for gestational age

questions.initialExplanation:
At 39 weeks the infant is term, but 2000 g is low birth weight and small for gestational age.

---

## Neonatal Temperature and Early Adaptation
questions.detailedExplanation: Since the infant in question was more than 38 weeks gestational age, she is not premature. She is, however, of low birth weight (<2500 g) and is small for gestational age. This can be confirmed by the use of standard intrauterine growth charts. (Note: Answers (A), (C), and (D) are correct, but (D) is the BEST answer.)

questions.stem: A newborn is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with multiple concerning symptoms. The infant has microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, hepatosplenomegaly, marked hyperbilirubinemia, and thrombocytopenia. Given these clinical findings, which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly are classic clues to congenital CMV.

---

## Neonatal Hepatitis B Prevention
questions.detailedExplanation: Congenital cytomegalovirus is the most common sort of congenital infection, with infection estimates ranging from 0.4% to 2.4% of all live births. Many cases are asymptomatic; others may develop cytomegalic inclusion disease, a multiorgan manifestation including intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, petechiae or purpura, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications. More than half of infants with this congenital infection develop sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.stem: You are advised by the obstetrician that the mother of a baby she has delivered is a carrier of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg-positive). Which of the following is the most appropriate action in managing this infant?

options.label: B
options.text: Isolate the infant with enteric precautions.

options.label: C
options.text: Screen the mother for hepatitis B “e” antigen (HBeAg).

options.label: D
options.text: Administer hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccine to the infant.

options.label: E
options.text: Do nothing because transplacentally acquired antibody will prevent infection in the infant.

questions.initialExplanation:
Give both HBIG and hepatitis B vaccine promptly to an infant born to an HBsAg-positive mother to prevent perinatal infection.

---

## Newborn Vascular Lesions
questions.detailedExplanation: The infant of a mother who is a carrier of hepatitis B surface antigen has a significant risk of acquiring infection. This usually occurs at the time of delivery, but infection can also be acquired during pregnancy and postnatally. A small percentage of infected neonates develop acute icteric hepatitis, but the majority remain asymptomatic. Of these infected asymptomatic infants, 80% or more will develop chronic infection, the long-term consequences of which are chronic liver disease and, possibly, hepatocellular carcinoma. Combined passive-active immunoprophylaxis in the form of hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccine affords protection not only from immediate perinatal infection but also from infection that may be acquired as a result of continued exposure in the household of a chronic carrier. Immunization in this infant is indicated regardless of the presence of hepatitis B “e” antigen in the mother. It is not necessary to isolate infants born to carriers of HBsAg, and screening of neonates for HBsAg is not indicated. Testing for HBsAg and anti-HBsAg at least 1 month after the third dose of hepatitis B vaccine will determine the efficacy of these measures.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant is in your office for a well-child examination. The mother is asking you about a red macule on the infant's cheek. She describes it as getting larger over the past few weeks. You suspect this is a capillary or cavernous hemangioma. The natural history of an elevated capillary or cavernous hemangioma is best described by which of the following statements?

options.label: A
options.text: No significant change in size after birth.

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in size during the first few years after birth and then regression.

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in size during the first decade of life and then no further change.

options.label: D
options.text: A slow but progressive increase in size throughout life.

options.label: E
options.text: A slow but progressive decrease in size starting shortly after birth.

questions.initialExplanation:
Infantile hemangiomas often grow during early infancy and then gradually shrink over subsequent years; treatment is reserved for complications.

---

## Necrotizing Enterocolitis
questions.detailedExplanation: Most capillary or cavernous hemangiomas are small or even invisible at birth. During the first weeks or months of life, they begin to grow and may become very large before finally starting to regress after a few years. Spontaneous regression usually (but not invariably) is complete or nearly so. Recognition of the natural history of this lesion permits reassurance of parents and avoidance of unnecessary therapy. The best cosmetic results are achieved by natural regression. Active intervention (surgery or laser therapy) should be advised only when a complication such as trapping of platelets (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome), erosion of tissue, or impairment of a life-threatening function (eg, vision, breathing) is a problem.

questions.stem: The nurse from the level 2 neonatal intensive care nursery calls you to evaluate a baby. The infant, born at 32 weeks' gestation, is now 1 week old and had been doing well on increasing nasogastric feedings. This afternoon, however, the nurse noted that the infant has vomited the last two feedings and seems less active. Your examination reveals a tense and distended abdomen with decreased bowel sounds. As you are evaluating the child, he has a grossly bloody stool. The plain film of his abdomen demonstrates distended loops of bowel with air in the bowel wall. The next step in your management of this infant should include which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Surgical consultation for an emergent exploratory laparotomy.

options.label: B
options.text: Continued feeding of the infant, as gastroenteritis is usually self-limited.

options.label: C
options.text: Stool culture to identify the etiology of the bloody diarrhea and an infectious diseases consultation.

options.label: D
options.text: Stopping feeds, beginning intravenous fluids, ordering serial abdominal films, and initiating systemic antibiotics.

questions.initialExplanation:
Pneumatosis intestinalis and bloody stool suggest NEC. Initial treatment is bowel rest, IV fluids, gastric decompression, antibiotics, and close serial monitoring; surgery is for perforation or deterioration.

> **Source note:** The fifth option is cut off at the bottom of the scanned screen; the first four options and the correct answer D are visible.

---

## Neonatal Bleeding
questions.detailedExplanation: The infant presented in the question has necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), a potentially life-threatening disease of the neonate; the radiograph demonstrates distended loops of bowel with air in the bowel wall. NEC is more common in premature infants, but has been described in term infants as well. Although several organisms have been isolated from NEC patients, no clear cause for this condition has been identified. Patients present with feeding intolerance and a distended abdomen; about a quarter have grossly bloody stool. Pneumatosis intestinalis is found on plain radiograph of the abdomen and is diagnostic for NEC in this age group. Management depends initially on the presence or absence of perforation; if no evidence of free peritoneal air is found, the infant should be put on bowel rest with nasogastric decompression, and systemic antibiotics are initiated. Electrolytes and vital signs should be monitored closely, and serial abdominal films should be performed to evaluate for perforation. If free air is identified on plain radiographs or if the infant clinically worsens with medical management, surgical consultation is required. An exploratory laparotomy is usually performed, and any necrotic intestinal tissue is removed. Occasionally, removal of necrotic gut will result in an infant without adequate intestinal surface area to absorb nutrition, a condition known as short bowel syndrome.

questions.stem: A full-term infant is born after a normal pregnancy; delivery, however, is complicated by marginal placental separation. At 12 hours of age, the child, although appearing to be in good health, passes a bloody meconium stool. For determining the cause of the bleeding, which of the following diagnostic procedures should be performed first?

options.label: E
options.text: A platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time

questions.initialExplanation:
The Apt test distinguishes swallowed maternal blood from blood originating in the newborn.

---

## Meconium Aspiration Syndrome
questions.detailedExplanation: Hematemesis and melena are not uncommon in the neonatal period, especially if gross placental bleeding has occurred at the time of delivery. The diagnostic procedure that should be done first is the Apt test, which differentiates fetal from adult hemoglobin in a bloody specimen. The test is based upon the finding that fetal hemoglobin is alkali resistant, while adult hemoglobin will convert to hematin upon exposure to alkali. If the blood in an affected infant's gastric contents or stool is maternal in origin, further workup of the infant is obviated.

questions.stem: A 3200-g (7 lb 1-oz) female neonate develops respiratory distress ten minutes after a cesarean delivery at 42 weeks' gestation. The delivery was complicated by oligohydramnios and meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Despite high Apgar scores, the infant shows signs of respiratory distress and an X-ray reveals findings suggestive of meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). Given these clinical findings, which intervention is most appropriate for managing this newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Administration of surfactant via endotracheal tube

options.label: E
options.text: Administration of intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin

questions.initialExplanation:
Initial care for meconium aspiration is supportive, with oxygen as needed; other interventions depend on complications.

---

## Neonatal Seizure Prognosis
questions.detailedExplanation: The treatment for meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS) typically involves supportive care, including supplemental oxygen to maintain adequate oxygenation. While surfactant therapy may be used in some cases of severe MAS with RDS, the initial step in management would be to provide oxygen. The other options are not indicated in this scenario without further evidence of complications such as infection (which would necessitate antibiotics) or persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (which might be treated with medications such as indomethacin).

questions.stem: A neonatologist is counselling the parents of a newborn who experienced seizures shortly after birth. The parents are understandably concerned about their infant's prognosis. Based on the neonate's current condition and type of seizures experienced, which has the most favorable prognosis?

options.label: C
options.text: Seizures after prolonged and recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia.

questions.initialExplanation:
Late hypocalcemic seizures often respond to calcium and usually have a better prognosis than seizures caused by structural, infectious, hypoxic, or recurrent metabolic injury.

---

## Birth Trauma and Respiratory Complications
questions.detailedExplanation: Infants with late hypocalcemic seizures generally have a good prognosis because these seizures are typically transient and respond well to calcium supplementation. Seizures due to other causes listed, such as congenital malformations, recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia, CNS infections, or asphyxia, are more concerning as they may indicate more severe underlying issues and are associated with a higher risk of long-term neurological impairment.

questions.stem: A term 4.3-kg infant is delivered vaginally to a 33-year-old woman with juvenile-onset diabetes. The delivery was complicated by severe shoulder dystocia and the infant experienced a brachial plexus injury with limited movement of the right arm. At 72 hours of age, the infant is noted to be tachypneic but he is pink and well perfused. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his tachypnea?

options.label: E
options.text: Cystic adenomatoid malformation of the lung

questions.initialExplanation:
The phrenic nerve can be injured along with the brachial plexus during shoulder dystocia, causing one-sided diaphragmatic paralysis and tachypnea.

---

## Neonatal Seizure Signs
questions.detailedExplanation: Brachial plexus injury results from stretching of the plexus and nerve roots. The upper roots (C5 and C6) are most vulnerable to injury. Phrenic nerve injury on the same side of the injury may occur, which results in diaphragmatic paralysis. The risks are highest for brachial plexus injury if the infant is large for gestational age and/or the labor and delivery is complicated. Respiratory distress syndrome is uncommon in term infants and almost always presents initially in the first 24 hours of life. Pulmonary hemorrhage, pneumothorax, and cystic adenomatoid malformation can cause cyanosis and respiratory distress but have no association with brachial plexus injury.

questions.stem: A 4-day-old premature infant is brought to the pediatrician by concerned parents who have observed unusual episodes which occur several times a day, often clustered together. The pediatrician is suspecting subtle seizures as the cause of his symptoms. Subtle seizures include all of the following except?
questions.initialExplanation:
The source lists eye, mouth, limb, heart-rate, blood-pressure elevation, and apnea manifestations; hypotension is the exception.

---

## Maternal Diabetes and Neonatal Hypoglycemia
questions.detailedExplanation: Subtle seizures include transient eye deviations, nystagmus, blinking, mouthing, abnormal extremity movements (rowing, swimming, bicycling, pedaling, and stepping), and fluctuations in heart rate, hypertension episodes, and apnea. Subtle seizures occur more commonly in premature than in full-term infants.

questions.stem: A full-term baby girl is born by cesarean section secondary to failure to progress to a G3P3 woman with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus. The baby's birth weight is 4.6 kg. Two hours following her delivery, the baby displays tremors and an exaggerated Moro reflex. Glucose oxidase strip analysis shows a glucose level of 30 mg/dL and serum glucose concentration is measured at 25 mg/dL. Of the following, what is the most appropriate next step in the management of this baby?

options.label: A
options.text: Observe closely and repeat serum glucose levels in 1 hour

options.label: B
options.text: Wrap the baby tightly in a blanket and place her under the infrared warming lights

options.label: C
options.text: Bring the baby to the mother for breastfeeding

options.label: D
options.text: Give the baby 0.4 units of normal insulin intramuscularly

options.label: E
options.text: Give an intravenous infusion of 8 mL of 10% glucose solution

questions.initialExplanation:
A symptomatic infant with a serum glucose of 25 mg/dL needs immediate IV dextrose, not warming alone or insulin.

---

## Birth Trauma and Hemorrhage
questions.detailedExplanation: Hypoglycemia is a common finding in infants of diabetic mothers, especially if maternal blood glucose concentrations were poorly controlled throughout pregnancy. The infant in the vignette is large for gestational age, likely secondary to increased circulating insulin concentrations during development. At birth, this increased insulin concentration is abruptly stopped but the residual insulin increases the risk of falling blood glucose concentrations in the hours following delivery. Infants at risk for hypoglycemia should be monitored with glucose oxidase strip testing every few hours in the nursery. If the strips report a glucose concentration below 40 to 50 mg/dL, confirmation with serum glucose testing should be undertaken. The infant in the vignette demonstrates clinical signs of hypoglycemia with increased tremors and an exaggerated Moro reflex. Symptomatic hypoglycemia needs to be addressed immediately with intravenous infusion of 10% dextrose solution. (A) Asymptomatic hypoglycemia can be monitored closely with repeat serum glucose levels and feeding. (B) The tremors described in the vignette are secondary to hypoglycemia rather than cold stress so wrapping the baby in a blanket and placing under warming lights would not address the underlying cause. (C) Breastfeeding should be encouraged once the acute symptomatic hypoglycemia is properly treated with glucose. (D) Administration of normal insulin would cause lower serum glucose concentrations and therefore is contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old boy in the neonatal intensive care unit has been found to have both conjunctival and retinal hemorrhages. He was born following a difficult labor that necessitated the use of forceps. Considering the birth history and clinical findings, which etiology is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.initialExplanation:
Retinal and conjunctival bleeding immediately after a difficult forceps delivery is most consistent with birth trauma.

---

## Neonatal Skin Infection
questions.detailedExplanation: Conjunctival and retinal hemorrhages in a newborn can occur as a result of birth trauma, especially with instrumental deliveries such as with forceps. The use of forceps can cause increased pressure on the baby's head, which may lead to these hemorrhages. This is more likely the cause in the immediate neonatal period rather than child abuse or hematologic conditions like vitamin K deficiency, which can also cause bleeding but are less common in the absence of other signs or risk factors.

questions.stem: A full-term, ill appearing, infant presents with vesicles and large bullae shortly at birth. Which of the following is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation:
A sick newborn with large bullae should be assessed urgently for infection; the source identifies Staphylococcus aureus as most likely.

---

## Apgar and Neurologic Prognosis
questions.detailedExplanation: The most immediate task when an infant presents with vesicles and bullae at birth is to rule out infection. Although rare in the newborn period, the infections listed can present with severe disease which may be life threatening if the infant is not adequately treated with appropriate antibacterial or antiviral therapy and supportive therapy for fluid and electrolyte issues. Decreased immune defenses and a fragile fluid and electrolyte balance can make the situation worse in the newborn period. Staphylococcus aureus infection is most likely. Herpes simplex and gram-negative infections do not generally present with bullous lesions. Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited diseases in which the skin cannot withstand friction and thus skin blistering develops, but is very rare. Severe forms of the disease can also be life threatening. Maternal diabetes is not associated with these skin findings at birth.

questions.stem: A family with an infant in the neonatal intensive care unit is very concerned that their child will have long-term neurologic abnormalities. Of the following, which correlates best with subsequent neurologic abnormalities?

options.label: E
options.text: Seizures in the first 36 hours of life

questions.initialExplanation:
Early neonatal seizures are a stronger warning sign for later neurologic problems than an isolated low Apgar score.

---

## Birth Trauma and Scalp Swelling
questions.detailedExplanation: Most infants who experience fetal bradycardia during labor are not severely asphyxiated at birth and ultimately have a good neurologic outcome. Likewise, most infants who fail to breathe initially or are cyanotic at birth and have a low 1-minute Apgar score recover promptly and do well neurologically. Although a low 5-minute Apgar score generally indicates more prolonged oxygen problems and correlates somewhat better with outcome than does the 1-minute score, most of these infants also will be normal. In contrast, a substantial population of newborns with low Apgar scores and seizures in the first 36 hours of life will show neurologic abnormalities on long-term follow-up.

questions.stem: As a medical student in the newborn nursery, you correctly identify a scalp swelling as a cephalohematoma. Your attending physician then asks you to describe how you would differentiate this from caput succedaneum. Which of the following best describes the way to differentiate a cephalohematoma from caput succedaneum?

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of a history of prolonged or difficult labor

options.label: B
options.text: Limitation of swelling to the area over one bone

questions.initialExplanation:
Cephalohematoma is subperiosteal and cannot cross suture lines, so it is limited to one bone; caput is diffuse and crosses sutures.

---

## Apgar and Newborn Assessment
questions.detailedExplanation: Both cephalohematoma and caput are associated with prolonged and difficult labor and delivery. They are also associated with a normal neurologic examination, unless there has been concomitant intracranial trauma. Caput, however, is diffuse and poorly demarcated edema of the scalp, whereas a cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal collection of blood. Therefore, a cephalohematoma is sharply demarcated and limited to a single bone. Cephalohematomas may be bilateral, but each is separate and sharply demarcated.

questions.stem: A full-term baby girl is born to a mother who has received several intravenous medications during labor including magnesium sulfate. The baby is immediately brought to the warmer and the appropriate resuscitation protocol is begun. After 1 minute, the baby is lying awake in the crib with some crying and flexion of her extremities. Her body is mostly pink but her hands and feet are blue. Her heart rate is 132 beats per minute. She grimaces with nasal suctioning. At 5 minutes of life, the baby's activity has progressed and she is now more active and vigorous. She continues to have nasal discharge and sneezes with suctioning of her nares. Her cardiac, respiratory, and skin examinations are unchanged. Of the following, which is the correct Apgar score at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively?
questions.initialExplanation:
Apgar scores combine heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex response, and color. The source key gives 7 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes.

---

## Respiratory Support
questions.detailedExplanation: The Apgar scoring system is a quick way to assess a newborn infant's transition from intrauterine to extrauterine life. The 1-minute Apgar score evaluates an infant's distress during the birthing procedure, while 5-, 10-, 15-, and 20-minute scores can act as indicators or predictors of the successful resuscitation. Apgar scores do not predict neurologic outcomes.

questions.stem: After surfactant therapy, the infant with respiratory distress syndrome is treated with continuous positive airway pressure. Which of the following is the major goal of continuous positive airway pressure?
questions.initialExplanation:
CPAP keeps alveoli open, improves functional residual capacity, and improves oxygenation, thereby increasing arterial oxygen tension.

---

## Neonatal Resuscitation and Meconium Aspiration
questions.detailedExplanation: The purpose of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is to increase the functional residual capacity and improve oxygenation by improving ventilation and perfusion mismatch. Improvement of ventilation (a decreased arterial CO2) and maintenance of an adequate cardiac output is desired when providing CPAP, but these parameters may be adversely affected if the appropriate pressure is not provided for the individual patient. Pneumothorax is one of the complications of treatment with continuous positive airway pressure. There is no evidence that continuous positive airway pressure prevents infection. To the contrary, the invasive technology (eg, endotracheal tube) often required can predispose to infection.

questions.stem: At 43 weeks' gestation, a long, thin infant is delivered. The infant is apneic, limp, pale, and covered with “pea soup” amniotic fluid. Which of the following is the best first step in the resuscitation of this infant at delivery?

options.label: A
options.text: Intubation and suction of the trachea; provision of oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: Artificial ventilation with bag and mask

questions.initialExplanation:
A depressed post-term infant with meconium-stained fluid needs immediate airway management and oxygenation; the source specifies intubation and tracheal suction for this presentation.

---

## Small-for-Gestational-Age Infants
questions.detailedExplanation: Infants who are postmature (more than 42 weeks' gestation) and show evidence of chronic placental insufficiency (low birth weight for gestational age and wasted appearance) have a higher than average chance of being asphyxiated, and passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid places these infants at risk for meconium aspiration. Ideally the obstetrician suctions the mouth, nose, and hypopharynx immediately after delivery of the infant's head but before delivery of the remainder of the body. If the infant's heart rate is more than 100 beats per minute and respirations are unlabored, routine neonatal management is appropriate. However, if the heart rate is less than 100 beats per minute in a floppy, depressed infant, then endotracheal intubation is accomplished along with suctioning and providing oxygen.

questions.stem: Two new mothers are discussing their infants outside the neonatal intensive care unit. Both were born at 36 weeks' gestation. One infant weighs 2600 g (5 lb, 12 oz) while the other infant weighs 1600 g (3 lb, 8 oz). The mother of the second infant should be told that her child is more likely to have which of the following conditions?
questions.initialExplanation:
Severe fetal growth restriction is associated with more congenital anomalies and growth-related complications than prematurity alone.

---

## Congenital Anomalies and Respiratory Distress
questions.detailedExplanation: Small-for-dates infants are subject to a different set of complications than preterm infants whose size is appropriate for gestational age. Small-for-dates infants have a higher incidence of major congenital anomalies and are at increased risk for future growth retardation, especially if length and head circumference as well as weight are small for gestational age. They are also more prone to neonatal asphyxia and meconium aspiration syndrome, which can lead to pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, or pulmonary hemorrhage. These, rather than hyaline membrane disease, are major pulmonary problems in small-for-gestational-age infants. Because neonatal symptomatic hypoglycemia is more commonly found in small-for-dates infants, careful blood glucose monitoring and early feeding are appropriate precautions. Normal or elevated hematocrit also is more common in these infants.

questions.stem: A 1-hour-old newborn boy is being evaluated for tachypnea. His prenatal history is unremarkable and the delivery was uncomplicated. On examination, he has a respiratory rate of 65 breaths/min and auscultation reveals the absence of breath sounds on the left side of the chest and his abdomen is scaphoid in shape. Of the following, which is the most likely cause for this patient's respiratory distress?
questions.initialExplanation:
A scaphoid abdomen with absent breath sounds on one side suggests abdominal organs have entered the chest through a diaphragmatic defect, impairing lung growth.

---

## Newborn Assessment and Apgar
questions.detailedExplanation: Pulmonary hypoplasia. The likely cause of the respiratory distress for the patient in the case is pulmonary hypoplasia due to a diaphragmatic hernia. A diaphragmatic hernia is a congenital abnormality in which a malformation of the diaphragm allows for the abdominal organs to move into the chest cavity, inhibiting proper lung development. The most common kind of diaphragmatic hernia is the Bochdalek hernia, in which a defect in the posterolateral corner of the diaphragm allows for passage of the abdominal organs into the chest cavity. Most diaphragmatic hernias occur on the left side. Infants present with tachypnea and respiratory distress shortly after birth. On physical examination, the abdomen is scaphoid secondary to displacement of the abdominal organs into the chest cavity. Lung auscultation demonstrates markedly decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side. Diagnosis is confirmed with chest radiography, which demonstrates bowel in the chest. Treatment is surgical. (A, B, E) Neonatal RDS, meconium aspiration syndrome, and pneumothorax all present with varying degrees of respiratory distress but are not accompanied by the physical examination findings described. (C) In dextrocardia, lung sounds should be normal, but heart sounds are auscultated on the right side of the chest.

questions.stem: A newborn with a high level of activity and a strong cry is being assessed one minute after birth. The attending physician notes a strong heart rate, reflex irritability, and overall pink coloration, but observes one parameter that seems inconsistent with the otherwise good condition of the newborn. Which of the following findings would not align with a near-perfect Apgar score of 9?
questions.initialExplanation:
Apgar assigns points for muscle tone. Limp tone scores zero and prevents a near-perfect score of 9.

---

## Newborn Assessment and Growth
questions.detailedExplanation: A limp tone gives a score of 0, which is simply incompatible with a score of 9 because even if all other parameters were perfectly normal the score would be 8. The other points mentioned can be compatible with a score of 9 if all other parameters are normal.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old female infant is brought to the pediatric clinic for a routine check-up. The parents express concern that their baby's head seems less rounded at the top than that of other babies. Upon examination, the pediatrician notes that the infant's anterior fontanelle is closed. The baby is otherwise healthy, with normal developmental milestones and a head circumference within the normal range for her age. Which of the following findings should prompt further investigation and possible interference?

options.label: A
options.text: Blue pigmented area in neonate lower back.

options.label: B
options.text: Head circumference measuring 47 cm in a one-year-old child.

options.label: D
options.text: Closed anterior fontanelle in a 4-month-old infant.

options.label: E
options.text: Vaginal discharge in a 2 days old girl.

questions.initialExplanation:
The anterior fontanelle usually remains open until roughly 12–18 months; closure at 4 months may require investigation for craniosynostosis.

> **Source note:** The stem contains the printed number “66”; the gray question marker in the PDF is 34.

---

## Neonatal Seizures and Birth Asphyxia
questions.detailedExplanation: The anterior fontanelle typically closes between 12 to 18 months of age. Early closure could indicate craniosynostosis or other underlying conditions, which might need further evaluation, including imaging studies. A blue pigmented area in the lower back is often a benign condition known as a Mongolian spot. Enlarged breasts in newborns are usually transient due to maternal hormones. Vaginal discharge in a newborn girl can occur due to maternal hormone withdrawal and is generally self-limiting.

questions.stem: A nurse in the special care nursery reports that a baby is moving strangely. The baby was delivered 12 hours ago by emergency cesarean section for nonreassuring heart tones to a G2P2 mother at 37 weeks' gestation. Apgar scores were 5 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The 1-minute Apgar score was reduced secondary to respiratory depression among other findings. He was admitted to the special care nursery for observation and has had an uneventful course until now. On examination, the baby's eyes are deviated to the right and he continues to move his hands and arms despite attempts to hold them still. His fontanelle is flat and nonbulging. He has no heart murmur and the remainder of his examination is unremarkable. Blood glucose level is 87 mg/dL. Of the following, what is the most likely cause of this baby's presentation?
questions.initialExplanation:
Eye deviation and movements that cannot be stopped by holding the infant still suggest a seizure; the low early Apgar supports birth-related hypoxia.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Infants in the neonatal period are susceptible to seizure activity for a variety of reasons, including metabolic derangements, infectious causes, and anatomic abnormalities. Tonic-clonic seizures are not the norm in this age group due to immature brain myelination that hinders electrical propagation throughout the neonatal brain. The seizures described for the patient in the vignette are caused by the most common etiology of neonatal seizures, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. This patient's hypoxic event likely occurred at birth and is reflected in the low 1-minute Apgar score.
