Long-term prognosis is good in children similar to the one in the vignette who only have a short period of hypoxia. Metabolic issues may lead to seizures in the neonatal period, but the baby in the vignette does not show any signs supporting these possibilities. (A) Hyponatremia can cause neonatal seizures and is often seen secondary to incorrect formula mixing. (B) Hypoglycemia can cause jitteriness or exaggerated startle reflexes as well as seizures and is often seen in infants of diabetic mothers. (D) Hypocalcemia does not often cause seizures within the first 5 days of life. (E) Normal neonatal jitteriness would be easily stopped with attempts to hold the infant still and would not be associated with eye deviation.

questions.stem: A neonate is evaluated in the NICU due to the onset of seizures. The healthcare team reviews the most likely etiologies to establish a targeted approach for treatment. Which of the following is the most common cause of neonatal seizures?
questions.initialExplanation:
Birth-related lack of oxygen or blood flow to the brain is the most common cause of neonatal seizures in this source.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is the most common cause of seizures in the neonatal period. HIE results from a lack of oxygen and/or blood flow to the brain around the time of birth, which can lead to seizures. Other causes include vascular events, intracranial infections, brain malformations, and metabolic disturbances, but HIE is the primary concern due to the vulnerability of the neonatal brain to hypoxia and ischemia.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old newborn boy is brought to the emergency department by his concerned parents due to episodes of unusual movements. His parents describe intermittent episodes where the baby exhibits rhythmic jerking of his limbs, lip smacking, and brief periods of unresponsiveness. The MOST common cause of neonatal seizures is?
questions.initialExplanation:
HIE is a leading cause of neonatal seizures and commonly presents during the first 12 hours after birth.

---

## Newborn Skin and Birthmarks
questions.detailedExplanation: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy is the most common cause of neonatal seizures, accounting for 50–60% of patients. Seizures secondary to this encephalopathy occur within 12 hr of birth.

questions.stem: A 1-week-old black infant presents to you for the first time with a large, fairly well-defined, purple lesion over the buttocks bilaterally. The lesion is not palpable, and it is not warm nor tender. The mother denies trauma and reports that the lesion has been present since birth. This otherwise well-appearing infant is growing and developing normally and appears normal upon physical examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action in this infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Report the family to child protective services

options.label: B
options.text: Reassurance of the normality of the condition

options.label: C
options.text: Soft tissues films of the buttocks to identify calcifications

options.label: E
options.text: Measurement of bleeding time as well as factor VII and XI levels

questions.initialExplanation:
A congenital, flat blue-gray patch over the buttocks is usually a Mongolian spot and needs reassurance, not a child-abuse workup by itself.

---

## Neonatal Jaundice and Temperature
questions.detailedExplanation: The pictured lesion is a Mongolian spot, a bluish-gray lesion located over the buttocks, lower back, and occasionally the extensor surfaces of the extremities. These are common in blacks, Asians, and Latin Americans. They tend to disappear by 1 to 2 years of age, although those on the extremities may not fully resolve. Child abuse is unlikely to present with bruises alone; children frequently present with more extensive injuries. Subcutaneous fat necrosis, which may ultimately result in subcutaneous calcifications in the affected area, is usually found as a sharply demarcated, hard lesion on the cheeks, buttocks, and limbs but is usually red. Hemophilia and vitamin K deficiency rarely present with subcutaneous lesions as described and are more likely to present as a bleeding episode.

questions.stem: Parents bring a 5-day-old infant to your office. The mother is O negative and was Coombs positive at delivery. The term child weighed 3055 g (6 lb, 1 oz) at birth and had measured baseline hemoglobin of 16 g/dL and a total serum bilirubin of 3 mg/dL. He passed a black tar-like stool within the first 24 hours of life. He was discharged at 30 hours of life with a stable axillary temperature of 36.5°C (97.7°F). Today the infant's weight is 3000 g, his axillary temperature is 35°C (95°F), and he is jaundiced to the chest. Parents report frequent yellow, seedy stool. You redraw labs and find his hemoglobin is now 14 g/dL, and his total serum bilirubin is 13 mg/dL. The change in which of the following parameters is of most concern?
questions.initialExplanation:
Weight loss and a bilirubin rise can occur during normal transition. A low temperature in a term newborn is concerning for infection.

---

## Newborn Assessment and Gestational Age
questions.detailedExplanation: There is a loss of body weight of 1.5% to 2% per day for the first 5 days of life for a normal newborn infant as excessive fluid is excreted. One might think this would tend to cause hemoconcentration and produce an increase in hematocrit, but, to the contrary, the hematocrit falls as an adaptation to an environment of higher oxygen. Infants usually have several meconium stools during the first day or two of life, changing to soft yellow stools after 1 to 2 days of life. As the hematocrit falls, there is a corresponding increase in serum bilirubin that peaks around 3 to 5 days of life. Temperature should not change; temperature instability in a term infant is frequently a sign of serious infection.

questions.stem: An infant is born precipitously to a mother without prenatal care and you are requested to determine the infant's gestational age. Of the following, which physical finding is most indicative of a full-term infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Veins and tributaries are seen over the abdomen

options.label: B
options.text: Long lanugo is present on the back

options.label: C
options.text: Palpable breast tissue of less than 1 cm

questions.initialExplanation:
The source keys the palpable breast tissue option as the full-term clue; soft, easily folded ears and abundant lanugo suggest prematurity.

> **Source note:** The keyed choice is C in the source, although the wording “less than 1 cm” is unusual beside the explanation that breast tissue is more developed in term infants.

---

## Neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus
questions.detailedExplanation: Breast hypertrophy is common in full-term infants. The less mature the infant, the smaller the amount of breast tissue. Long lanugo, translucent skin, and a soft ear pinna that does not readily recoil are indicative of prematurity. The Ballard scoring system uses physical findings such as these to determine the gestational age of the newborn. Veins and tributaries over the abdomen and pitting edema over the tibia are associated with pathological conditions and are not used in gestational age assessment.

questions.stem: During a prenatal care visit, a mother notifies you that her partner has been diagnosed with herpes simplex virus (HSV). She is asking about risks for the infant if she has HSV. Which of the following is the most important risk factors for neonatal HSV infection?

options.label: B
options.text: Cold sore on mother’s lip at time of delivery

options.label: C
options.text: Primary maternal genital infection during pregnancy

options.label: E
options.text: Rupture of membranes greater than 4–6 hours

questions.initialExplanation:
A first genital HSV infection during pregnancy carries the highest neonatal transmission risk because maternal antibodies are not yet present.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Approximately 75% of neonatal disease is due to HSV 2 (typically genital herpes). Transmission most commonly occurs at delivery due to virus in the birth canal (95%). In utero infection from ascending or transplacental passage is also possible (5%). A primary maternal genital infection is the single greatest risk for disease in the infant due to the presence of a high viral replication load, longer viral excretion, and lack of maternal antibody passage to the infant. The risk for disease in the infant during a primary maternal infection is 10–20 times higher than in the presence of maternal secondary or recurrent lesions. In most neonates with disease, there is no maternal clinical history of HSV. Prolonged rupture of membranes increases the risk of ascending infection. Fetal scalp monitoring may break the infant's skin barrier and thus is contraindicated in the presence of known maternal HSV infection. Prematurity is also a risk factor likely due to low transplacental IgG antibodies in premature infants.

questions.stem: A week-old infant is brought to the pediatric emergency department with a high fever and focal seizure. The parents are extremely concerned about their child's sudden illness. Given the clinical presentation, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Fever and focal seizures in a 1-week-old infant raise concern for neonatal HSV, which can involve the central nervous system and requires acyclovir.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Transmission of HSV from mother to newborn can happen in utero, intrapartum, and postnatally. Intrapartum transmission is most common. Infants born vaginally to a mother with a primary genital herpes infection are at highest risk for disease, with up to 50% risk of perinatal transmission. About half the infants of congenital HSV are born to mothers who are unaware of their infection. Infants can display isolated CNS involvement, isolated cutaneous infection, or systemic generalized infection. Treatment usually is with acyclovir; even with therapy, morbidity is high in infants with CNS involvement.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has cramping abdominal pain and a rash mainly on the back of his legs and buttocks as well as on the extensor surfaces of his forearms. Laboratory analysis reveals proteinuria and microhematuria. You diagnose Henoch-Schonlein, or anaphylactoid, purpura. In addition to his rash and abdominal pain, what other finding is he likely to have?
questions.initialExplanation:
HSP is an IgA small-vessel vasculitis. Along with purpura and abdominal symptoms, joint pain or arthritis is a common associated feature.

---

## Nephrotic Syndrome and Glomerular Disease
questions.detailedExplanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP), or anaphylactoid purpura, is a systemic IgA-mediated vasculitis. The rash of anaphylactoid purpura most often involves extensor surfaces of the extremities; the face, soles, palms, and trunk are less often affected. Other significant symptoms include edema, arthralgia or arthritis, colicky abdominal pain with GI bleeding, acute scrotal pain, and renal abnormalities ranging from microscopic hematuria to acute renal failure. As HSP is a systemic vasculitis, any organ system can be affected. The prognosis, however, is excellent, with only a small percentage of children going on to end-stage renal failure. Seizures are an uncommon complication of CNS involvement; more commonly, patients will complain of headache and will have behavioral changes. Unilateral lymphadenopathy and nonpurulent conjunctivitis are not typical of HSP (but are criteria for Kawasaki disease, another pediatric vasculitis).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy without significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with a swollen face, hands, and feet for the last 2 days. His mother reports he has no other complaints. She denies any new food or environmental exposures. A laboratory workup reveals hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria. Of the following, which is the next best step in the treatment of this patient?
questions.initialExplanation:
Primary childhood nephrotic syndrome is commonly due to minimal change disease and is initially treated with corticosteroids. A biopsy is usually considered when the child does not respond as expected.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Steroid therapy. Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical condition caused by massive loss of protein in the urine due to glomerular pathology, specifically injury at the epithelial cells and basement membrane. The findings include proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. The most common cause for nephrotic syndrome is minimal change disease (MCD); therefore, any child presenting with primary nephrotic syndrome is considered to have MCD and should initially be treated with steroids. (B) If the patient does not respond to steroid therapy, a renal biopsy may be warranted to assess for other potential causes of nephrotic syndrome. Patients with nephrotic syndrome are at risk for bacterial infections such as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and bacteremia due to loss of significant amounts of immunoglobulin, complement factors, and antibodies in their urine. (A) However, without any symptoms of infection, prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely used. (C) Patients with edema due to anaphylaxis require aggressive management with intramuscular or intravenous epinephrine and antihistamines. The patient in the vignette does not present with anaphylaxis. Patients with nephrotic syndrome have significant edema from loss of albumin, which leads to a decrease in oncotic pressure intravascularly. There is a subsequent fluid shift from the intravascular space to the interstitial space. Total body water may remain normal. The fluid management of patients with nephrotic syndrome can be difficult as initially the patients may be intravascularly depleted. Treatment includes replacement of albumin and the administration of diuretic medications, which result in fluid shift to the intravascular space. (D) Patients with nephrotic syndrome often need fluid and salt restriction to regulate their fluid balance. The aggressive management of fluids is needed for all cases of nephrotic syndrome, but does not treat the underlying cause of the nephrotic syndrome itself.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with a known history of nephrotic syndrome is brought to the emergency department by their parents due to fever, increasing swelling, and generalized malaise. The parents report that the child has been less active and developed a cough over the past few days. On examination, the child appears lethargic, and there is increased abdominal distension and facial puffiness. Blood pressure is within the normal range. Lab tests reveal elevated white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, and a urinary tract infection is confirmed. Children with nephrotic syndrome are especially susceptible to infections such as cellulitis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and bacteremia; all the following are contributory factors EXCEPT?
questions.initialExplanation:
Nephrotic syndrome increases infection risk through urinary loss of IgG and complement proteins, impaired opsonization, and immunosuppressive treatment. IgA urinary loss is not listed as a major mechanism here.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Children with nephrotic syndrome are indeed more susceptible to infections due to factors like urinary losses of immunoglobulin G (A), urinary loss of complement factors (B), impaired opsonization of microorganisms (C), and immunosuppressive therapy (D). However, immunoglobulin A (IgA) is primarily involved in mucosal immunity, and its urinary losses are not a significant contributory factor to the increased susceptibility to infections seen in nephrotic syndrome. The other factors listed are more directly associated with compromising the immune system in these patients.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with generalized edema, decreased urine output, and fatigue. The parents report that the child was previously healthy with no significant medical history. Laboratory tests reveal hypoalbuminemia with a serum albumin of 1 g/dL, hypercholesterolemia with a cholesterol level of 560 mg/dL, normal complement levels, and normal liver enzymes. Based on these findings, the pediatrician is considering a primary glomerular disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
A young child with edema, heavy protein loss, low albumin, high cholesterol, and normal complement levels fits minimal-change nephrotic syndrome.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Minimal-change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and is characterized by hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, and often, a normal complement level. It is typically responsive to steroid therapy, and unlike poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, it is not associated with a preceding infection. Membranous glomerulonephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis usually present later in life and have different laboratory findings. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis may present with similar symptoms but is less common than MCD in this age group and often does not respond as well to steroids.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is seen in the emergency room with edema and shortness of breath. He was previously healthy, but his mother has noted worsening edema over the past 2 weeks and over the past 2 days he appears increasingly dyspneic. Physical examination reveals mild tachypnea, periorbital edema, decreased lung sounds in the bilateral bases, and pitting edema of bilateral lower extremities. CXR reveals bilateral pleural effusions. CBC are normal. Urinalysis reveals 3+ protein. Serum albumin is markedly decreased with a value of 2 g/dL. A 24-hour urine collection reveals 4 grams of protein. Light microscopy of a kidney biopsy would most likely reveal:

options.label: B
options.text: Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane

questions.initialExplanation:
Minimal-change disease usually looks normal on light microscopy. The characteristic podocyte foot-process effacement is seen with electron microscopy.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation of a 3-year-old boy with edema, shortness of breath, significant proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and pleural effusions is highly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome. In pediatric patients, particularly those around the age of 3, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome is minimal change disease (MCD). The characteristic finding on light microscopy for MCD is typically normal. Effacement of podocyte foot processes is seen in electron microscopy, rather than light microscopy.

questions.stem: The finding of a low serum concentration of the C3 component of complement in a child with nephrotic syndrome indicates which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: A high likelihood of spontaneous remission

options.label: B
options.text: A high likelihood of good response to steroid therapy

options.label: C
options.text: The presence of focal segmental sclerosis

questions.initialExplanation:
Low C3 is atypical for minimal-change nephrotic syndrome and points toward membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis in this context.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Low serum concentration of the C3 component of complement in a child with nephrotic syndrome almost always indicates the presence of membranoproliferative disease (assuming that the child does not have a systemic lupus, endocarditis, or a shunt infection). Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is very unlikely either to respond to corticosteroids or to remit spontaneously.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old patient arrives late to your office with his father and a sign-language translator. They are very apologetic, but the father communicates that he had car trouble at his dialysis center and thus was late picking up the child from day care. The father is concerned about his child's having intermittent red, bloody-looking urine. A gross inspection of the child's urine in your office looks normal, but the dipstick demonstrates 3+ blood. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this child's hematuria?
questions.initialExplanation:
Alport syndrome can cause recurrent microscopic or visible hematuria and is associated with hereditary renal disease and hearing loss. The vignette's family clue supports this diagnosis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The most common type of hereditary nephritis is Alport syndrome. Clinically, patients present with asymptomatic microscopic hematuria, but gross hematuria is also possible, especially after an upper respiratory infection. Hearing loss, eventually leading to deafness, is associated with Alport syndrome in 30% to 75% of cases. End-stage renal disease, as hinted in the question (the father was at a dialysis center), is common by the second or third decades of life. This syndrome is most commonly an X-linked dominant disorder, which explains the more severe course in males. Other findings include ocular abnormalities (30% to 40%) and, rarely, leiomyomatosis of the esophagus or respiratory tree. Berger nephropathy (IgA nephropathy) results from IgA deposits within the mesangium of the glomerulus in the absence of systemic disease; it can be associated with microscopic or gross hematuria, but is not associated with a hereditary condition resulting in deafness and end-stage renal disease. Idiopathic hypercalciuria, which may be autosomal dominant, causes recurrent gross hematuria, persistent microscopic hematuria, and complaints of dysuria or abdominal pain without stone formation. Membranous glomerulopathy is an unusual cause of hematuria in children occurring in the second decade of life when seen; it is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It usually presents with signs and symptoms of nephrotic syndrome. Goodpasture syndrome results in pulmonary hemorrhages in addition to the signs and symptoms of glomerulonephritis; it is a rare disease in children.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents to the pediatric nephrology clinic with complaints of recurrent episodes of visible blood in his urine, particularly following upper respiratory infections. The child's parents report that these episodes have been occurring intermittently for the past few months. On examination, the child appears well and is in no acute distress. Urinalysis reveals the presence of red blood cells and proteinuria. Serum creatinine and electrolytes are within normal limits. Based on these findings, which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis for this child?
questions.initialExplanation:
IgA nephropathy often causes episodes of hematuria around the time of an upper respiratory infection, while kidney function may initially remain normal.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: IgA nephropathy is characterized by the deposition of IgA immune complexes in the glomeruli of the kidneys. It often presents with recurrent episodes of gross or microscopic hematuria, particularly following upper respiratory tract infections or other mucosal infections. Proteinuria may also be present.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old male diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome after presenting with edema and heavy proteinuria. Which of the following investigation is TRUE?
questions.initialExplanation:
In typical minimal-change nephrotic syndrome, complement levels are normal; low complement suggests another glomerular disorder.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Minimal change disease does not typically affect the complement pathway, so C3 and C4 levels remain within the normal range. This differentiates it from other glomerular diseases, such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis, which can be associated with low complement levels.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is referred to the pediatric nephrology clinic with swelling around his ankles and abdomen. His parents mention that his appetite has decreased and he has gained weight despite not eating well. Laboratory tests reveal heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia. His serum cholesterol level is noted to be elevated. The pediatric nephrologist is considering a diagnosis of childhood nephrotic syndrome. Which of the following statements is TRUE about childhood nephrotic syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Majority of childhood nephrosis is idiopathic

options.label: D
options.text: Group B-streptococcal peritonitis is a common complication

options.label: E
options.text: Associated with reduced levels of complement

questions.initialExplanation:
Most childhood nephrotic syndrome is idiopathic and commonly represents minimal-change disease. Cholesterol is usually high, and complement is usually normal.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The majority of cases of childhood nephrotic syndrome are idiopathic, meaning they have no identifiable cause and are often diagnosed as minimal change disease. It is more common in boys than in girls. In nephrotic syndrome, serum cholesterol levels are typically elevated due to the liver's increased synthesis of lipoproteins in response to hypoalbuminemia. Group B-streptococcal peritonitis is not a common complication; infections are a concern due to the loss of immunoglobulins in urine and the use of corticosteroids, but they are not typically caused by Group B strep. Childhood nephrotic syndrome is not associated with reduced levels of complement; this is more characteristic of post-infectious glomerulonephritis such as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Therefore, statement A is correct.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy and his family have recently visited a local amusement park. Several of the family members developed 'gastroenteritis' with fever and diarrhea, but the 4-year-old's stool was slightly different, as it contained blood. His mother reports that in the past 24 hours he developed pallor and lethargy; she relates that his face looks swollen and that he has been urinating very little. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hematocrit of 28% and a platelet count of 72,000/µL. He has blood and protein in the urine. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to explain these symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation:
Bloody diarrhea followed by pallor, thrombocytopenia, reduced urine output, and renal findings strongly suggests HUS, often related to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Hemolytic-uremic syndrome is most common in children younger than 4 years of age and is characterized by an acute microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia from increased platelet utilization, and renal insufficiency from vascular endothelial injury and local fibrin deposition. Ischemic changes result in renal cortical necrosis and damage to other organs such as colon, liver, heart, brain, and adrenal. Laboratory findings associated with hemolytic-uremic syndrome include low hemoglobin level, decreased platelet count, hypoalbuminemia, and evidence of hemolysis on peripheral smear (for example, helmet cells, schistocytes). Usually patients have a history of gastroenteritis, which is typically due to verotoxin-producing E. coli O157:H7, which has been implicated as a cause of hemolytic-uremic syndrome. This organism is a pathogenic E. coli. Outbreaks associated with undercooked contaminated hamburgers have been reported in several states. Roast beef, cow's milk, and fresh apple cider have been implicated as well. The symptoms are not specific to this type of hemolytic anemia. Henoch-Schonlein purpura is a vasculitis that presents with petechial-like rash on the lower extremities (but the platelet count is normal); it is not usually associated with fever, but microscopic blood in the stool or urine are possible as is colicky abdominal pain. IgA nephropathy can cause hematuria, but none of the other findings in the question typically are noted. Intussusception is seen in children of this age, but the lack of episodic colicky abdominal pain or emesis makes this diagnosis unlikely. Meckel diverticulum causes painless bloody stool without fever or other associated symptoms; it does not cause anemia.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child is referred to the pediatric nephrology clinic with a history of nephrotic syndrome that has been resistant to conventional corticosteroid therapy. The parents report that despite multiple courses of oral prednisone, the child continues to experience persistent proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and recurrent episodes of edema. On examination, the child exhibits periorbital and lower extremity edema. Regarding steroid resistance nephrotic syndrome is defined as failure to achieve remission after?
questions.initialExplanation:
In this question, steroid resistance is defined as failure to achieve remission after eight weeks of corticosteroid treatment.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is usually caused by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (80%), minimal change nephrotic syndrome, or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child is referred to the pediatric nephrology clinic due to generalized swelling and frothy urine. The parents report that the child has been more fatigued and has gained weight recently. The child exhibits periorbital edema and mild abdominal distension. Blood pressure is within the normal range. Considering the clinical presentation, the medical team suspects minimal change disease (MCD) as a cause of nephrotic syndrome. When you investigate for first attack of minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS), one of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Microscopic hematuria is present in 20% of children

options.label: B
options.text: Spot urine protein:creatinine ratio should be <2.0

options.label: E
options.text: Hypertension is usually present in half of the cases

questions.initialExplanation:
Typical first-episode minimal-change disease has normal complement, marked proteinuria, and usually does not require routine biopsy; microscopic hematuria can occur in a minority.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Microscopic hematuria is present in 20% of children. A spot urine protein:creatinine ratio should be >2.0. Serum complement levels are normal, and a renal biopsy is not routinely performed if the patient fits the standard clinical picture of MCD and the urinalysis reveals 3+ or 4+ proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic by concerned parents due to swelling around the eyes and ankles. The parents report that the child has been less active and has noticed only little urine over the past few weeks. On examination, the child exhibits periorbital edema and pitting edema in the lower extremities. The medical team suspects minimal change disease. In treatment of minimal change nephrotic syndrome, all the following are true EXCEPT?

options.label: A
options.text: Tuberculosis must be ruled out prior to starting immunosuppressive therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Steroid therapy may be initiated without a diagnostic renal biopsy

options.label: C
options.text: Prednisone should be administered as a single daily dose of 60 mg/m²/day

options.label: D
options.text: Remission consists of urine protein less than 1+ on urine dipstick for 3 consecutive days

options.label: E
options.text: Pleural effusion is a potential complication of parenteral albumin therapy

questions.initialExplanation:
The answer key marks E, but the accompanying explanation seems to support rather than refute the statement. Review this item against the original teaching source before relying on it.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The source marks option E as the correct answer. Its explanation states: 'Pleural effusion, is a potential complication of parenteral albumin therapy. Symptomatic volume overload, hypertension, heart failure, and pulmonary edema, is a potential complication of parenteral albumin therapy, particularly when administered as rapid infusions.' This explanation appears to describe albumin-related volume overload as a potential complication, which does not clearly support an EXCEPT stem. The source's answer/explanation pair is therefore internally inconsistent and has been preserved rather than silently corrected.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with the rash seen in the picture below, left knee pain, and crampy abdominal pain. He is admitted for observation and treated with supportive care. He continues to have normal BP readings, laboratory studies, and urinalysis. Over the next day, he quickly improves and is stable for discharge. Of the following, which is the next best step for monitoring this patient upon discharge home?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat a urinalysis weekly during active disease and then monthly for 6 months

options.label: E
options.text: No further workup unless patient develops clinical symptoms

questions.initialExplanation:
HSP can involve the kidneys after the rash and joint or abdominal symptoms. Serial urinalysis is important because renal involvement may appear or progress after the initial presentation.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Repeat a urinalysis weekly during active disease and then monthly for 6 months. The symptoms described in the vignette are consistent with a presentation of Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP). HSP is one of the most common systemic small-vessel vasculitides of childhood. It is characterized by a palpable, purpuric rash, arthritis, and less frequently gastrointestinal pain or involvement. Children with HSP and renal involvement can have either acute or chronic conditions. Most cases are mild and self-limited with isolated microscopic hematuria; however, patients can progress to severe glomerulonephritis with hematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency within the first few months of presentation. Therefore, aggressive monitoring with urinalysis is recommended. If a patient is found to have hematuria with proteinuria, renal insufficiency, or hypertension, consultation with pediatric nephrology may be warranted. Although the patient in the vignette does not warrant a renal biopsy at this time, if a biopsy were to be performed, findings would appear similar to patients with immunoglobulin (IgA) nephropathy: increased mesangial cellularity and IgA deposition on immunofluorescence.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with a history of minimal change disease presents to the emergency department with increasing facial edema. His mother states that these are similar symptoms to when he was first diagnosed, except this time he appears more ill, and he complains of abdominal pain and fever. He is currently on steroid treatment. Of the following, which is the most common organism and condition responsible for this patient's presentation?
questions.initialExplanation:
Nephrotic syndrome causes urinary loss of immune proteins and steroid treatment adds risk. Pneumococcus is the classic organism associated with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in these children.

---

## Acute Kidney Injury, Dialysis, and Electrolytes
questions.detailedExplanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae; SBP. A common complication for patients with nephrotic syndrome is an increased susceptibility to serious infections, such as bacteremia and SBP. Patients lose significant amounts of protein in the urine. This lost protein includes immunoglobulins, complement factors, and antibodies and can lead to immune compromise. Steroid dependency can also predispose these patients to an immunocompromised state. The most common microorganism seen in SBP in patients with nephrotic syndrome is Streptococcus pneumoniae, followed by gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli. If there is a concern for SBP, appropriate antibiotic therapy should be initiated.

topics.name: Acute Kidney Injury, Dialysis, and Electrolytes

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is admitted to the pediatric emergency department with a history of vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased urine output for the past 24 hours. On examination, she appears dehydrated, blood pressure is within normal range for her age, and there are no signs of fluid overload. Indications for dialysis in acute kidney injury include all the following EXCEPT:
questions.initialExplanation:
The source seems to intend the distinction between persistent hyperkalemia and hypercalcemia. Because the displayed answer and its note conflict, verify this item against the original reference before using it.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The source answer box shows 'persistent hypercalcemia' and then adds the note 'Persistent hyperkalemia not hypercalcemia.' This indicates an internal wording inconsistency in the source: the question is about dialysis indications, and the explanation appears to distinguish hyperkalemia from hypercalcemia, but the answer line itself says hypercalcemia. The source text is retained here without silently changing the answer.

questions.stem: Olivia, a 5-year-old girl, is brought to the pediatric clinic with complaints of bloody diarrhea and vomiting. Her parents mention that Olivia had been enjoying a family picnic a few days ago. Upon examination, Olivia is visibly fatigued and pale. Laboratory tests reveal anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated serum creatinine. Based on the clinical presentation and positive stool culture, Olivia is diagnosed with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). A pediatric nephrologist is promptly involved for comprehensive renal assessment. In the treatment of diarrhea-associated hemolytic-uremic syndrome, one of the following options has no beneficial role?
questions.initialExplanation:
Eculizumab is used for complement-mediated atypical HUS, not as routine beneficial therapy for typical diarrhea-associated HUS.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Eculizumab is an anti-C5 antibody that inhibits complement activation, a pathway that contributes to active disease in some forms of atypical HUS. For patients with diarrhea-associated HUS, subsequent systematic analysis showed no benefit from either plasma exchange or eculizumab, despite initial reports that suggested eculizumab provided benefit in patients with diarrhea-associated HUS.

questions.stem: Olivia, a 5-year-old girl, is brought to the pediatric clinic with complaints of bloody diarrhea and vomiting. Her parents mention that Olivia had been enjoying a family picnic a few days ago. Upon examination, Olivia is visibly fatigued and pale. Laboratory tests reveal anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated serum creatinine. In hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS), the following, which is the MOST correct statement?

options.label: A
options.text: The majority of patients with diarrhea-associated enteropathic HUS develop HUS

options.label: B
options.text: Stool culture is often positive in patients who have diarrhea-associated HUS

options.label: C
options.text: Kidney biopsy is rarely indicated to diagnose HUS

options.label: D
options.text: Partial thromboplastin and prothrombin times are usually low

options.label: E
options.text: Coombs test is usually negative in pneumococci-induced HUS

questions.initialExplanation:
HUS is usually diagnosed from the clinical pattern and laboratory findings; kidney biopsy is rarely needed, especially during the acute illness.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Kidney biopsies are only rarely performed in HUS because the diagnosis is usually established by clinical criteria and the risks of biopsy are significant during the acute phase of the disease. The organisms that cause HUS may be carried, therefore, the stool culture is often negative in patients who have diarrhea-associated HUS. Partial thromboplastin and prothrombin times are usually normal. The Coombs test is usually positive, with the exception of pneumococci-induced HUS, where the Coombs test is usually positive.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old male presented with diarrhea and vomiting, then turned lethargic and started to have slightly difficult and rapid breathing. The mother tells urine output was reduced significantly. Initial labs showed raised blood urea and serum creatinine. What is the first line of management?

options.label: B
options.text: Start intravenous normal saline for hydration

options.label: E
options.text: Give diuretic challenge to enhance urine output

questions.initialExplanation:
The child appears volume-depleted from gastrointestinal losses. Initial management is IV isotonic fluid to restore circulation and kidney perfusion.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The child is showing signs of acute kidney injury (AKI), likely secondary to dehydration from diarrhea and vomiting. Hydration is critical in this scenario to restore intravascular volume, improve perfusion to the kidneys, and address the underlying cause of the AKI. Intravenous normal saline is the best immediate intervention to correct the fluid deficit and stabilize the child.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is admitted to the pediatric emergency department with a history of vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased urine output for the past 24 hours. On examination, she appears dehydrated, blood pressure is within normal range for her age, and there are no signs of fluid overload. Many patients with acute kidney injury require dialysis support for 1-3 weeks, which of the following is TRUE statement:

options.label: A
options.text: Intermittent hemodialysis is useful in patients with unstable hemodynamic status

options.label: B
options.text: Continuous renal replacement therapy is useful in patients with stable hemodynamic status

options.label: C
options.text: In peritoneal dialysis, hypo-osmolar dialysate is infused into the peritoneal cavity

options.label: D
options.text: Anticoagulation is not necessary in peritoneal dialysis

options.label: E
options.text: Urea and creatinine clearance is greater with peritoneal dialysis than intermittent hemodialysis

questions.initialExplanation:
Peritoneal dialysis does not usually require systemic anticoagulation. Intermittent hemodialysis is generally used in more hemodynamically stable patients, while continuous replacement is useful when patients are unstable.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Intermittent hemodialysis is useful in patients with relatively stable hemodynamic status, while continuous renal replacement therapy is useful in patients with unstable hemodynamic status. Continuous renal replacement therapy, or ultrafiltration, is infused into the peritoneal cavity via a surgically or percutaneously placed peritoneal dialysis catheter; urea and creatinine clearance are more with intermittent hemodialysis than peritoneal dialysis.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl had bloody diarrhea for several days. One week later she develops periorbital edema and fatigue. What is the most likely laboratory finding?
questions.initialExplanation:
HUS after bloody diarrhea produces hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, often with acute kidney injury.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The patient exhibits signs and symptoms of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) after an episode of gastroenteritis most likely caused by enterohemorrhagic strain of E. coli. This syndrome is characterized by microangiopathic hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. The typical history, clinical picture, and laboratory findings confirm the diagnosis in most patients. Treatment is mainly supportive; frequent peritoneal dialysis needs to be initiated. Mortality is less than 10% with aggressive management of the acute renal failure. Most of the patients recover normal renal function.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 3-year-old boy presents with a sudden onset of lethargy, pallor, and bloody diarrhea. The parents report that he was active until the diarrhea started 4 days ago, which was initially thought to be gastroenteritis. Over the past 2 days, his condition has worsened, with reduced urine output. There is no significant travel or medication history that could contribute to his symptoms. On examination, he is found to have mild hypertension and a petechial rash, along with signs of dehydration. Which of the following statements regarding the suspected diagnosis is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Given the nature of this patient's symptoms and his young age, he is most likely to have atypical HUS

options.label: B
options.text: Parenteral antibiotic treatment with gentamicin is indicated for the treatment of suspected Escherichia coli hemorrhagic colitis

options.label: C
options.text: Although he has a petechial rash, his platelet count will be normal

options.label: D
options.text: The prognosis is poor; he will likely have a chronic relapsing course, with a high chance of end-stage renal disease (ESRD)

options.label: E
options.text: The renal impairment is caused by toxin binding to renal vascular endothelial cells

questions.initialExplanation:
Typical Shiga toxin-associated HUS causes kidney injury when the toxin damages vascular endothelium. The source notes that gentamicin is not recommended in suspected E. coli hemorrhagic colitis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation is suggestive of typical hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), which is often preceded by gastroenteritis symptoms, including bloody diarrhea. HUS can occur after infections with certain strains of E. coli, which produce Shiga toxin that binds to endothelial cells in the kidneys, leading to renal impairment. Atypical HUS is less common and is associated with complement dysregulation rather than preceding diarrhea. Antibiotics like gentamicin are not recommended as they can increase the release of Shiga toxin. The prognosis of HUS varies; some patients may progress to ESRD, while others may recover with appropriate management, including supportive care and, in some cases, dialysis.

questions.stem: The 14-year-old boy with APSGN is found to have a potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L, which is high, and ECG changes suggestive of hyperkalemia. What is the next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide and normal saline

questions.initialExplanation:
Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane when hyperkalemia is causing ECG changes. Other therapies are then used to shift or remove potassium.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In the setting of hyperkalemia with ECG changes, the immediate goal is to stabilize the cardiac membrane. Intravenous calcium gluconate is used for this purpose and can help protect the heart from the effects of elevated potassium levels. This does not lower the potassium level itself but is a critical first step in acute management. Other treatments like insulin and glucose, albuterol, or hemodialysis are used to actually lower the potassium level and would follow the initial stabilization with calcium gluconate.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old female with acute simple gastroenteritis and anuria. On examination she was severely dehydrated and acidotic breathing. Which of the following is TRUE regarding urine examination?
questions.initialExplanation:
In dehydration-related prerenal AKI, the kidneys conserve sodium and concentrate urine. A high urine osmolality is therefore expected.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In the context of a 10-month-old female with acute simple gastroenteritis, anuria, severe dehydration, and acidotic breathing, it is important to understand the typical findings associated with prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI) due to dehydration. In such a scenario, the kidney attempts to conserve sodium and water to maintain intravascular volume. Therefore, the most likely true statement regarding urine examination is: d. Urine osmolality >400 mOsm/kg. This reflects the kidney's ability to concentrate the urine. In prerenal AKI, urine osmolality is typically high because the kidneys are functioning in response to conserve water as possible to counteract the effects of dehydration. Here is a brief explanation of why the other options are less likely: a. Specific gravity <1.010 - In dehydration, the specific gravity is typically high (>1.020) because the urine is concentrated. b. RBC casts - These are more indicative of glomerulonephritis or another form of intrinsic renal disease, not prerenal AKI from dehydration. c. Urine Na >40 mEq/L - In prerenal AKI, urine sodium is typically low (<20 mEq/L) as the kidneys conserve sodium to preserve volume. e. Fractional excretion of Na >1% - In prerenal AKI, the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is typically low (<1%) because the kidneys are reabsorbing sodium to conserve volume.

questions.stem: Four days after admission to the hospital for severe dehydration due to profuse, bloody diarrhea, a 10-year-old boy is evaluated for decreased urine output. Physical examination shows generalized abdominal tenderness and numerous punctate, non-blanching macules on the trunk and extremities. Serum creatinine and urea nitrogen are elevated. A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following sets of laboratory values is most likely in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal PT, normal PTT, increased bleeding time, decreased platelet count

options.label: B
options.text: Increased PT, increased PTT, normal bleeding time, normal platelet count

options.label: C
options.text: Increased PT, increased PTT, increased bleeding time, decreased platelet count

options.label: D
options.text: Normal PT, normal PTT, increased bleeding time, normal platelet count

options.label: E
options.text: Normal PT, increased PTT, normal bleeding time, normal platelet count

questions.initialExplanation:
HUS causes platelet consumption and thrombocytopenia, while the coagulation tests PT and PTT are generally normal.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The source explanation states that option A is the most appropriate set of laboratory values for this patient, indicating a condition like HUS, which typically features normal PT and PTT with an increased bleeding time due to platelet consumption, and a decreased platelet count.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy and his family have recently visited a local amusement park. Several of the family members developed 'gastroenteritis' with fever and diarrhea, but the 4-year-old's stool was slightly different, as it contained blood. His mother reports that in the past 24 hours he developed pallor and lethargy, and that his face looks swollen and that he has been urinating very little. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hematocrit of 28% and a platelet count of 72,000/µL. He has blood and protein in the urine. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to explain these symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation:
Bloody diarrhea followed by anemia, low platelets, edema, and reduced urine output is the classic pattern of HUS.

---

## Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis and Hematuria
questions.detailedExplanation: The source identifies hemolytic-uremic syndrome as the correct diagnosis. The syndrome is characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal insufficiency, often following bloody gastroenteritis. (The detailed HUS explanation is reproduced under question 46, where the same vignette and full source explanation appear.)

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with a history of 'brown urine.' He had a sore throat two weeks prior that resolved without intervention. His physical exam shows hypertension and periorbital edema. Which of the following findings is inconsistent with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN)?

options.label: C
options.text: Red cell casts in urine microscopy

questions.initialExplanation:
APSGN typically lowers C3 while C4 remains normal. A reduction in both C3 and C4 is therefore inconsistent with the usual pattern.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In APSGN, complement levels, particularly C3, are often low, while C4 typically remains normal. This is due to the classical pathway not being typically activated in APSGN. Therefore, both C3 and C4 being low is less consistent with APSGN, as C4 would usually remain within the normal range in this condition.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with red-coloured urine and bilateral pitting leg oedema, you suspect acute post streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Which of the following is the most important to measure?
questions.initialExplanation:
APSGN commonly causes hypertension from renal inflammation and fluid retention, so blood pressure is the key measurement to monitor.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Blood pressure. Hypertension is a significant clinical feature of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Monitoring blood pressure is crucial as hypertension can be a presenting symptom and may require management to prevent complications such as hypertensive encephalopathy or heart failure. While monitoring other vital signs like temperature, respiratory rate, heart rate, and SpO2 is also important for assessing overall clinical status, in the context of APSGN, blood pressure monitoring is particularly critical due to the risk of hypertension.

questions.stem: You are discussing the management options and the prognosis for an 8-year-old boy who presented earlier with gross hematuria and later diagnosed with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis with his parents. Which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.label: E
options.text: Microscopic hematuria after 1 year should suggest other diagnosis

questions.initialExplanation:
Microscopic hematuria can persist after APSGN and does not automatically mean another diagnosis. Most children recover with supportive care.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The source explains that persistent microscopic hematuria after 1 year is typical for APSGN and should NOT prompt further investigation for alternative diagnoses. The diagnosis is clinical and is based on a typical history along with elevated ASO titers; renal biopsy is not usually required. Most patients with PSGN will recover spontaneously with conservative management and without the need for dialysis.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has hematuria and an increased serologic titer to antistreptolysin O (ASO). What will be the most likely finding?
questions.initialExplanation:
A positive ASO with hematuria and low C3 supports poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The differential diagnosis of hematuria in children includes glomerular diseases, extraglomerular renal diseases, and various nonrenal diseases. The glomerular diseases include acute or chronic glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, benign familial hematuria, Alport syndrome, systemic vasculitis, and hemolytic uremic syndrome. Hypercalciuria can also cause hematuria. Serum complement, both total and C3, is decreased in conditions such as poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and bacterial endocarditis. Hematuria with a positive ASO and decreased C3 levels confirms a diagnosis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with complaints of dark urine and puffiness of his face, particularly around the eyes. He had a sore throat and fever which resolved two weeks ago. On examination, his blood pressure is elevated, and he has mild edema in the lower extremities. The physician is suspecting acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Which of the following is NOT commonly associated with this condition?
questions.initialExplanation:
APSGN is a nephritic syndrome with hematuria, edema, hypertension, and possible renal dysfunction. High cholesterol is more characteristic of nephrotic syndrome.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) commonly presents with symptoms such as high blood pressure, gross hematuria, possible renal insufficiency, and edema due to inflammation of the glomeruli following a streptococcal infection. However, high cholesterol levels are more typically associated with nephrotic syndrome, not APSGN, which primarily presents with nephritic symptoms. Therefore, high cholesterol level is the correct exception for APSGN.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a history of upper respiratory tract infection three weeks ago. He now presents with puffy eyes, reduced urine output, and brown-colored urine. On examination, he has mild periorbital edema. His mother mentions that the boy had a sore throat a month ago but did not take any medication. The physician suspects a post-infectious glomerulonephritis. Which of the following statements is true about his condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Typical patient develops nephritic syndrome 1-2 weeks following streptococcal skin infection

options.label: C
options.text: Most common in children below 3 years

options.label: D
options.text: The earliest symptom is mild periorbital edema

options.label: E
options.text: ASO titer is commonly elevated after skin infection

questions.initialExplanation:
Postinfectious glomerulonephritis follows a streptococcal infection and commonly produces proteinuria, hematuria, edema, and hypertension.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis typically presents with proteinuria due to the inflammation of the glomeruli caused by the immune response following a streptococcal infection. This disease is more common in children aged 3-7 years after a pharyngeal or skin streptococcal infection. ASO titers can be elevated, especially following pharyngeal infections. Nephritic syndrome usually develops a few weeks after the infection, characterized by hematuria, hypertension, and edema. It is not the most common in children below 3 years, and while periorbital edema can occur, it is not always the earliest symptom. Proteinuria is a key feature and thus the correct statement.

questions.stem: The parents of a 6-year-old boy bring him to the clinic for evaluation of cola-colored urine and mild swelling of his extremities. The symptoms started a few days prior, but he had slowly increased in severity. He was sent home from school 3 weeks ago for having a fever and sore throat, which improved without intervention. Of the following, which statement is true concerning this boy's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) is the result of direct bacterial infection of the glomerular basement membrane

options.label: B
options.text: APSGN is not seen following streptococcal skin infections

options.label: C
options.text: Treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis with antibiotics would have prevented APSGN

options.label: D
options.text: Only specific nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes trigger the immune response that causes APSGN

options.label: E
options.text: Urine cultures in patients with APSGN will be positive for S. pyogenes

questions.initialExplanation:
APSGN is an immune-mediated complication of infection with nephritogenic strains of group A Streptococcus. It can follow throat or skin infection and is not prevented reliably by treating the original infection.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Only specific nephritogenic strains of S. pyogenes trigger the immune response that causes APSGN. APSGN is one of the most common causes of acute nephritic syndrome in children and consists of hematuria, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. APSGN results from inflammation due to an immune-mediated response, specifically to a nephritogenic strain of S. pyogenes. This response is directed at the glomerular capillary wall, leading to complement activation and eventual cell proliferation and injury. APSGN occurs 5 to 21 days following an initial infection, usually of the pharynx or skin, such as impetigo. If the patient has an active infection at the time of diagnosis, antibiotics are needed; however, appropriate treatment does not prevent the immune response that leads to APSGN. (E) APSGN is not the result of an active urinary infection. (C) Appropriate therapy of streptococcal pharyngitis does prevent rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents to the clinic with dark urine and facial puffiness. His parents report that he had a sore throat and skin rash three weeks prior, which resolved on its own. On physical examination, he has mild hypertension and edema. The physician is considering post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis as a differential diagnosis. Regarding this condition, which of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The most common cause of gross hematuria

options.label: B
options.text: Follows a group B-beta hemolytic streptococcal infection

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease in C3 level is seen

options.label: D
options.text: Requires long-term prophylactic penicillin to prevent recurrence

options.label: E
options.text: Rapidly progressive disease is seen in the majority of affected children

questions.initialExplanation:
APSGN commonly causes a temporary reduction in C3 and follows group A, not group B, streptococcal infection.

---

## Urinary Tract Infection, Reflux, and Obstructive Uropathy
questions.detailedExplanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically follows an infection with group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, not group B. It is one of the causes of gross hematuria, but not necessarily the most common cause overall. A decrease in complement level, specifically C3, is commonly seen in this condition due to the activation of the complement system as part of the immune response against the streptococcus. This disease is not typically rapidly progressive, and while antibiotic treatment for streptococcal infection is important, it does not eliminate the risk of developing glomerulonephritis if the immune response has already been triggered.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Infection, Reflux, and Obstructive Uropathy

questions.stem: After her first urinary tract infection, a 1-year-old has a voiding cystourethrogram shows reflux into the ureters and into the kidney, with dilation of the renal pelvis. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option?

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate surgical reimplantation of the ureters

questions.initialExplanation:
The source describes reflux with renal pelvic dilation and recommends conservative management with daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis for lower-grade reflux, reserving surgery for more severe persistent cases.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The radiograph shows reflux into the ureters and into the kidney, with dilation of the renal pelvis, making the diagnosis of vesicoureteral reflux. The higher the reflux into the renal system, especially if the renal pelvis is dilated, the more likely it is for renal damage to occur; the grading system is based upon these radiographic observations. Grade I VUR is reflux of urine into an undilated ureter. Reflux into the ureter and collecting system without dilation is called grade II. Grade III lesions have dilatation of the ureter and collecting system without blunting of the calyces. Grade IV lesions are characterized by blunting of the calyces, and grade V lesions demonstrate even more dilatation and tortuosity of the ureter. Low-grade lesions (grade I and grade II) are conservatively managed with close observation, daily low-dose antibiotics, and urinalyses and cultures every 3 to 4 months. Grade V lesions (and some grade IV lesions) require surgical reimplantation of a ureter if the findings persist. Lesions in between these two extremes are treatment dilemmas.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department with a fever and irritability. His mother reports that he is feeding poorly and has had vomiting. The clinical examination is non-specific but considering his symptoms, a urinary tract infection is suspected. The pediatrician decides to order diagnostic tests to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate any complications. Which of the following statements is FALSE about urinary tract infections in this context?

options.label: A
options.text: Are more common in males in the neonatal period

options.label: B
options.text: In childhood are more likely to be due to ascending infection

options.label: C
options.text: Gram-negative E. coli is the most common organism

options.label: D
options.text: Scarring is more likely to occur if there has been a delay in treatment

options.label: E
options.text: An ultrasound is the best way of detecting renal scarring

questions.initialExplanation:
Ultrasound can assess the urinary tract, but a DMSA renal scan is more sensitive for demonstrating renal cortical scarring.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Urinary tract infections are more common in males compared to females in the neonatal period, and in childhood they are often due to ascending infections with E. coli being the most common causative organism. Renal scarring can occur if treatment is delayed. However, while an ultrasound can detect changes suggestive of scarring, it is not considered the best way for detection. A DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) renal scan is more sensitive for detecting renal cortical defects, which indicate scarring. Thus statement E is false as it does not represent the most accurate method for detecting renal scarring.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old child is being evaluated for a fever of unknown etiology. As part of the laboratory evaluation, a urine specimen was obtained that grew E. coli with a colony count of 2000/µL. These findings would be definite evidence of a urinary tract infection if which of the following is true about the sampled urine?

options.label: A
options.text: It has a specific gravity of 1.008

options.label: B
options.text: It is from a bag attached to the perineum of an uncircumcised boy

options.label: C
options.text: It is from an ileal-loop bag

options.label: D
options.text: It is from a suprapubic tap

options.label: E
options.text: It is the first morning sample

questions.initialExplanation:
A positive culture with a low colony count is most convincing when the sample is collected by suprapubic aspiration, which minimizes contamination.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The mechanism by which urine is collected is paramount in determining the interpretation of cultures. No bacteria should grow in a properly obtained urine sample from a suprapubic tap unless infection is present. For children who undergo bladder catheterization, colony counts of 10³ to 10⁴ are considered significant. Ileal-loop bags are usually contaminated and are not useful. Bag specimens in smaller children (obtained by placing an adhesive, sealed, sterile collection system onto the perineum) can be helpful if the culture is negative. Contamination is common, especially in girls and in uncircumcised boys; positive cultures in this latter group of children, if they contain more than one organism, are suspect. In properly obtained midstream clean-catch urines, colony counts greater than 10⁵ in the asymptomatic child and colony counts of 10⁴ in the symptomatic child may be significant. Clean-catch urine samples in an uncircumcised male who cannot retract the foreskin are also suspect.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with complaints of dysuria and vague suprapubic abdominal pain. Her parents report they have been trying to teach the child the proper way to wipe after stooling. She also has a history of constipation, but reports no other complaints, and has been tolerating solids and liquids well. A urinalysis is obtained, which demonstrates nitrites, leukocyte esterase, and many bacteria. A urine culture is pending. Of the following, which antibiotic is most appropriate to initiate for this patient?
questions.initialExplanation:
This is uncomplicated lower UTI (cystitis), most often due to E. coli. The source lists trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as the best choice among the options.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The patient in the vignette presents with signs of acute cystitis, or lower urinary tract infection (UTI), limited to the bladder. Older children have symptoms similar to adults that include low-grade fever, frequency, urgency, dysuria, and hematuria. A common cause for UTIs is E. coli, which results from ascending infection of exterior fecal flora into the urinary tract. Constipation is another common risk factor for UTIs as it can contribute to some voiding dysfunction. The organisms implicated in UTIs in this age group are those found in fecal flora, specifically Escherichia coli. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the best choice for first-line uncomplicated acute cystitis. Nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin, and cephalosporins can also be used as outpatient treatment of UTI based on the sensitivity reports of the microorganism involved. (A) Ciprofloxacin has appropriate coverage against most gram-negative organisms that cause UTIs; however, it is generally avoided in young children, secondary to concern for potential cartilage damage. (B) Azithromycin does not have activity against E. coli. (D) Gentamicin and piperacillin-tazobactam can be used in inpatient management of patients with pyelonephritis, who may not be responsive to third-generation cephalosporin therapy.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl presents to the clinic with symptoms of a urinary tract infection. She has a history of a previous UTI treated with antibiotics three months ago. The symptoms resolved completely until this week, when she developed dysuria and frequency again. There are no accompanying fevers or flank pain. A urine dipstick confirms the presence of leukocyte esterase and nitrites. Which is the most appropriate plan for a child with a recurrent UTI?

options.label: A
options.text: Urinalysis, urine culture, and VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram)

questions.initialExplanation:
A recurrent UTI needs confirmation with culture and evaluation for vesicoureteral reflux; VCUG is included in the source's recommended plan.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: For children with recurrent UTIs, it is important to perform a urinalysis and urine culture to identify the causative organism and determine appropriate antibiotic sensitivity. Additionally, a VCUG is recommended to evaluate for vesicoureteral reflux, a condition that can predispose children to recurrent UTIs. This imaging test can help guide long-term management and prevention strategies.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her parents with complaints of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) over the past few months. The parents report that she has had three episodes of UTI in the last six months, each characterized by fever, dysuria, and urgency. Despite completing courses of antibiotics prescribed by her pediatrician, the symptoms have recurred. On examination, the child appears well, with no signs of fever or distress. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, with no tenderness or palpable masses. Urinalysis reveals pyuria and bacteriuria consistent with a UTI. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this child's recurrent UTIs?

options.label: A
options.text: Referral to a pediatric urologist for further evaluation

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat urine culture and sensitivity testing

options.label: C
options.text: Renal ultrasound to assess for structural abnormalities

options.label: E
options.text: Reassurance as repeated UTIs are normal in this age group

questions.initialExplanation:
Repeated UTIs warrant imaging to look for reflux, obstruction, or congenital urinary tract abnormalities. The source selects renal ultrasound as the immediate next investigation.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Recurrent UTIs in children can be indicative of underlying structural or functional abnormalities of the urinary tract, such as vesicoureteral reflux, obstructive uropathy, or other congenital anomalies. A renal ultrasound is a non-invasive imaging modality that can help identify such abnormalities, guiding further management and treatment to prevent future infections and potential kidney damage. While other steps may be relevant in the overall management (such as culture and sensitivity testing to guide antibiotic therapy, or referral to a pediatric urologist if abnormalities are found), the renal ultrasound is the most immediate and essential investigation to identify any underlying causes of the recurrent infections.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with fevers and chills for the past 2 days. Her parents report she is also complaining of back pain and nausea. On examination, she has tenderness to her right flank area. Her laboratory workup reveals a leukocytosis with a left shift and elevated inflammatory markers. Her urinalysis reveals many bacteria, white blood cells, nitrites, and leukocyte esterase. Of the following, which is her most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Fever, chills, nausea, and flank tenderness with infected urine point to kidney infection rather than simple bladder cystitis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Acute pyelonephritis. Acute pyelonephritis refers to a urinary tract infection (UTI) that involves the kidney. Pyelonephritis can clinically manifest with systemic signs of fever, nausea, vomiting, malaise, and focal signs of pain radiating to the back, abdomen, or flank region. In younger children, fever may be the only symptom. Most acute pyelonephritis infections occur from ascending UTIs; however, cases of hematogenous spread can be possible as well. The patient in the vignette has clinical symptoms, laboratory findings, and urine results consistent with acute pyelonephritis. Patients are typically hospitalized for initial treatment with intravenous antibiotics. (A) The patient in the vignette unlikely has a simple acute cystitis with infection only limited to the bladder, given the pain, fever, and chills, indicative of a more systemic or involved process. (C) Vertebral osteomyelitis can present similar to pyelonephritis with fever and back pain; however, vertebral osteomyelitis should not present with urine findings consistent with an infection. (D) Patients with pneumonia and acute appendicitis will not have infectious urine findings, but both conditions can present with back pain, nausea, and fever. Acute appendicitis may cause a sterile pyuria, noted with white blood cells in the urine without a negative urine culture.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl with no significant past medical history is hospitalized after 4 days of fever. The results of her partial septic workup reveal a urinary tract infection (UTI) with Escherichia coli. Antibiotics are initiated and her fevers have subsided. A renal ultrasound demonstrates that her right kidney is larger than her left. Of the following tests, which is the next best step in evaluation of this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis

questions.initialExplanation:
A febrile UTI in an infant plus an abnormal renal ultrasound warrants assessment for vesicoureteral reflux. The source identifies VCUG as the appropriate test.

---

## Other Renal and Urinary Topics
questions.detailedExplanation: Voiding cystourethrogram. Based on the age and findings of a febrile UTI and abnormal renal ultrasound of the patient in the vignette, the patient warrants further evaluation for vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). VUR is an abnormal or retrograde movement of urine from the bladder into the ureters and/or kidneys. VUR can predispose patients to pyelonephritis, which can result in renal injury or scarring. The best test to evaluate VUR is a voiding cystourethrogram in which a catheter is placed through the urethra into the bladder, filled with contrast, and then monitored under fluoroscopy to look for abnormal retrograde flow from the bladder toward the kidneys. VUR is typically the result of an abnormal vesicoureteral junction, although the degree of reflux can be variable, and management can vary from supportive care to medical management to surgical intervention. (B) A computed tomography scan would not provide superior information for the patient in the vignette and delivers a significant amount of radiation. (D) A 24-hour urine collection is not an appropriate test to evaluate for VUR. (C, E) Cystoscopy or exploratory laparotomy would be considered invasive tests and unnecessary.

questions.stem: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most frequent malignant tumor of the genitourinary tract in childhood. The most common presenting sign of this neoplasm is which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation:
Wilms tumor most often presents as a painless abdominal or flank mass found by a parent or on examination.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: An abdominal or flank mass is the most common presenting sign in children with Wilms tumor. Often, the mass is discovered on routine examination or during examination for a minor illness. This underscores the importance of a thorough examination at every physician visit. Occasionally, the parents will bring the child to the physician because they note an enlarging abdomen or feel the mass themselves.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to the pediatrician by their parents due to a painless abdominal swelling noticed over the past few weeks. The parents report that the child's appetite has decreased, and they have observed blood in the child's urine on several occasions. On examination, a firm, non-tender mass is palpable in the child's left upper abdomen. There are no other significant findings on physical examination. Laboratory investigations reveal microscopic hematuria. Ultrasound imaging of the abdomen confirms the presence of a solid renal mass. Based on these findings, which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis for this child?
questions.initialExplanation:
A child with a painless abdominal mass and a solid renal mass on ultrasound should raise concern for Wilms tumor.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Wilms tumor is the most common renal malignancy in children, typically presenting as a painless abdominal mass with or without other symptoms such as hematuria and abdominal pain. It is characterized by a solid renal mass, as described in this case.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency room because her urine is red. She has been healthy her whole life, and has recently returned from an outing with her grandmother to a local amusement park. Her urine dip for heme is positive, suggesting which of the following is a possibility?
questions.initialExplanation:
Food pigments can turn urine red but do not make the heme dipstick positive. Myoglobin can cause a positive heme test without intact red blood cells.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: A number of pH-dependent substances can impart a red color to urine. Use of phenolphthalein, a cathartic agent, or phenazopyridine, an anticoagulant, can cause red urine; ingestion of blackberries, red Kool-Aid, or beets also can lead to red coloration ('beeturia'). None of these choices, however, would cause the heme test to be positive. Myoglobin, on the other hand, is the only choice listed that can test positive for heme. Myoglobinuria occurs in rhabdomyolysis with skeletal muscle damage and increased serum creatine kinase. Another possible cause of heme-positive urine with no red cells is hemoglobinuria resulting from hemolysis.
