questions.detailedExplanation: Tumor lysis syndrome follows rapid breakdown of malignant cells, releasing intracellular potassium and phosphate and increasing uric acid from nucleic acid metabolism. These abnormalities can cause acute kidney injury and dangerous cardiac or neurologic complications. The source screenshot shows the keyed choice D, but its table headings are cropped; the exact column labels cannot be fully read from the provided image.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child from Diyala presents with a persistent fever, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Upon examination, the child’s spleen and liver are palpably enlarged. Further investigation confirms the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis. One of the following investigations is highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis:
questions.initialExplanation:
The rK39 test detects antibodies against *Leishmania donovani* and is a highly useful specific test for visceral leishmaniasis. The other listed tests may support the diagnosis but are less specific.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The recombinant antigen K39 is indeed highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis. This diagnostic test detects antibodies against the K39 antigen, which is specific to the *Leishmania donovani* parasite, the primary cause of visceral leishmaniasis. It has been shown to have high sensitivity and specificity, making it a valuable tool for diagnosing this condition, particularly in endemic regions where other diagnostic methods may be less reliable. Abdominal ultrasound, blood culture, complete blood picture, and liver function tests can provide supportive information but may not offer the same level of accuracy and specificity as the K39 antigen test for diagnosing visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.stem: You started treatment with Sodium Antimony agents to a two-year-old boy recently diagnosed with Kala-Azar; the mother is worried about the abdominal distension and inquiring about the time her son’s abdomen comes back to normal. The best response will be within:

options.label: A
options.text: Time depends on duration of treatment

questions.initialExplanation:
The enlarged liver and spleen do not return to normal immediately after treatment. Their size usually decreases gradually over weeks to months.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
The best response to the mother’s concern about her son’s abdominal distension due to Kala-Azar (visceral leishmaniasis) and when it might resolve is “C. Weeks to months.” This timeframe is realistic as the spleen and liver enlargement (leading to abdominal distension) that occurs with this disease usually begins to resolve after effective treatment starts. However, the process is gradual.

The reduction in spleen and liver size and the associated decrease in abdominal distension depend on the body’s ability to clear the infection and repair the inflammation caused by the disease. Although treatment with sodium antimony agents is effective in killing the parasites, the recovery of organ size and function is not immediate and can take weeks to months, varying from one patient to another depending on the severity of the infection and the individual’s response to treatment.

questions.stem: A nine-year-old girl from Diyala presents to the local health clinic with complaints of persistent fever, significant weight loss, and weakness over the past three months. Her parents also note that her abdomen has been gradually swelling. On physical examination, the child appears pale and malnourished. Given the endemic nature of the region and the clinical presentation, the clinician suspects visceral leishmaniasis. The following is WRONG?

options.label: A
options.text: Is characterized by splenomegaly and pancytopenia.

options.label: B
options.text: Fatalities are usually the result of secondary bacterial infections.

options.label: C
options.text: Antimony products are not always effective.

options.label: D
options.text: The epidemiology of Leishmania is tightly linked with the epidemiology of the sandfly.

questions.initialExplanation:
Leishmania amastigotes live inside macrophages, so the organism is intracellular rather than extracellular. The remaining statements describe recognized features of visceral leishmaniasis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
“The organism is characteristically extracellular” is incorrect regarding visceral leishmaniasis. The parasite that causes visceral leishmaniasis is primarily an intracellular organism. It resides within the macrophages of the host’s immune system. This intracellular lifestyle is a key aspect of the parasite’s ability to evade the host’s immune response and sustain infection.

Here is why the other statements are correct:

- **A. Is characterized by splenomegaly and pancytopenia.** Visceral leishmaniasis often leads to enlargement of the spleen (splenomegaly) and a decrease in all types of blood cells (pancytopenia), which are characteristic clinical signs of the disease.
- **B. Fatalities are usually the result of secondary bacterial infections.** Patients with visceral leishmaniasis are at increased risk of secondary bacterial infections due to immune system dysfunction caused by the disease, and these infections can be fatal.
- **C. Antimony products are not always effective.** Although antimony-containing compounds have been a mainstay in the treatment of leishmaniasis, resistance to these drugs has been reported, and they are not always effective, especially in certain geographic areas where resistance has developed.
- **D. The epidemiology of Leishmania is tightly knit with the epidemiology of the sandfly.** Leishmania parasites are transmitted by the bite of infected female sandflies, making the distribution and behavior of these insects crucial to the epidemiology of the disease.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child from Diyala presented to the clinic with persistent fever, weakness, and weight loss. Upon examination, the child exhibited hepatosplenomegaly (enlargement of the liver and spleen), pallor, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests revealed pancytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, and hypergammaglobulinemia. Further investigation, including a bone marrow biopsy, confirmed the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar. The MOST common cause of death in kala-azar is?
questions.initialExplanation:
Visceral leishmaniasis can impair host defenses. Secondary bacterial infections are a major cause of death in advanced disease.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The late stage of the illness is often complicated by secondary bacterial infections, which frequently are a cause of death.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl who presented with fever, anorexia, weight loss, and abdominal distension for the last three weeks is likely to have:
questions.initialExplanation:
Prolonged fever, weight loss, poor appetite, and abdominal enlargement from hepatosplenomegaly are typical clues to visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar), especially in an endemic area.

---

# 2. Mumps
questions.detailedExplanation: The most likely diagnosis for a 3-year-old girl presenting with fever, anorexia, weight loss, and abdominal distension for the last three weeks is option D, Kala-Azar, also known as visceral leishmaniasis. Kala-Azar is a parasitic infection caused by the protozoan *Leishmania donovani*. It is characterized by prolonged fever, often lasting for several weeks to months, accompanied by symptoms such as anorexia, weight loss, and abdominal distension due to hepatosplenomegaly (enlargement of the liver and spleen). Kala-Azar is endemic in certain regions, particularly in parts of Africa, Asia, and South America, and is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected sandflies. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications and reduce mortality associated with the disease.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child was admitted to the hospital with complications arising from mumps infection. Initially presenting with classic symptoms of mumps, including swelling and tenderness of the parotid glands, the child’s condition deteriorated over the following days. The MOST common complication of mumps is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Mumps can involve the central nervous system. Aseptic meningitis is a recognized and common complication; the other listed complications are less common.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The most common complications of mumps are meningitis, with or without encephalitis, and gonadal involvement. Uncommon complications include conjunctivitis, optic neuritis, pneumonia, nephritis, pancreatitis, and thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents in the clinic with an illness notable for swelling in front of and in back of the ear on the affected side, as well as altered taste sensation. Correct statements about this condition include which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Arthritis is a common presenting complaint in children.

options.label: B
options.text: The disease could have been prevented by prior immunization with killed whole cell vaccine.

options.label: C
options.text: Involvement of the central nervous system (CNS) may occur 10 days after the resolution of the swelling.

options.label: D
options.text: Orchitis can occur and is almost exclusively seen in prepubertal males.

options.label: E
options.text: Subendocardial fibroelastosis is a common complication in a child of this age.

questions.initialExplanation:
Mumps is a systemic viral infection, not just parotitis. Aseptic meningitis may occur during parotitis or about 10 days later. Orchitis is more typical after puberty, and the vaccine is live attenuated.

---

# 3. Roseola Infantum / Human Herpesvirus 6
questions.detailedExplanation: The child in this question likely has mumps. Although mumps is usually thought of as a parotitis (presenting as swelling as described in the question), it is a generalized infection and, as such, can have widespread effects and a variety of clinical presentations. Many infections with the mumps virus are unrecognized because of the substantial rate of subclinical attacks. Meningitis, pancreatitis, and renal involvement can occur as part of the disease. Many patients with mumps have some WBCs in their spinal fluid. The meningitis that occurs with mumps can occur at the same time as the parotitis, or following the parotitis by about 10 days. Orchitis, seen most frequently in postpubertal males, has been reported in young children as well. All of these problems can be prevented by prior immunization with live attenuated virus vaccine; widespread use of this vaccine has reduced the number of cases in the United States to less than 500 per year. Arthritis is rare in children. Subendocardial fibroelastosis in a newborn was once thought to be associated with prenatal infection with mumps, but this does not appear to be true.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old previously healthy infant presented with a history of an abrupt onset of a high fever that reached 40°C, which lasts for 5 days with nonspecific complaints and was accompanied by a single episode of generalized tonic-clonic convulsion attributed to the rapid rise of temperature by the family physician. On the fourth day, the mother noticed that the temperature had decreased rapidly with the onset of a mild, pink rash over the trunk. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Roseola typically causes several days of high fever followed by rapid defervescence and a pink rash that starts on the trunk. Febrile seizures can occur during the fever.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The most likely diagnosis in this case is option A, Roseola infantum. Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease or exanthema subitum, typically presents with a sudden onset of high fever, often reaching 40°C, which lasts for several days. During the fever phase, the child may appear irritable or lethargic and may experience nonspecific symptoms. In some cases, the rapid rise in temperature can lead to febrile seizures, as observed in this infant. Following the resolution of the fever, a characteristic rash appears, starting on the trunk and spreading to the extremities. This sequence of symptoms, including the fever, convulsion, and subsequent rash, is consistent with the clinical presentation of Roseola infantum.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy presented with evanescent, erythematous, maculopapular rash following the rapid defervescence of several days of high fever. The rash appeared mainly on the trunk, then spreads to the face and extremities. Which of the following is the most likely infectious organism?
questions.initialExplanation:
HHV-6 is the main cause of roseola. The typical pattern is high fever for several days followed by a transient rash as the fever resolves.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Roseola (exanthema subitum) is a common acute illness of young children (such as the 9-month-old child with fever and transient rash), characterized by several days of high fever followed by a rapid defervescence and the appearance of an evanescent, erythematous, maculopapular rash. Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) has been identified as its main cause.

questions.stem:
A 15-month-old presents to the clinic the day after a visit to the emergency department for his first seizure. He had tactile fevers per his mother for each of the 3 days prior to presentation. She describes the seizure episode as shaking of his entire body and lasting approximately 4 minutes. It stopped without intervention before the ambulance arrived. He had returned to his baseline by the time they arrived at the emergency department. He was observed for several hours with no further adverse events and subsequently discharged home. In the clinic today, his mother reports he feels better than he had earlier this week except he has a rash on his body as shown in Figure. He has not felt warm since yesterday and his appetite has returned. Of the following, what is the most likely etiologic agent causing this patient's rash?

**Figure**  
The source includes a photograph of a diffuse pink/maculopapular rash on the infant’s trunk.
questions.initialExplanation:
The fever-then-rash sequence in a child younger than 2 years, with a febrile seizure during the fever, strongly supports roseola due to HHV-6. The source screenshot does not show all five options, but its explanation identifies HHV-6 as the answer (C).

---

# 4. Measles (Rubeola)
questions.detailedExplanation: Human herpesvirus-6. The boy in the vignette has a viral exanthem caused by human herpesvirus-6 or -7 known as roseola, or erythema subitum. This condition is a common exanthem seen most often in children younger than 2 years old. It is characterized by isolated and sustained high fevers for several days and followed by defervescence and eruption of a pink, morbilliform rash that fades within 24 hours. The rash appears similar to other exanthematous eruptions, but may be distinguished by the characteristic fever curve. Febrile seizures are associated with the high spiking fevers during the first few days of the illness. The remaining options are associated with characteristic rashes as well, but unlikely to cause the presentation of the child in the vignette. (A) Coxsackie virus causes hand-foot-and-mouth disease and is characterized by the abrupt onset of papules and vesicles in the oral mucosa on the extremities including the palms and soles. (B) Human parvovirus B19 causes an exanthem called erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease. Patients present with the characteristic slapped cheek rash and occasionally progress to a widespread pink morbilliform rash. (D) VZV causes varicella (chicken pox) and zoster. Both infections present with crops of vesicular lesions in diffuse (varicella) or dermatomal (zoster) distributions. (E) Rubeola is the causative virus for the measles exanthem. Measles includes a severe prodrome lasting 3 to 5 days including fever, cough, and coryza that is followed by the typical exanthematous eruption that includes intense mucous membrane erythema, pinpoint white macules on the buccal surface called Koplik spots, and progression to a diffuse rash of discrete erythematous macules and papules on the face, trunk, and extremities.

questions.stem: Sophie, a 3-year-old girl, was admitted to the pediatric outpatient clinic complaining from classic symptoms of measles including high fever, cough, and rash. Her parents are asking you about the complications of measles. You tell them that the MOST common complication of measles is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Otitis media is the most common complication of measles. Pneumonia is more serious and is the most common cause of death from measles.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Acute otitis media is the most common complication of measles and pneumonia is the most common cause of death in measles.

questions.stem: Emily, a 5-year-old girl, was brought to the pediatrician’s office by her worried parents after developing a high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes over the past few days. Upon examination, the pediatrician noticed characteristic small white spots on the inside of Emily’s cheeks. All the following are true about her condition EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: These spots have been reported in 50–70% of measles cases.

options.label: C
options.text: The rash begins on the forehead, behind the ears, and on the upper neck.

options.label: D
options.text: The rash fades over about 3 days in the same progression as it evolved.

options.label: E
options.text: In more severe cases, generalized lymphadenopathy may be present.

questions.initialExplanation:
The question is testing the duration and direction of the measles rash. The source marks D as the exception, while its explanation gives approximately 7 days rather than 3 days for fading.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
The source gives the answer as D and states in its answer line: “the rash fades over about 7 days in the same progression as it evolved, often leaving a fine desquamation of skin in its wake.”

**Source discrepancy**  
The option says **about 3 days**, while the explanation says **about 7 days**. Both wordings are retained as shown; the PDF itself contains this discrepancy.

questions.stem: A 17-month-old previously healthy but unimmunized child develops fever, malaise, and upper respiratory symptoms, including cough, runny nose, and conjunctivitis, that worsen over several days. The fever increases gradually up to 39.5°C over several days. Two days later, an erythematous, maculopapular rash appears on the head and spreads from head to toe over the next 3 days. The fever resolves on the fourth day of the rash, which persists for about a week as does the cough. The most likely provisional diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation:
An unimmunized child with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a rash spreading from the head downward has a classic measles presentation.

---

# 5. Epstein–Barr Virus / Infectious Mononucleosis
questions.detailedExplanation: The most likely provisional diagnosis based on the provided symptoms is option E, measles. Measles typically presents with fever, malaise, and upper respiratory symptoms such as cough, runny nose, and conjunctivitis, followed by the characteristic erythematous, maculopapular rash that starts on the head and spreads downward. The fever often peaks before the rash appears and resolves shortly after the rash emerges. The duration of the rash and cough aligns with the typical course of measles, which can persist for about a week. Additionally, the fact that the child is unimmunized further increases the likelihood of measles, as vaccination is highly effective in preventing the disease.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with fever, fatigue, and sore throat. Examination reveals exudative pharyngitis, generalized lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show elevated WBC count with presence of atypical lymphocytes. What is the best action?

options.label: A
options.text: No participation in contact sports for next 2–4 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: 2-week treatment with oral acyclovir and prednisone

questions.initialExplanation:
EBV can cause splenomegaly, making the spleen vulnerable to rupture after trauma. Avoid contact sports for several weeks and until splenic enlargement has resolved; routine steroids or acyclovir are not indicated.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Signs and symptoms in this patient are consistent with infectious mononucleosis most likely caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). A presumptive diagnosis can be made with typical clinical presentation and presence of atypical lymphocytosis. Serologic testing can confirm the diagnosis. Very healthy adolescents with infectious mononucleosis experience severe complications. The most feared complication is splenic rupture which has a reported occurrence rate of 0.2% in adults and is usually associated with blunt trauma to the abdomen. Participation in contact sports should therefore be avoided for several weeks or until splenomegaly has resolved. Corticosteroids are indicated only if there is severe airway obstruction because of tonsillar enlargement. Acyclovir does not alter the course of the disease.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is seen in the ER because of a 3-week history of fever between 38.3°C and 38.9°C (101°F and 102°F), lethargy, and a 2.7-kg (6-lb) weight loss. Physical examination reveals marked cervical and inguinal adenopathy, enlarged tonsils with exudate, small hemorrhages on the soft palate, a WBC differential that has 50% lymphocytes (10% atypical), and a palpable spleen 2 cm below the left costal margin. Which of the following therapies should be initiated?

options.label: C
options.text: IV infusion of immunoglobulins and high-dose aspirin

questions.initialExplanation:
The findings strongly suggest EBV infectious mononucleosis. Because the spleen is enlarged, the key advice is to avoid contact sports to reduce the risk of splenic rupture.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: To prove a diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a triad of findings should be present. First, physical findings can include diffuse adenopathy, tonsillar enlargement, an enlarged spleen, small hemorrhages on the soft palate, and periorbital swelling. Second, the hematologic changes should reveal a predominance of lymphocytes with at least 10% of these cells being atypical. Third, the characteristic antibody response should be present. Traditionally, heterophil antibodies can be detected when confirming a diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis. These antibodies may not be present, however, particularly in young children. Alternatively, specific antibodies against viral antigens on the EBV can be measured. Antibodies to viral capsid antigen (VCA) and to anti-D early antigen are elevated prior to the appearance of EBV nuclear antigen (EBNA) and are therefore markers for acute infection. VCA IgG and EBNA persist for life, whereas anti-D disappears after 6 months. Adolescents with this condition, because of the enlarged spleen, should avoid contact sports until the splenomegaly has resolved. While some features of the other conditions can overlap with EBV infection, the totality of the presentation in the case strongly suggests EBV as the causative agent. Initiation of zidovudine would be indicated if the child were proven to have HIV disease. IV acyclovir might be indicated for varicella infection. IV infusion of immunoglobulins and high dose aspirin is indicated for Kawasaki disease, which is usually not seen at this age. Intramuscular penicillin might be helpful in streptococcal pharyngitis, but atypical lymphocytes are not usually seen with this condition.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl presented 3 days ago to an urgent care clinic at her local pharmacy with complaints of 4 days of fever, runny nose, sore throat with exudates, and fatigue. She was prescribed amoxicillin for presumed streptococcal pharyngitis and presents today to her pediatrician’s clinic with a rash on her trunk and extremities. On examination, she is mildly ill-appearing and her temperature is 38.3°C. Her left tympanic membrane is dull and opaque without erythema. Her pharynx is erythematous and her tonsils have white exudates. Her abdomen is soft and a spleen tip is palpable. She has an erythematous macular rash on her trunk and extremities that spares her palms and soles. Of the following, what is the most likely cause of her presentation?
questions.initialExplanation:
A teenager or child with exudative pharyngitis, splenomegaly, and a rash after amoxicillin is suggestive of EBV infectious mononucleosis rather than a true immediate allergic reaction.

---

# 6. Varicella (Chickenpox)
questions.detailedExplanation: Epstein-Barr virus. Infectious mononucleosis is a viral syndrome characterized by fatigue, fever, lymphadenopathy, sore throat, exudative pharyngitis, headache, splenomegaly, and rarely a faint morbilliform rash. It is most often caused by infection with Epstein-Barr virus and affects children from school-age to adolescence. Because diagnosis is often made based on suggestive history and physical examinations, antibiotic therapy with penicillins or macrolides is often prescribed for concurrent diagnosis of otitis media or bacterial pharyngitis. The presentation and rash in the vignette are typical for patients with clinically diagnosed infectious mononucleosis receiving amoxicillin therapy. (A, B, C) Infections with influenza virus, *S. pyogenes*, and *S. pneumoniae* are not associated with rash eruption following antibiotic therapy. (E) The rash described is not characteristic of anaphylaxis or drug rash. These reactions are mediated by mast cell degranulation and more commonly lead to urticarial eruptions. Skin rash alone without involvement of other systems is not sufficient to diagnose anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old unimmunized child presents with fever and vesicular rash. You notice about 300 lesions, some of which were crusted. You suspect varicella infection. Which of the following is a TRUE statement about varicella?

options.label: A
options.text: It has an incubation period of 5–7 days.

options.label: B
options.text: The rash is confluent, centrifugal, and pustular.

options.label: C
options.text: It is associated with Koplik spots.

options.label: D
options.text: There is a high risk of shingles.

options.label: E
options.text: It can cause visceral dissemination in the immunocompromised host.

questions.initialExplanation:
Varicella causes crops of itchy lesions in different stages. Immunocompromised patients, especially those with impaired T-cell function, are at risk of severe disseminated disease.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The rash of varicella follows an incubation period of 10–21 days. There is then onset of a very pruritic rash, with crops of lesions that begin as papules and progress to vesicles and finally crusted scabs. Typically, all three stages are identified on clinical examination. Fever usually is mild to moderate. While a generally self-limited and benign course is noted, severe disease may occur occasionally in the otherwise healthy host, especially adolescents and adults. A progressive and severe disease with visceral dissemination is seen in 30%–50% of children with lymphoproliferative malignancies, solid tumors, or posttransplantation with the development of hepatitis, encephalitis, and pneumonia. Fatal disease has also been reported in those treated with high-dose corticosteroids and in those with other defects of T-cell function.

questions.stem: Acyclovir is sometimes needed for the treatment of chicken pox in children. In which of the following situations acyclovir is NOT indicated?

options.label: A
options.text: A 13-year-old with a negative past medical history

options.label: B
options.text: A 2-year-old who had contact with his 4-year-old sibling who has chickenpox

options.label: C
options.text: A 6-year-old who is taking aspirin for a prolonged time

options.label: D
options.text: A 5-year-old who is receiving treatment for leukemia

options.label: E
options.text: A 9-year-old who is currently taking corticosteroids for nephrotic syndrome

questions.initialExplanation:
Routine acyclovir prophylaxis is not indicated for an otherwise healthy young child after exposure. Older children and patients with chronic illness, aspirin or steroid use, or immunocompromise may need treatment consideration.

---

# 7. Parvovirus B19 (Erythema Infectiosum)
questions.detailedExplanation:
There is no need to use acyclovir prophylactically in otherwise healthy children who have been exposed to chickenpox, as they typically handle the infection well without complications. Acyclovir is generally reserved for use in patients who are at higher risk of severe disease.

Oral acyclovir may be considered for children older than 12 years, persons who have chronic disease, and persons who are taking chronic aspirin or corticosteroid therapy. Intravenous acyclovir should be used for immunocompromised patients.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old child presents to your office with a high fever, and an intense, red rash on the cheeks with circumoral pallor. What is the most likely etiology of this febrile exanthem?
questions.initialExplanation:
A bright “slapped-cheek” rash with circumoral pallor is typical of erythema infectiosum, caused by parvovirus B19.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical manifestations of human parvovirus B-19 include erythema infectiosum (healthy child), polyarthropathy syndrome (adults especially women), chronic anemia/pure red cell aplasia (immunocompromised hosts), transient aplastic crisis (sickle cell patients), and hydrops fetalis/congenital anemia (fetus). Erythema infectiosum is most commonly diagnosed and easily recognized. A distinctive rash featuring a “slapped cheek” appearance is noted that is often associated with circumoral pallor. Coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71 are causes of hand-foot-and-mouth syndrome. Enterovirus 71 is also associated with encephalitis. Adenovirus is not associated with a characteristic exanthem, however it may cause conjunctivitis. Rubeola virus is the causative agent of measles, and generally presents with a triad of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, as well as Koplik spots and rash.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has a mild febrile illness with mild URI symptoms. She has an erythematous rash on both cheeks. Her pregnant mother had arthralgias of the hands, wrists, knees, and ankles a week ago. What should be the next action?

options.label: A
options.text: Closely monitor the child’s sibling who has spherocytosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Exclude the child from daycare until rash has resolved.

options.label: C
options.text: Exclude the pregnant daycare providers until no further cases are diagnosed for 2 weeks.

options.label: E
options.text: Give the sibling with spherocytosis IVIG.

questions.initialExplanation:
Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid precursor cells and can trigger aplastic crisis in people with chronic hemolytic disorders such as hereditary spherocytosis. The sibling should therefore be monitored. The source states that IVIG postexposure prophylaxis is not indicated.

---

# 8. Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
questions.detailedExplanation: The child and mother exhibit classical symptoms of human parvovirus B19 infection also called fifth disease or erythema infectiosum. Prodromal symptoms are usually mild and diagnosis is often made on the characteristic rash appearance. Initially the rash starts on the face and children have what is often described as a “slapped-cheek” appearance. The rash spreads readily to the rest of the body with a diffuse macular erythema. Central clearing of the macules then occurs rapidly and gives the rash a lacy, reticulated appearance. Joint symptoms are very common in adults and may be the only clinical manifestation of parvovirus B19 infection. The primary target of parvovirus B19 is the erythroid cell line. Children with erythema infectiosum are most infectious prior to the onset of the rash, therefore, exclusion from school or day care after the rash develops is not indicated. Pregnant women in day care or schools need not be excluded. Parvovirus B19 has also been associated with hydrops fetalis in pregnant women. It can also cause a more serious transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic hemolytic diseases. Postexposure prophylaxis with IVIG for pregnant women or patients with chronic hematologic disorders is not indicated.

questions.stem: The mother of a family who declines immunization develops paroxysmal cough. Her infant is subsequently admitted to the hospital with apneic episodes. Which of the following white blood cell counts is most suggestive of pertussis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Pertussis classically produces marked absolute lymphocytosis, often with a total white blood cell count around 20,000–30,000/mm³.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Pertussis is usually associated with a marked absolute lymphocytosis. Peripheral white blood cell counts in the range of 20,000–30,000/mm³ with a majority of lymphocytes are characteristic of this infection. This is a useful and important diagnostic feature.

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant presents with apnea. The infant was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. The mother of this baby had rhinorrhea and cough that started 3 weeks ago and now she has a severe persistent cough with post-tussive emesis. Which treatment should be initiated?
questions.initialExplanation:
A neonate with apnea and a mother with prolonged paroxysmal cough should be treated for suspected pertussis. Azithromycin is the preferred option among those listed.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: There are many causes of apnea in infants. The extent of the diagnostic workup depends on many factors such as history and physical examination findings. In this case, the symptoms of the mother should raise significant concern for the presence of pertussis, a well-recognized cause for apnea in young infants. Pertussis, caused by *Bordetella pertussis*, is endemic and the annual incidence has risen in the past year. Coughing adolescents and adults currently are the major reservoir for *B pertussis*. Erythromycin for 14 days in the past has been the standard treatment but current recommendations suggest azithromycin is effective and a shorter duration of therapy is needed. It should be instituted when pertussis is suspected or confirmed to limit the spread of infection; the clinical benefit to the patient who has been coughing for longer than 2 weeks is negligible. New vaccines recently have been licensed for booster immunizations of adolescents and adults (Tdap) and will hopefully serve to reduce the risk of exposure of young infants to the pool of susceptible older patients.

questions.stem: The 3-year-old sister of a newborn baby develops a cough diagnosed as pertussis by nasopharyngeal culture. The mother gives a history of having been immunized as a child. Which of the following is a correct statement regarding this clinical situation?

options.label: A
options.text: The mother has no risk of acquiring the disease because she was immunized.

options.label: B
options.text: Hyperimmune globulin is effective in protecting the infant.

options.label: C
options.text: The risk to the infant depends on the immune status of the mother.

options.label: D
options.text: Erythromycin should be administered to the infant.

options.label: E
options.text: The 3-year-old sister should be immediately immunized with an additional dose of pertussis vaccine.

questions.initialExplanation:
Maternal vaccination does not reliably protect a newborn from pertussis exposure. The source recommends erythromycin for the exposed infant; hyperimmune globulin is not effective.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Newborn infants exposed to pertussis are at considerable risk of being infected regardless of the immune status of the mother. In contrast to other childhood infectious diseases, pertussis is not entirely prevented by transplacentally acquired antibody. Hyperimmune globulin is ineffective and not recommended. Natural immunity conferred by infection is lifelong. Because immunity acquired by immunization declines with age, however, many adults who were immunized in infancy are susceptible to pertussis. The Tdap vaccine has been introduced specifically to address this waning immunity; now, instead of merely receiving a scheduled tetanus (and diphtheria) booster with Td, adults may receive the Tdap which includes a pertussis booster. Erythromycin achieves high concentrations in respiratory secretions and is effective in eliminating organisms from the respiratory tract of patients. In exposed, susceptible persons, erythromycin may be effective in preventing or lessening severity of the disease if administered during the preparoxysmal stage. Immunization against pertussis is unnecessary if the patient has had culture-proven pertussis.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old female develops a persistent cough with progressively worsening paroxysms and cyanosis. There is occasional post-tussive emesis. The child is afebrile. Between coughing spells, the physical examination is normal. Her birth weight was 3.4 kg. She is a breastfed baby, had never been vaccinated yet. There is no history of consanguinity or early infant deaths in relatives with a negative family history of reactive airways disease. The white blood cell count on the patient is 32,000/mm³, with 80% lymphocytes and 2% mononuclear cells. What is the most appropriate next step at this time?

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat the blood count in 24 hours

questions.initialExplanation:
Paroxysmal cough, cyanosis, post-tussive vomiting, and marked lymphocytosis strongly suggest pertussis. Start azithromycin and provide supportive monitoring.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most appropriate next step in this scenario is to prescribe oral azithromycin. The presentation of persistent cough with worsening paroxysms, cyanosis, and post-tussive emesis in a 6-month-old infant, particularly with a high white blood cell count predominantly consisting of lymphocytes, suggests a likely diagnosis of pertussis, also known as whooping cough.

Given the severity of the symptoms and the potential for complications in infants, initiating antibiotic treatment with azithromycin is crucial. Azithromycin is effective in treating pertussis and can help reduce the severity and duration of symptoms, as well as limit transmission to others. Additionally, providing supportive care, such as ensuring hydration and monitoring for any respiratory distress, is important in managing the condition.

questions.stem: There has been a recent increase in cases of pertussis in your community. When counselling a family who declines immunization, you should inform them of the common manifestations of pertussis. Which of the following is a typical presentation of pertussis infection?

options.label: A
options.text: 4 or 5 days of high fever followed by croupy cough

options.label: B
options.text: Sudden onset of fever and cough

options.label: C
options.text: Gradual onset of cough, followed by abrupt onset of fever and whooping

options.label: D
options.text: Mild upper respiratory symptoms followed by paroxysmal cough

questions.initialExplanation:
Pertussis starts like a mild upper respiratory infection, then progresses to repeated severe coughing fits. A high fever is not typical.

---

# 9. Meningococcal Disease / Meningococcemia / Sepsis
questions.detailedExplanation: Pertussis classically begins with a catarrhal stage indistinguishable from a common cold and lasts up to a week. This is followed by gradual worsening of the cough, finally reaching the paroxysmal stage, characterized by thick, tenacious secretions and fits of forceful coughing that often end in a whoop as the child is finally able to take a full breath. Fever is usually mild or absent.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has been hospitalized for 2 days with *Neisseria meningitidis* meningitis that has been confirmed by culture. He is responding well to intravenous antibiotics therapy. He has a healthy 8-year-old twin brother. Of the following, the best choice for prophylaxis for his twin brother is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Household contacts of invasive meningococcal disease need chemoprophylaxis. Rifampicin is the answer specified by this source.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
The best choice for prophylaxis for the twin brother of a child with *Neisseria meningitidis* is **D. Rifampicin**.

Rifampicin is recommended for prophylactic treatment in close contacts of individuals diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. This antibiotic is effective in eradicating the *Neisseria meningitidis* bacteria from the nasopharynx, thereby reducing the risk of developing the disease. Close contacts, especially household members like a twin brother, are at increased risk of contracting meningococcal meningitis, making prophylaxis crucial.

Rifampicin is therefore the standard choice for prophylaxis in children who have been in close contact with cases of meningococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following drug regimens is the most appropriate chemoprophylaxis for adult household contacts of a child with meningococcal meningitis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Close household contacts have a much higher risk of meningococcal infection. This question specifies adult contacts and the source identifies single-dose ciprofloxacin.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Household contacts of those with meningococcal disease are at 500–1000 times greater risk for acquisition of meningococcal infection than the general population. Although several drug regimens for prophylaxis of contacts of meningococcal disease are acceptable, the primary regimen recommended at this time is rifampin, 10 mg/kg every 12 hours (q12h) for a total of four doses for children and a single dose of ciprofloxacin for those older than 18 years.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old adolescent presents with temperature of 103.1°F (39.5°C) and purpuric skin lesions. The child is found to have a blood pressure of 60/30 and heart rate of 180 with bounding pulses and a respiratory rate of 40. What infectious agent is the most likely to cause the above symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation:
Fever, rapidly progressive purpura, and shock are classic for meningococcemia. The purpura fulminans reflects severe systemic infection and may indicate DIC.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Although the combination of fever, hemorrhagic eruption, and shock can be seen with bacteremic infection caused by a wide variety of organisms including *H. influenzae*, *S. pneumoniae*, *S. aureus*, and beta-hemolytic streptococcus, this combination of findings is most commonly seen with meningococcal (*N. meningitidis*) infection. The hemorrhagic skin lesions (purpura fulminans) suggest disseminated intravascular coagulation, an ominous prognostic sign.

questions.stem: A three-year-old girl is rushed to the emergency department by her concerned parents due to a sudden onset of high fever, rapid breathing, and lethargy. Over the past two days, she had been mildly irritable with a slight cough, but this morning she became markedly less responsive and developed a blotchy rash. Her medical history is notable for a recent ear infection treated with antibiotics. Upon examination, she displays signs of hypotension and tachycardia, with cold extremities and delayed capillary refill, indicating poor perfusion. Most crucial step for management her condition is:
questions.initialExplanation:
The source selects prompt IV antibiotics as the key action in this sepsis question. The child also has signs of shock and poor perfusion, so the clinical vignette describes an emergency requiring rapid sepsis management.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most crucial step for managing sepsis in a three-year-old child is **A - Intravenous antibiotics**. This step is critical because sepsis is a systemic response to infection, and the primary goal is to eliminate the underlying infection as quickly as possible to prevent further progression of the disease. Intravenous antibiotics allow for rapid administration and high serum levels of the medication, which are essential for combating the widespread infection efficiently.

Here’s why the other options, though important, are not the most crucial:

- **B - Monitoring vitals** is essential for assessing the child’s condition and response to treatment, but it is secondary to initiating treatment.
- **C - Fluid resuscitation** is vital for managing sepsis, especially in stabilizing blood pressure and improving circulation, but the initial focus must be on treating the cause of the sepsis.
- **D - Vasopressors and inotropic agents** are used to support blood pressure and heart function if the child does not respond to fluid resuscitation alone, but this is a later step after addressing the infection.
- **E - Blood and blood product transfusion** may be necessary if there are complications like severe anemia or coagulopathies, but again, it is not the first-line action.

Therefore, initiating intravenous antibiotics is the most critical and immediate step when managing a child with sepsis, as it directly targets the infection causing the systemic inflammatory response.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old adolescent presents with temperature of 103.1°F (39.5°C) and purpuric skin lesions. The child is found to have a blood pressure of 60/30 and heart rate of 180 with bounding pulses and a respiratory rate of 40; what is the first priority in management of the child?

options.label: E
options.text: Complete blood count and blood culture

questions.initialExplanation:
This patient is in shock. The immediate priority among the listed choices is circulatory support with IV fluids; cultures and antibiotics should follow rapidly when feasible.

---

# 10. Tuberculosis
questions.detailedExplanation: While all of the answers are important in clinical evaluation and treatment of the child with meningococcemia, starting with the ABCs of basic life support still applies. As airway management choices are not available, addressing the circulatory status with intravenous fluids would be the most appropriate initial step. Antibiotic administration should occur rapidly and preferably after blood cultures have been drawn. Initial CSF evaluation including culture is helpful, but is not always feasible depending on the degree of illness of the child. It should be completed prior to antibiotics when possible; however it can still be useful after antibiotic administration to evaluate for pleocytosis.

questions.stem: A ten-year-old girl presents to the clinic with persistent cough, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. Her mother mentions that the cough is worse at night and occasionally the girl coughs up small amounts of blood. She also adds that she has been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 6 months ago and was prescribed anti-tuberculous medications. The major cause behind secondary resistance in tuberculosis treatment is:

options.label: A
options.text: Lack of steroids at the start of therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Being infected with resistant strain of mycobacteria

questions.initialExplanation:
Irregular treatment or stopping TB drugs early allows surviving organisms to persist and select for drug resistance. Adherence to the full prescribed regimen is essential.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The major cause behind secondary resistance in tuberculosis (TB) treatment is E. Poor adherence to treatment. This occurs when patients do not follow their prescribed medication regimen correctly, either by not taking the drugs consistently or by prematurely stopping the therapy. When TB medications are taken irregularly or discontinued too soon, it allows tubercle bacilli that are not completely eradicated to mutate and develop resistance to the drugs being used. This results in a form of the disease that is harder to treat with standard TB drugs, often requiring second-line medications, which can be more toxic and less effective.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and cough. A diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis infection was made based on chest X-ray and tuberculin skin testing. The mother of the child asks when her child may return to day care or school. When can a child diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis infection return to day care or school?

options.label: A
options.text: As soon as effective therapy has been instituted

options.label: C
options.text: Once negative sputum smears are confirmed

options.label: E
options.text: Whether they are receiving therapy or not

questions.initialExplanation:
The source states that children with uncomplicated primary pulmonary TB are generally noninfectious and may attend school or child care while receiving therapy. More extensive, cavitary, laryngeal, or smear-positive disease requires precautions.

---

# 11. Diphtheria
questions.detailedExplanation: In general, children with uncomplicated primary pulmonary tuberculosis are noninfectious and do not require isolation. This is believed to relate to the scanty sputum production, lack of expectoration, and the small number of organisms that can be recovered from sputum or gastric culture. In contrast, children with laryngeal involvement, with cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis, extensive pulmonary infection, positive sputum AFB smears, or suspected congenital tuberculosis should be considered contagious and appropriate precautions should be taken. Children with tuberculosis disease can attend school or child care if they are receiving therapy.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presented to the emergency room with a severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and a high-grade fever. Upon examination, the child exhibited a grayish-white membrane covering the tonsils and throat, along with swollen neck lymph nodes. Of the following, the mainstay of therapy is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Diphtheria toxin causes the major systemic injury. Give diphtheria antitoxin promptly on clinical suspicion; antibiotics are also used but do not replace antitoxin.

---

# 12. Rubella / Congenital Rubella Syndrome
questions.detailedExplanation: The picture is suggestive of Diphtheria. Specific antitoxin is the mainstay of therapy and should be administered on the basis of clinical diagnosis. The role of antimicrobial therapy is to halt toxin production, treat localized infection, and prevent transmission of the organism to contacts.

questions.stem: You are counseling a primigravid woman who has been found to be rubella nonimmune on prenatal laboratory evaluation. She asks you if her fetus is at risk for malformations. When is maternal infection with rubella virus most commonly associated with congenital defects?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first 4 weeks of gestation

options.label: C
options.text: In the third or fourth month

questions.initialExplanation:
The risk of congenital defects is highest when maternal rubella infection occurs very early in pregnancy, especially during the first four weeks.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Congenital malformations, stillbirths, and abortions all have been reported with rubella infection during pregnancy. The congenital rubella syndrome consists of ophthalmologic, cardiac, auditory, and neurologic abnormalities with rates as high as 85% if infection occurs in the first 4 weeks of gestation, decreasing to 20%–30% during the second month, and 5% during the third or fourth month. These infants may continue to excrete rubella virus for 1 year or more after birth and pose a risk of infection for susceptible hosts.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant was diagnosed with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), a condition resulting from the mother’s rubella infection during pregnancy. The parents were devastated upon learning about the diagnosis, as they had not realized the severity of the consequences of maternal rubella infection during pregnancy. The MOST common finding among infants with congenital rubella syndrome is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common finding in congenital rubella syndrome according to the source.

---

# 13. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
questions.detailedExplanation: Nerve deafness is the single most common finding among infants with congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.stem: An infant is born to a mother who acquired primary CMV infection during pregnancy. What will be the most likely finding in this infant?
questions.initialExplanation:
Most congenitally CMV-infected infants are asymptomatic or have subclinical infection at birth, although some may later develop hearing loss.

---

questions.detailedExplanation: Approximately 1%–4% of pregnant women in the United States acquire primary CMV infection during pregnancy. A fetus may become infected as a result of primary and recurrent maternal infection, but risk for fetal infection is greater with maternal primary CMV infection. Only 5% of all infected infants show the full spectrum of congenital CMV disease with intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, purpura, microcephaly, and intracranial calcifications. Another 5% of congenitally infected infants have mild infection. About 90% of congenitally infected infants have subclinical but chronic infection. Sensorineural hearing loss occurs in approximately 7% of infected infants and can even occur in infants who were asymptomatic at birth.

questions.stem: Mohammed is a 5-month-old infant who has been seen repeatedly by his general practitioner because of colic. His mother brings him to the Accident and Emergency department as he is having episodes of suddenly throwing his head and arms forward. These episodes occur in repetitive bursts. His mother thinks they may be something more than just colic, as he is now not smiling or supporting his head as well as he did previously. He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery and has no other medical problems. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.label: C
options.text: Childhood Rolandic epilepsy (benign epilepsy with centro-temporal spikes)

questions.initialExplanation:
Repeated clusters of sudden flexor or extensor spasms in an infant, especially with developmental regression, suggest infantile spasms. The characteristic EEG pattern is hypsarrhythmia.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Infantile spasms (West Syndrome) Correct. Vijay has violent flexor spasms of the head, trunk and limbs followed by extension. These are known as infantile spasms. He also has developmental regression. The EEG shown is characteristic, called hypsarrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with chronic seizures involving the left arm and leg. He is febrile, lethargic and meningeal irritation signs are non-evident. Emergent head computed tomography scan shows low density in the right temporal lobe. Of the following, the most appropriate next step is:

options.label: C
options.text: Brain magnetic resonance imaging with contrast

questions.initialExplanation:
Fever, altered mental status, seizures, and a temporal-lobe lesion strongly raise concern for HSV encephalitis. Treatment with IV acyclovir should begin promptly rather than waiting for definitive confirmation.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation along with temporal lobe finding highly suggest HSV encephalitis. Acyclovir is the drug of choice for treating HSV encephalitis. It helps to inhibit viral replication and improve outcomes when administered promptly. Due to the potential severity of herpes simplex encephalitis, especially in the temporal lobe, early initiation of acyclovir is recommended even before the definite diagnosis is confirmed.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl was brought to the emergency department because of lower limb weakness for one-day. One week ago, she had a 3-day episode of flu-like symptoms that resolved without treatment. She has not yet received any routine childhood vaccinations. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the right lower extremity and absent in the left lower extremity. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid shows a leukocyte count of 38 cells/mm3 (68% lymphocytes), a protein concentration of 49 mg/dL, and a glucose concentration of 60 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.initialExplanation:
Polio can cause asymmetric acute flaccid weakness with reduced or absent reflexes. A preceding viral-like illness, lack of vaccination, and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis support the diagnosis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Poliomyelitis is caused by the poliovirus and typically presents with acute flaccid paralysis, which manifests as sudden onset weakness or paralysis of one or more limbs. The asymmetrical involvement of the lower extremities, with absent deep tendon reflexes in one leg and diminished reflexes in the other leg, is characteristic of poliomyelitis. The absence of routine childhood vaccinations, including the polio vaccine, further raises concern for susceptibility to poliovirus infection. The patient’s history of flu-like symptoms preceding the onset of lower limb weakness is consistent with the prodromal phase of poliovirus infection, which may include fever, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis findings of lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly elevated protein concentration, and normal glucose concentration are nonspecific but can be seen in poliomyelitis.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old female patient with a long history of epilepsy, controlled with medication for the past years, visits her neurologist for a routine follow-up. She reports recent concerns including significant hair loss and weight gain. Her medical history is otherwise unremarkable, and she has not started any new medications. Weight gain and alopecia are side effects of the following antiepileptic drugs AEDs?
questions.initialExplanation:
Valproic acid can cause weight gain and hair loss. It can also cause hyperammonemia, tremor, menstrual irregularities, and potentially serious liver or pancreatic toxicity.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The source states: “Side effects of valproic acid: weight gain, hyperammonemia, tremor, alopecia, and menstrual irregularities. Serious: hepatic and pancreatic toxicity.”

questions.stem: A 15-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department shortly after a 2-minute episode of rhythmic eye blinking and uncontrolled shaking of all limbs. She was unresponsive during the episode. For the past few days, the girl has had a fever and mild nasal congestion. Her immunizations are up-to-date. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). She is sleepy but opens her eyes when her name is called. The neck is supple with normal range of motion. An oral dose of acetaminophen is administered. On re-evaluation, the girl is alert and playing with toys in the examination room. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Perform a CT scan of the head

questions.initialExplanation:
A well-appearing child who returns to baseline after a brief simple febrile seizure and has no signs of CNS infection can usually be discharged with parental advice and reassurance. Routine EEG, CT, or antiseizure medication is not indicated in this scenario.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: This patient has regained normal mental status after her first simple febrile seizure, which was likely related to a viral upper respiratory syndrome. She has no history or examination findings that would suggest CNS infection (meningitis or encephalitis) and can safely be discharged with reassurance. While the exact pathophysiology of simple febrile seizures is unknown, high fever, viral infection (especially HHV-6 and influenza), a family history of febrile seizure, and recent immunization (especially DTP and MMR) are all known risk factors.

questions.stem: You are presented with the case of an 18-year-old patient who has a medical history marked by recurrent fractures and optic gliomas. Recently, this patient has been diagnosed with a malignant schwannoma. Which underlying medical condition is most frequently associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.initialExplanation:
NF1 is an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous disorder associated with café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic gliomas, and characteristic bone lesions.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a progressive neurocutaneous syndrome that results from a defect in neural crest differentiation and migration during the early stages of development. It has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance; the gene locus has been identified on chromosome 17. Any organ or system can be affected, neurologic complications are frequent, and patients are at high risk of developing malignant neoplasms of various types. The presence of any two of the following confirms the diagnosis of NF1: (1) Five or more café-au-lait spots over 5 mm in diameter in prepubertal patients; six or more over 15 mm in diameter in postpubertal patients; (2) axillary freckling; (3) two or more Lisch nodules (hamartomas of the iris); (4) two or more neurofibromas, typically involving the skin and appearing during adolescence or pregnancy, or one plexiform neurofibroma involving a nerve tract present at birth; (5) bony lesions leading to pathologic fracture and kyphoscoliosis; (6) optic glioma; (7) NF1 in a first degree relative.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is rushed to the emergency department by her parents due to a sudden onset of high fever, severe headache, and vomiting. Over the past few hours, she has become increasingly lethargic and irritable. Her medical history is unremarkable, and she is up-to-date with her vaccinations. On examination, she appears acutely ill and drowsy. She has a temperature of 39.5°C, and her neck is stiff when flexed. The MOST common neurologic sequela of his condition is?
questions.initialExplanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss is a frequent and important complication of bacterial meningitis. Hearing should be assessed in every child with bacterial meningitis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common sequela of bacterial meningitis and, usually, is already present at the time of initial presentation. It is a result of cochlear infection and occurs in as many as 30% of patients with pneumococcal meningitis, 10% with meningococcal, and 5-20% of those with H. influenzae type b meningitis. Hearing loss may also be caused by direct inflammation of the auditory nerve. All patients with bacterial meningitis should undergo careful audiologic assessment before or soon after discharge from the hospital. Frequent reassessment on an outpatient basis is indicated for patients who have a hearing deficit.

questions.stem: A 2-week-old male presents with irritability, decreased feeding, and fever. Cerebrospinal fluid examination reveals cloudy fluid with 5500 WBC/mm3 and a low glucose. Gram stain revealed no bacteria. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
questions.initialExplanation:
A neonate with fever, poor feeding, cloudy CSF, high white-cell count, and low CSF glucose is concerning for bacterial meningitis. Group B Streptococcus is a major cause of meningitis in this age group.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The elevated white blood cell count and low glucose in the cerebrospinal fluid are most suggestive of a bacterial pathogen, of which group B streptococcus would be the most likely. Though a Gram stain of CSF provides presumptive evidence in the evaluation of meningitis, it frequently is misleading. The gold standard for diagnosis of a bacterial pathogen is the culture of the spinal fluid.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presented with headache, fever and neck stiffness. Acute bacterial meningitis is suspected and further tests to confirm the suspected diagnosis is being considered. Contraindications to performing a lumbar puncture include the following EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: Suspected mass lesion of the brain

options.label: B
options.text: Suspected mass lesion of the spinal cord

options.label: C
options.text: Symptoms and signs of impending cerebral herniation

options.label: D
options.text: Skin infection at the site of the lumbar puncture

questions.initialExplanation:
The source identifies severe thrombocytopenia below 20 × 10^9/L as a contraindication. A platelet count of 49,000 is therefore the exception in this question's stated answer key.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Thrombocytopenia with a platelet count <20 × 10^9/L is a contraindication for LP.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with a known diagnosis of cerebral palsy is brought to a pediatric neurologist by his parents due to recent onset of seizure activity. The boy was diagnosed with cerebral palsy shortly after birth, which was attributed to complications during delivery leading to a period of hypoxia. He has been receiving physical therapy and occupational therapy, which have helped with his motor skills and independence in daily activities. The MOST common type of cerebral palsy (CP) associated with seizures is?
questions.initialExplanation:
Spastic hemiplegia affects one side of the body and is the answer specified in the source for the CP subtype associated with seizures.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Individuals with Spastic Hemiplegia (Option A) experience increased muscle tone and stiffness on one side of their body, affecting either the left or right side.

questions.stem: There are several predictors of epilepsy after febrile seizures, the highest percent of the risk factor for subsequent epilepsy after febrile seizure is?
questions.initialExplanation:
Among the risk factors listed, a focal complex febrile seizure carries the highest subsequent epilepsy risk in the source's explanation.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Focal complex febrile seizure has 29% risk for subsequent epilepsy. While all these factors can increase the risk of epilepsy following a febrile seizure, focal complex febrile seizures represent the highest risk. This is likely due to the more significant underlying brain involvement suggested by the focal nature of these seizures.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old female presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of runny nose and fever to 38.8°C. On examination, her temperature is 39.3°C, HR 140 beats per minute, and a RR 30 times per minute. She is alert and playful with copious rhinorrhea. After the examination is complete, she becomes stiff and displays tonic-clonic movements of all four extremities. Rectal acetaminophen is given. The patient quickly becomes alert, happy, and playful. She is afebrile and has a normal examination. All ordered tests are normal. Which of the following management plans is most appropriate at this time?

options.label: A
options.text: Discharge home after instructions regarding home management of fever and seizures

options.label: C
options.text: Discharge home with alternating doses of ibuprofen and acetaminophen every 3 hours for the next 3 days

questions.initialExplanation:
A child who has a brief simple febrile seizure, returns to normal, and has no concerning examination findings can generally go home with clear advice about fever, seizure first aid, and when to seek urgent care. Long-term antiseizure medication is not routinely used.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Febrile seizures are convulsions brought on by a fever in infants or small children. During a febrile seizure, it’s important to focus on preventing injury and ensuring the child’s safety. The seizure described was self-limited, and the child returned to a normal state of alertness and playfulness afterward. The normal physical examination and the absence of nuchal rigidity or other signs of serious illness suggest that this was a simple febrile seizure. The management of simple febrile seizures does not typically include antiseizure medications like phenytoin or phenobarbital for prevention, as the risks of these medications outweigh the benefits in most cases. Alternating doses of ibuprofen and acetaminophen are generally recommended for fever management, but not at fixed intervals for three days unless the fever persists. Admission for observation and MRI is not indicated in the absence of neurological signs or a complicated febrile seizure.

questions.stem: Jordan is a 7-year-old child born in Yemen who presents to the children’s outpatient department. His mother is concerned regarding a number of skin marks, which she has noticed over the last year. She was not initially concerned about them, but they are becoming more numerous and larger in size. She reports that Jordan’s father also had similar skin marks before he passed away from ‘cancer’. On examining Jordan you see the skin lesions shown in Fig. 29.2. He also has a large number of freckles in his axilla region. He has no other medical problems and is not on any medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Multiple café-au-lait macules together with axillary freckling and a compatible family history strongly support NF1.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
A. Ataxia telangiectasia: The skin lesions in ataxia telangiectasia are small dilated blood vessels near the surface of the skin or the mucous membranes.  
B. Friedreich ataxia: Friedreich ataxia does not present with skin lesions.  
C. Neurofibromatosis: Correct. The lesions seen in the image are café-au-lait spots. This is an autosomal dominant neurological disorder. There are criteria for making the diagnosis. This boy meets the diagnosis as he has six or more café-au-lait spots, has axilla freckles and it is likely he has a family history, related to his father.  
D. Sturge-Weber syndrome: In Sturge-Weber syndrome there is a port-wine stain present on the face.  
E. Tuberous sclerosis: In tuberous sclerosis there are a number of different skin lesions: depigmented, ‘ash leaf’-shaped patches, which fluoresce under ultraviolet light (Wood’s light), roughened patches of skin (shagreen patches) usually over the lumbar spine and/or adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromata) in a butterfly distribution over the bridge of the nose and cheeks.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy who had a simple brief febrile seizure comes to your clinic a day after his ED visit. He is currently afebrile, is happily pulling the sphygmomanometer off the wall, and is taking antibiotics for an ear infection diagnosed the previous day. His mother wants to know what to expect in the future regarding his neurologic status. You correctly tell her which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: He has no risk of further seizures because he was 2 years at the time of his first febrile seizure.

options.label: B
options.text: He will need to take anticonvulsant medications for 6 to 12 months to prevent further seizure activity.

options.label: C
options.text: You want to schedule an EEG and a magnetic resonance scan of his head.

options.label: D
options.text: Although he does have a risk of future febrile convulsions, seizures of his type are generally benign and he is likely to outgrow them.

options.label: E
options.text: This is an isolated disorder, and his children will not have seizures.

questions.initialExplanation:
Simple febrile seizures are usually benign and do not themselves increase mortality or epilepsy risk. Recurrence can occur, but most children outgrow them.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
Simple FS do not carry a risk of epilepsy or mortality, but it may recur in ~30% of infants & children after the first episode. However, there are several risk factors that can predict recurrence of FS including:  
Major criteria: age <1 yr, fever 38-39°C, and fever duration <24 hr (i.e. an infant with simple and short duration of fever).  
Minor criteria: family history of FS or epilepsy, complex FS, male, day care, and hyponatremia.  
If a patient has no risk factor, the recurrence rate is only 12%, but this number is doubled or tripled with increasing risk factors.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old girl is brought to the physician because she is unable to sit and has not learned how to crawl. She keeps her hips and elbows flexed and her parents have to use considerable force to passively extend her joints. She attained neck control at 4 months and could roll from front to back at 5 months of age. She does not engage in play, reach for toys, or maintain eye contact. She babbles and doesn't mimic sounds. She does not follow simple instructions. She is at the 25th percentile for length and 10th percentile for weight. Neurological examination shows increased muscle tone in all extremities. The ankle clonus and extensor plantar responses are present bilaterally. The Moro reflex is present. An MRI of the head shows periventricular leukomalacia. Which of the following is the most important risk factor for the development of this condition?
questions.initialExplanation:
Periventricular leukomalacia is strongly associated with prematurity and can injure developing motor pathways, increasing the risk of cerebral palsy.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation, including difficulty sitting, lack of crawling, joint stiffness, delayed developmental milestones, impaired play and social interaction, difficulty swallowing, and the presence of neurological signs like increased muscle tone, ankle clonus, and extensor plantar responses, suggests cerebral palsy. Cerebral palsy can be caused by various prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal factors, but in this case, the presence of periventricular leukomalacia seen on MRI is indicative of damage to the white matter around the lateral ventricles, often associated with prematurity.

questions.stem: The diagnosis of diffuse CNS infections depends on examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) obtained by lumbar puncture (LP). The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein may reach 3,000 (mg/dL) in which of following conditions?
questions.initialExplanation:
Very high CSF protein, potentially reaching 3,000 mg/dL, is described in the source as a feature of tuberculous meningitis, particularly when CSF flow is obstructed.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In tuberculous meningitis, CSF protein is 100-3,000; may be higher in presence of block, while in other options, it may reach 500.

questions.stem: The parents of a 21-month-old boy are concerned because he used to say a few words and more recently, he is just babbling with no recognizable words. They are worried these may be features of autism. Which of the following is a feature that characterizes autistic spectrum disorders?

options.label: B
options.text: Use of 2 word phrases by 18 months

options.label: E
options.text: Lack of sensitivity to textures or sounds

questions.initialExplanation:
Reduced eye contact and impaired social communication are common early concerns in autism spectrum disorder. The question's answer key identifies decreased eye contact.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired socialization, impaired verbal and nonverbal communication, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior. Early recognition of autism, preferably before the second year of life, is critical. Referral criteria in the second year of life include no pointing or waving by 18 months, a preference for solitary play, diminished eye contact, and an oversensitivity to textures and noises. Nystagmus is more likely to be associated with an ocular disorder. Lack of use of two-word phrases is a concern after the age of 2 years.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to the pediatrician by concerned parents who have observed motor difficulties and delayed milestones. The child has noticeable stiffness and spasticity in the lower extremities, with a tendency to walk on tiptoes. The parents are worried about the possibility of cerebral palsy. In cerebral palsy, one of the statements below is INAPPROPRIATE:

options.label: A
options.text: Baclofen have primarily been used in the management of spasticity

options.label: B
options.text: The diagnosis of cerebral palsy is generally based on laboratory tests

options.label: C
options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is the diagnostic neuroimaging study of choice

options.label: D
options.text: Cerebral palsy is the leading cause of childhood disability affecting function and development

options.label: E
options.text: Equinus, or toe walking, and varus or valgus of the hind foot is common in cerebral palsy

questions.initialExplanation:
Cerebral palsy is diagnosed mainly from the child's history, development, and neurologic examination. Brain MRI can help identify underlying brain injury, but routine laboratory tests do not establish the diagnosis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Cerebral palsy is primarily diagnosed based on clinical assessment and observation of motor impairments, developmental delays, and associated features. Laboratory tests are not the mainstay for diagnosing cerebral palsy.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is referred to a pediatric neurologist by her primary care physician due to a history of seizures and a distinctive facial birthmark. Since birth, she has had a large port-wine stain covering most of the left side of her face, including the eyelid. Her parents report that she experienced her first seizure at the age of two, characterized by twitching on the right side of her body. These seizure episodes have become more frequent and are accompanied by periods of temporary weakness in her right arm and leg. The facial port-wine stain of Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is characterized by the following EXCEPT

options.label: C
options.text: Always involves the upper face and eyelid

options.label: D
options.text: Its distribution is consistent with the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

options.label: E
options.text: Most children with facial port-wine stain have SWS

questions.initialExplanation:
A facial port-wine stain can occur without Sturge-Weber syndrome. The source notes that only a minority of children with a port-wine stain have SWS.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: It is important to note that not all children with facial port-wine stain have SWS. In fact, the overall incidence of SWS has been reported to be 8-33% in those with a Port-wine stain.

questions.stem: Examination of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of an 8-year-old, mildly febrile child with nuchal rigidity and intermittent stupor shows the following: WBCs 85/µL (all lymphocytes), negative Gram stain, protein 150 mg/dL, and glucose 15 mg/dL. A computed tomographic (CT) scan with contrast shows enhancement of the basal cisterns by the contrast material. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, high protein, very low glucose, and basal cistern enhancement are classic clues for tuberculous meningitis.
