**Source note:** The answer-key line says “Correct Answer is B,” while the label immediately below it prefixes the answer text with “A.” The answer text and option B match; the source's letter formatting is inconsistent.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
Included among those processes that can cause the clinical picture are viral meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, meningeal leukemia, and medulloblastoma, all of which can cause pleocytosis as well as elevated protein and lowered glucose concentrations in CSF. Of the four diseases (and the likely diagnosis of this patient), tuberculous meningitis is associated with the lowest glucose levels in CSF. The CT scan with contrast can be an excellent clue for diagnosing tuberculous meningitis. Exudate in the basal cisterns that shows enhancement by contrast material is typical; tubercles, ringed lucencies, edema, and infarction can be apparent; and hydrocephalus can develop. Confirmation with culture is mandatory. The x-ray of the chest will be likely to show signs of pulmonary tuberculosis. A high index of suspicion is necessary to diagnose tuberculous meningitis early.  
In pseudotumor cerebri, the constituents of CSF are generally normal except for low-protein content in some instances and high opening pressure. Acute bacterial disease must be considered for this patient, but typically causes polymorphonuclear cells and positive Gram stains. Neither tuberous sclerosis nor stroke typically cause these findings on CSF examination.

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-year-old bring her to the emergency center after she had a seizure. Although the parents report she was in a good state of health, the vital signs in the emergency center reveal a temperature of 39°C (102.2°F). She is now running around the room. Which part of the story would suggest the best outcome in this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: A CSF white cell count of 100/µL

options.label: D
options.text: The child was born prematurely with an intraventricular hemorrhage

options.label: E
options.text: The family reports the child to have had right-sided tonic-clonic activity only

questions.initialExplanation:
An associated, treatable infection such as otitis media can explain the fever in a child with a brief generalized febrile seizure. Prolonged or focal seizures and pre-existing neurologic injury are less reassuring features.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The child in the question likely had a febrile seizure. Febrile seizures usually occur in children between the ages of 9 months and 5 years, generally in association with upper respiratory illness, roseola, shigellosis, or gastroenteritis. The generalized seizures are mostly brief (2-5 minutes), and the CSF is normal. Since other more serious processes cause seizure and fever, each child must be carefully evaluated. Children younger than 12 to 18 months of age do not have a reliable neck examination for meningismus, so they will probably need a lumbar puncture to rule out CNS infection as a cause. In a simple febrile seizure, EEG and CNS imaging are not usually necessary. Infants who have seizures that are prolonged (longer than 15 minutes), focal, or lateralized, or who had neurologic problems before the febrile seizure (including intraventricular hemorrhage), are at a higher risk of developing an afebrile seizure disorder during the subsequent 5 to 7 years. CSF is usually normal after a seizure, so a pleocytosis requires evaluation for meningitis or encephalitis.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 1-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of irritability and fever for 2 days. His symptoms began shortly after returning from a family trip to Canada. His temperature is 39.2°C (102.5°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 92/55 mm Hg. Physical examination shows several purple spots over the trunk and extremities that are 1 mm in diameter. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A lumbar puncture is done; cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows abundant segmented neutrophils, decreased glucose concentration, and an increased protein concentration. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Ampicillin therapy for the patient and ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for contacts

options.label: B
options.text: Cefotaxime and vancomycin therapy for the patient and doxycycline prophylaxis for contacts

options.label: C
options.text: Vancomycin therapy for the patient and rifampin prophylaxis for contacts

options.label: D
options.text: Ceftriaxone and vancomycin therapy for the patient and rifampin prophylaxis for contacts

options.label: E
options.text: Cefotaxime and vancomycin therapy for the patient and no prophylaxis for contacts

questions.initialExplanation:
The petechial rash and bacterial CSF profile raise concern for meningococcal meningitis. Treat the patient urgently with the listed empiric regimen and provide prophylaxis to close contacts as specified in the source.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation, including fever, irritability, petechial rash, and abnormal CSF findings, raises concern for Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcal) meningitis. Prompt initiation of antibiotics is essential to treat the infection in the affected individual. Ceftriaxone and Vancomycin are commonly used for empiric treatment of bacterial meningitis, providing coverage against a range of pathogens. Additionally, considering the contagious nature of Neisseria meningitidis, prophylaxis for close contacts is crucial to prevent further spread. Rifampicin is one of the recommended prophylactic agents for contacts, helping to eradicate carriage of the bacteria.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is referred for new-onset seizures. Which of the following would mostly support a diagnosis of complex partial (psychomotor) seizures?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal mental state, consciousness, and responsiveness during seizure

options.label: E
options.text: Normal mental state, consciousness, and responsiveness after seizure

questions.initialExplanation:
Focal impaired-awareness seizures commonly include reduced responsiveness and automatisms such as lip-smacking or repetitive hand movements. A 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG pattern instead suggests absence seizures.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Complex partial seizures is the current name for what previously was termed temporal lobe or psychomotor seizures. Complex partial seizures are characterized by alterations of mental status, consciousness, or responsiveness. During the seizure, there may be confusion, emotional reactions, feelings of detachment, and hallucinations. Automatisms (semi purposeful but inappropriate motor acts) are frequent. There is no tonic or clonic component. Postictal confusion is common. The usual EEG finding is spike-wave activity over one or both temporal lobe regions. A three-per-second spike-and-wave pattern on EEG is characteristic of absence seizures.

questions.stem: On the second day of treatment for pneumococcal meningitis, a 10-month-old child who had been alert is noted to be lethargic. Serum electrolytes reveal: Na 120 meq/L; Cl 82 meq/L; K 3.1 meq/L; BUN 2 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause of the lethargy and electrolyte disturbance in this patient?
questions.initialExplanation:
CNS infections such as meningitis can trigger excess ADH release, causing water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. SIADH is the source's explanation for this child's lethargy and low sodium.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is a common complication of a variety of central nervous system problems, including bacterial meningitis. Usually the SIADH resolves as the meningitis is treated, even if a subdural effusion is present.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated in clinic for concerns of poor school performance and poor attention. She has had difficulty following along with the rest of her class and her teacher notes she frequently daydreams. In addition to asking both the mother and the teacher to fill out surveys to evaluate for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the pediatrician also orders an electroencephalogram (EEG). Of the following, which EEG finding is most consistent with this patient's presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: Spike discharges from the left temporal lobe

options.label: D
options.text: 6/second spike and wave discharge with photic stimulation

questions.initialExplanation:
Absence seizures cause brief staring spells with immediate return to activity. The classic EEG is generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave activity; ethosuximide is commonly used as initial therapy.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
The child in the vignette is having absence seizures. This type of childhood epilepsy is characterized by an abrupt pause in activity without loss of tone that lasts for several seconds and resolves as abruptly as it began with resumption of pre-seizure activities. Some children display automatisms during the seizure such as rapid eye-blinking or lip-smacking. There is no post-ictal state. (B, E) Because absence seizures may occur with a high frequency throughout the day, children often present with concerns for poor attention, but an EEG showing generalized 3/second spike and wave pattern is diagnostic for absence seizures. Ethosuximide is the antiepileptic treatment of choice for absence seizures.  
The remaining EEG findings are classic for other types of childhood epilepsy syndromes. Complex partial seizures may be characterized by a brief alteration of mental status with automatisms and could be confused with absence seizures. These seizures typically occur with less frequency than absence seizures and the disorder is less common among the pediatric population. (A) EEG findings of spike discharges in the temporal lobe are consistent with complex partial seizures. (C) Hypsarrhythmia, or a chaotic pattern of high-voltage, bilaterally asynchronous, slow-wave activity, is the EEG finding associated with infantile spasms. This type of epilepsy usually presents between 4 and 8 months of age and prognosis depends on the presence or absence of associated neurologic symptoms. (D) Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is a seizure disorder that presents during the early teenage years and is associated with significant myoclonic jerks especially during the morning and shows 4 to 6/second spike and wave discharge with photic stimulation. This type of epilepsy requires lifelong treatment.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic for a follow-up evaluation after experiencing his first febrile seizure two months ago. The seizure was a brief, generalized episode that occurred at the peak of a fever during a viral respiratory illness. The boy has fully recovered, and his medical history reveals no neurological issues or developmental delays. His immunizations are up to date, and there is no family history of epilepsy, although his older sister had a febrile seizure at the age of three. During the consultation, the pediatrician assesses the risk of recurrence. Regarding risk of febrile seizure recurrence, Major risk factors include?
questions.initialExplanation:
The source separates recurrence predictors into major and minor factors. Fever of 38-39°C is listed as a major factor; family history, daycare, male sex, and hyponatremia are listed as minor factors.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
Risk factors for recurrence of febrile seizure include:  
**MAJOR**  
- Age <1 yr  
- Duration of fever <24 hr  
- Fever 38-39°C (100.4-102.2°F)  
**MINOR**  
- Family history of febrile seizures  
- Family history of epilepsy  
- Complex febrile seizure  
- Daycare  
- Male gender  
- Lower serum sodium at time of presentation

questions.stem: In a pediatric emergency department, a 9-year-old child is admitted with acute respiratory insufficiency. The child’s parents report a recent viral illness preceding the sudden onset of limb weakness and difficulty in breathing. On examination, the child decreased lung function requiring immediate respiratory support. Acute respiratory insufficiency is often the MOST prominent clinical manifestation of:
questions.initialExplanation:
Guillain-Barre syndrome can progress rapidly after an infection and may weaken respiratory muscles, making acute respiratory support necessary.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Acute respiratory insufficiency is often the most prominent clinical manifestation of several acute neuromuscular disorders, such as high-level spinal cord injury, poliomyelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and botulism. Although much more insidious in its clinical course, respiratory dysfunction constitutes the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in progressive neuromuscular disorders (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy, congenital myotonic dystrophy, myasthenia gravis, and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease).

questions.stem: Data support the use of intravenous dexamethasone, 0.15 mg/kg/dose given every 6 hr for 2 days, in the treatment of children older than 6 wk with acute bacterial meningitis caused by H. influenzae type b. for the following reasons EXCEPT
questions.initialExplanation:
The source lists shorter fever duration, lower CSF protein and lactate, and less sensorineural hearing loss as benefits. It does not list lower mortality, making that the EXCEPT choice.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Among children with meningitis caused by H. influenzae type b, corticosteroid recipients have a shorter duration of fever, lower CSF protein and lactate levels, and a reduction in sensorineural hearing loss. Data in children regarding benefits, if any, of corticosteroids in the treatment of meningitis caused by other bacteria are inconclusive.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old boy presents to the ED with a 1-day history of fever to 104°F (40°C), increased irritability, decreased breast-feeding, and refusal of solid foods. The parents brought him in after two 30-second episodes of generalized jerking that occurred over a 20-minute span. Your examination reveals an awake but lethargic infant. The anterior fontanel is flat, the tympanic membranes and oropharynx are moist and not erythematous, the lungs are clear, and the heart and abdominal examinations are normal. He has no focal neurologic findings. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Discharge from ED to follow up with his primary care provider in 24 hours

questions.initialExplanation:
In an infant younger than 12 months, meningitis may be difficult to exclude by neck examination alone. The source recommends lumbar puncture in this clinical setting to evaluate for meningitis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Although this child ultimately may be diagnosed as having had a febrile seizure, the patient's age (<1 year) precludes a reliable neck examination for meningitis. An LP is required to evaluate the child for meningitis. Administering antibiotics before the LP (or other cultures are obtained) is inadvisable unless the patient's condition is such that he would not tolerate the procedure.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old school student is brought to the emergency department by her roommate after experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure for the first time. The seizure occurred suddenly while she was studying in her dorm room. Her roommate describes that she first stiffened up (tonic phase) and then began convulsing (clonic phase) for about two minutes. Following the seizure, she was confused and drowsy, a state known as postictal confusion. The current antiepileptic drug (AEDs) of choice for primary generalized tonic-clonic Seizures in children is:
questions.initialExplanation:
The source identifies valproate and lamotrigine as preferred options for primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and lists valproate as the keyed answer here.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Class I evidence demonstrates that phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, Primidone, valproate, topiramate, oxcarbazepine, and lamotrigine are effective for the Treatment of primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. On the basis of efficacy and Tolerability, valproate and lamotrigine have emerged as the current drugs of choice for Grand mal seizures.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because he has not been able to walk since waking up that morning. His mother said that when he tried to get out of bed he was unable to stand without support. He also complained of a prickling sensation in his hands and feet. Three weeks ago, he had a fever, a dry cough, and a sore throat. There is severe weakness in both lower extremities and mild sensory loss of the hands and feet. Knee and ankle jerk reflexes are absent. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
questions.initialExplanation:
Progressive symmetric weakness, tingling, and absent tendon reflexes after an infection suggest Guillain-Barre syndrome. IVIG is a standard immunomodulatory treatment.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: This decision is based on the clinical presentation, which is suggestive of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a post-infectious immune-mediated neuropathy. GBS often follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection and presents with progressive bilateral limb weakness, areflexia (absence of reflexes), and sensory symptoms. The boy’s recent history of fever, cough, and sore throat, followed by the acute onset of bilateral lower extremity weakness and areflexia, fits the typical pattern of GBS. IVIG is a treatment of choice for GBS as it can modulate the immune response and has been shown to reduce the duration of the disease and accelerate recovery.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl, previously healthy and well-adjusted, is brought to the pediatric clinic by her parents who are concerned about recent changes in her behavior and personality. Over the past three months, they have observed a marked shift in her demeanor, from being outgoing and interactive to withdrawn and irritable. Concurrently, the girl has experienced sporadic episodes characterized by sudden unresponsiveness, lip smacking, and fidgeting with her clothes, each lasting 1-2 minutes. These episodes are sometimes followed by a brief period of confusion. Regarding this, a history of personality change in a patient with seizure could suggest the following as a cause of seizure?
questions.initialExplanation:
New personality change together with seizures should raise concern for a structural brain process, including an intracranial tumor. The source contrasts this with regression in degenerative or metabolic disease.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: A history of personality change or symptoms of increased intracranial pressure can suggest an intracranial tumor. Similarly, a history of cognitive regression can suggest a degenerative or metabolic disease. Certain medications such as stimulants or antihistamines, particularly sedating ones, can precipitate seizures. A history of prenatal or perinatal distress or of developmental delay can suggest etiologic congenital or perinatal brain dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 5 year old child with known history of epilepsy since age of 4, that is poorly controlled with sodium valproic acid, presented to the E/R after an episode of generalized seizure without regaining consciousness. Status epilepticus is diagnosed if the episode should is lasting for more than:
questions.initialExplanation:
The source uses the modern 5-minute threshold: ongoing seizure activity for 5 minutes or longer, or recurrent seizures without recovery, is treated as status epilepticus.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In this case, the correct answer is A. Status epilepticus is a medical emergency characterized by prolonged or recurrent seizures without full recovery of consciousness between episodes. The typical duration used to define status epilepticus is 5 minutes or more of continuous seizure activity.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to a pediatric clinic by her parents for an evaluation of multiple skin lesions and a recent change in her behavior and academic performance. The parents report the presence of numerous “cafe-au-lait” spots on her skin since infancy, which have increased in number over the years. Recently, they have also noticed freckling in her underarm areas. The child’s teacher mentioned difficulties with attention and a decline in her school performance. The following are complications of neurofibromatosis (type 1) NF-1 EXCEPT?
questions.initialExplanation:
Cataracts are more characteristic of NF2-related ocular findings, whereas NF1 can be associated with learning difficulties, seizures, precocious puberty in some cases, and skeletal abnormalities such as scoliosis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Cataracts are found in 60-81% of patients with NF-2 but is not a complication of NF-1.

questions.stem: Ali, a 22-month-old boy, had been unwell with a runny nose and cough for a day when his father brings him to the Emergency Department. At lunch he suddenly became stiff, his eyes rolled upwards and both his arms and legs started jerking for 2 minutes. He felt very hot at the time. When examined 2 hours later, he has recovered fully. This is the first time this has happened. He has a normal neurological examination and is acquiring his developmental milestones normally. He has no other medical problems. The triage nurse performed a blood glucose test, which indicated a glucose level of 4.2 mmol/L (within normal range). What would be the most appropriate investigation?
questions.initialExplanation:
A first, brief generalized febrile seizure in a child who has returned to baseline and has a normal neurologic examination usually does not require routine CT, EEG, ECG, or glucose-tolerance testing.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
A. CT scan of the brain: Persistent signs, particularly asymmetric ones, should prompt imaging.  
B. ECG: Why the fever? Cardiac causes usually occur ‘out of the blue’ or following a specific trigger: exercise (hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) or shock (ventricular tachycardia).  
C. EEG (electroencephalography): Will be ‘abnormal’ in a significant proportion of normal children. This will lead to significant ‘overdiagnosis’ of epilepsy. Not indicated here.  
D. No investigation required: Correct. Ali had a simple febrile seizure, secondary to a respiratory tract infection. A febrile seizure is a clinical diagnosis and does not require investigation. Indeed, there is no confirmatory test.  
E. Oral glucose tolerance test: This is not required as the blood glucose is normal. It is rarely required in children to diagnose diabetes.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency room by her parents after experiencing a brief convulsive episode at home. Her parents describe that she suddenly started shaking all over her body with her eyes rolling back, lasting for about two minutes. This episode occurred in the context of a high fever, which developed earlier that day. The child has had no previous seizures, and her developmental milestones have been normal. Her past medical history is unremarkable except for a few episodes of otitis media. On examination, the child appears lethargic but is consolable by her parents. She has a temperature of 38.7°C and shows signs of a mild upper respiratory tract infection. No signs of meningitis or other focal neurological deficits are noted and febrile seizure is clinically diagnosed. Which one of the following factors, if detected, has the highest risk for subsequent epilepsy?
questions.initialExplanation:
The source ranks neurodevelopmental abnormalities as the strongest listed predictor of later epilepsy, with a stated risk of 33%.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
Risk factor for subsequent epilepsy:  
- Simple febrile seizure 1%  
- Recurrent febrile seizures 4%  
- Complex febrile seizures (more than 15 min duration or recurrent within 24 hr) 6%  
- Fever <1 hr before febrile seizure 11%  
- Family history of epilepsy 18%  
- Complex febrile seizures (focal) 29%  
- Neurodevelopmental abnormalities 33%

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents due to a high fever, severe headache, and confusion that started abruptly a few hours ago. He also complains of sensitivity to light and neck stiffness. His parents mention that he had a mild cold and sore throat a few days prior. On examination, the boy is irritable and drowsy, with a temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F). He shows signs of meningeal irritation, including neck stiffness and a positive Brudzinski’s sign. The MOST common cause of viral meningoencephalitis are?
questions.initialExplanation:
Enteroviruses are a common cause of viral meningitis and meningoencephalitis in children. The source identifies them as the most common cause among the listed options.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Enteroviruses are the most common cause of viral meningoencephalitis. As of 2014, more than 70 serotypes of these small RNA viruses have been identified.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department 25 minutes after an episode of loss of consciousness. The child began crying after his 4-year-old brother snatched a toy from him. The brief shrill cry was followed by a period of expiration; he then turned blue, became unconscious, and briefly lost his muscle tone, before he stiffened and had jerky movements of his arms and legs for 15 seconds. After this episode, he immediately regained consciousness. He had a similar episode. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation:
A stereotyped crying-expiration-cyanosis episode followed by brief loss of consciousness and rapid recovery in a toddler is typical of a breath-holding spell. The source recommends reassurance.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Breath-holding spells typically manifest between the age of 6-18 months. They are typically triggered by emotional distress, as is the case in this patient. The typical sequence includes crying, exhaling, and holding the breath, followed by cyanosis and loss of consciousness. Patients usually resume breathing and regain consciousness in less than 1 minute. Most importantly, parents should be reassured that the condition is benign and their child will outgrow it by the age of 4-7 years. The diagnosis is usually based on the clinical features and a detailed description of the episode; no treatment is required. Parents should be aware of the triggers of breath-holding spells, such as tantrums, minor injuries, and distress. However, they should not avoid reprimands for fear of triggering an episode.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with a long-standing history of epilepsy visits his neurologist for a routine check-up. He has been on therapy to control his seizure activity. Recently, he has noticed several concerning changes. He reports significant gum overgrowth, making it difficult for him to maintain oral hygiene. Additionally, he has observed an increase in facial hair growth and a general coarsening of his facial features. Over the past few months, he has also experienced balance problems and occasional involuntary eye movements, which he describes as his eyes “moving back and forth rapidly.” The neurologist recognizes these symptoms as potential adverse effects of?
questions.initialExplanation:
Phenytoin can cause gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarse facial features, ataxia, and nystagmus.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The symptoms described, including significant gum overgrowth (gingival hyperplasia), facial hair growth, coarsening of facial features, balance problems, and involuntary eye movements (nystagmus), are indicative of phenytoin use.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with a known history of epilepsy is rushed to the emergency department by her parents after experiencing a prolonged seizure at home. The seizure, characterized by continuous convulsions, has been ongoing for more than 30 minutes, and the parents report that it is unlike her typical seizure episodes, which usually last for a couple of minutes and respond to her regular seizure medication. The MOST common precipitant of status epilepticus in children is
questions.initialExplanation:
Fever or infection is the most common precipitant listed in the source, accounting for 36% of cases.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The source provides the following precipitant percentages: Fever/infection (36%), CNS infection (5%), medication change (20%), trauma (4%), unknown (9%), cerebrovascular (3%), metabolic (8%), ethanol/drug-related (2%), congenital (7%), tumor (1%), and anoxia (5%).

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child presents to the pediatrician with a history of brief, sudden lapses in consciousness without any convulsive movements. During these episodes, which last less than 20 seconds, the child seems to be staring into space and is unresponsive to verbal cues. There is no history of trauma, fever, or other systemic symptoms. The mother reports that these episodes have been occurring several times a day for the past two weeks. The child resumes her previous activity normally after these episodes and have no recall of them. The MOST appropriate initial treatment for his condition is:
questions.initialExplanation:
Brief staring spells with immediate recovery suggest absence seizures. Ethosuximide is the source's preferred initial treatment.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Absence seizures are most often initially treated with ethosuximide, which is as Effective and as less toxic than valproate and more effective than lamotrigine.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old male presents with a 48-hour history of headache, and meningismus. Evaluation of the CSF reveals clear fluid with normal protein and glucose content. The CSF cell count reveals 300 WBC/hpf, 90% lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.initialExplanation:
Clear CSF with lymphocyte predominance and normal glucose and protein suggests viral meningitis. Enterovirus is a common cause in children.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Clearly this child’s presentation suggests meningitis, a diagnosis which is confirmed by the CSF results. The relatively low number of total white blood cells, the predominance of lymphocytes, and the normal glucose and protein values are all suggestive of a viral illness. Therefore, the most likely etiologic agent is meningitis caused by enterovirus.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with a history of epilepsy is brought to his pediatric neurologist for a routine follow-up. He was diagnosed with epilepsy at the age of 4 and has been seizure-free for a while now. He is on levetiracetam. His development has been normal, and he has had no adverse effects from the medication. His parents express interest in exploring the possibility of discontinuing his epilepsy medication, given his seizure-free period and concern about long-term medication effects. Discontinuation of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) is usually indicated when children are free of seizures for at least?
questions.initialExplanation:
The source uses a seizure-free period of at least two years as the usual point at which discontinuation of antiepileptic medication may be considered.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Discontinuation of AEDs is usually indicated when children are free of seizures for at least 2 yr.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presented to the emergency department with a sudden onset of weakness and difficulty walking. The parents reported that the symptoms began a few days after a respiratory infection. Physical examination revealed symmetrical muscle weakness, areflexia, and loss of sensation in the lower limbs. The child had difficulty standing and required assistance to walk. Suspecting Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). Guillain-Barré syndrome can be a sequel in the following foodborne bacterial illness:
questions.initialExplanation:
Campylobacter jejuni infection can precede Guillain-Barre syndrome. The source identifies it as the foodborne bacterial illness associated with this neurologic complication.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Treatment of Campylobacter jejuni is supportive care. For severe cases, antibiotics, such as azithromycin and quinolones, may be indicated early in the diarrheal disease. Guillain-Barré syndrome can be a sequel.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is brought to the pediatric neurologist by concerned parents who have observed developmental delays and abnormalities in muscle tone. The child has difficulty with both fine and gross motor skills and exhibits involuntary movements. Seizure episodes have also been noted in the past few months. What is the MOST severe common type of cerebral palsy (CP) associated with seizure?
questions.initialExplanation:
Spastic quadriplegia affects all four limbs and is generally the most severe common spastic CP pattern.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Spastic quadriplegia is the most severe common type of cerebral palsy (CP) and is associated with significant motor impairment in both upper and lower extremities.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic by her mother who reports witnessing her daughter having a strange episode earlier that day. The mother describes that while playing, the child suddenly stopped responding, stared blankly, and began smacking her lips repeatedly. This behavior lasted for about two minutes, during which the girl seemed completely unaware of her surroundings. The mother also noticed her right hand making rhythmic twitching movements. After the episode, the child appeared confused but gradually returned to her normal self. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her condition?
questions.initialExplanation:
Lip-smacking, unilateral rhythmic movements, impaired awareness, and postictal confusion indicate a focal impaired-awareness seizure. Carbamazepine is one of the source's listed first-line options for focal seizures.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The focal symptoms (rhythmic twitching of the right hand) and the post-ictal confusion suggest that this is a case of complex partial seizure rather than absence seizure. In general, the drugs of first choice for focal seizures and epilepsies are oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine; for absence seizures, ethosuximide; for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, valproate and lamotrigine; for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, clobazam, valproate, topiramate, lamotrigine, and, most recently, as add on, rufinamide; and for infantile spasms, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to a pediatric neurologist by his parents due to concerns about developmental delay and recent onset of seizures. The parents describe episodes where the child exhibits brief periods of unresponsiveness, accompanied by subtle stiffening of the arms and blinking. These episodes have become more frequent over the past month. Additionally, the parents have noticed white patches on his skin and some areas with a rough, thickened appearance. During the examination, the neurologist observes several hypopigmented macules (‘ash leaf spots’) on the child’s skin and a shagreen patch on his lower back. Definite tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is diagnosed when at least 2 major or 1 major plus 2 minor features are present, all the following are minor features EXCEPT:

options.label: D
options.text: Not visible in the provided source page

options.label: E
options.text: Not visible in the provided source page

questions.initialExplanation:
Tuberous sclerosis is diagnosed from a combination of major and minor clinical features. A shagreen patch is a major feature in the criteria printed in this source. The last two answer choices are not visible in the PDF image, so they are not reconstructed.

**Source note:** The answer panel is on PDF page 55 and states “Correct Answer is: E — Tuberous sclerosis,” but that page belongs to the next numbered question (Question 50). The choices for Question 47 are cut off at the end of PDF page 54; only A-C are visible. The source's answer-to-question alignment is therefore unclear, and the E answer is retained as the adjacent answer-panel text rather than treated as independently verified for Question 47.

---
questions.detailedExplanation:
The source page lists the following clinical diagnostic criteria:  
**Major features:** Hypomelanotic macules (≥3, at least 5-mm diameter); angiofibromas (≥3) or fibrous cephalic plaque; ungual fibromas (≥2); shagreen patch; multiple retinal hamartomas; cortical dysplasias; subependymal nodules; subependymal giant cell astrocytoma; cardiac rhabdomyoma; lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM); angiomyolipomas (≥2).  
**Minor features:** “Confetti” skin lesions; dental enamel pits (>3); intraoral fibromas (≥2); retinal achromic patch; multiple renal cysts; nonrenal hamartomas.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a sudden-onset seizure. The child’s temperature is elevated, but there are no other signs of infection. One statement is NOT appropriate about the definition of simple febrile seizure:

options.label: C
options.text: Only two seizures in a 24-hour period

options.label: D
options.text: No evidence of central nervous system infection

questions.initialExplanation:
A simple febrile seizure is generalized, brief, occurs in the typical age range, and does not recur within the same 24-hour period. Recurrence within 24 hours makes it complex.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The key criteria for simple febrile seizures include generalized seizure activity, age range typically from 6 months to 5 years, no evidence of central nervous system infection, and a duration of less than 15 minutes. A simple febrile seizure occurs only once; if the seizure recurs in a 24-hour period then it is considered complex febrile seizure.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of high fever. His temperature prior to arrival was 40.0°C (104°F). There is no family history of serious illness. Development has been appropriate for his age. He is administered rectal acetaminophen. While in the waiting room, he becomes unresponsive and starts jerking his arms and legs back and forth. A fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 86 mg/dL. After 5 minutes, he continues having jerky movements and is unresponsive to verbal and painful stimuli. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation:
A seizure continuing for five minutes is treated as status epilepticus. IV lorazepam is the source's preferred initial medication because it acts rapidly.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Lorazepam, a benzodiazepine, is the preferred initial treatment for status epilepticus in children due to its rapid onset of action and efficacy in terminating seizures. IV lorazepam should be administered as soon as possible to halt the prolonged seizure activity and prevent further complications. While other antiepileptic medications such as phenobarbital, phenytoin, and valproate may be considered if seizures persist after lorazepam, lorazepam is the first-line agent for its rapid action.

questions.stem: You’re evaluating an infant who has been experiencing infantile spasms, exhibits a hypsarrhythmic EEG pattern, and has noticeable ash-leaf depigmentation on her back. Which underlying medical condition is most likely associated with these symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation:
Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia and hypopigmented ash-leaf macules are a characteristic combination for tuberous sclerosis complex.

---

## 2. Cerebral Palsy and Motor Disorders
questions.detailedExplanation: Tuberous sclerosis, an autosomal dominant condition, can result in severe mental retardation and seizures. Infantile spasms, a hypsarrhythmic EEG pattern, hypopigmented lesions (ash-leaf spots), cardiac tumors, sebaceous adenomas, a shagreen patch (a roughened, raised lesion over the sacrum), and calcifications on the CT scan are all features of this condition. No specific treatment is available.

questions.stem: The mother of a 2-year-old girl brings her to her pediatrician’s office for a checkup. When asked about discipline concerns, the mother expresses worry because the child gets mad and throws herself on the ground screaming. Which of the following statements regarding temper tantrums is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Most often indicate a serious psychosocial problem

options.label: B
options.text: Usually appear at the end of the first year

options.label: C
options.text: Peak prevalence is between 4 and 6 years

questions.initialExplanation:
Temper tantrums commonly begin near the end of the first year and peak around ages 2-4 years. Long or very frequent tantrums may warrant further assessment.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: As children mature, they learn what behaviors are acceptable and how much power they are able to wield by testing limits. Control is a central issue. Inability to control some aspect of the external world, such as how to make a certain toy work or when to leave, often results in a loss of internal control, that is, a temper tantrum. Fear, overtiredness, or physical discomfort can also evoke tantrums. When they are reinforced by intermittent rewards, as when the parent occasionally gives in to the child’s demands, tantrums can also become an entrenched strategy for exerting control by the toddler. Tantrums lasting more than 15 minutes or happening regularly more than three times daily can reflect underlying medical, emotional, or social problems. Tantrums normally appear at the end of the first year of life and peak at 2–4 years. Frequent tantrums after 5 years of age usually persist throughout childhood. Clearly, this is an undesirable outcome which, in nearly all children, is avoidable.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with CP comes to your clinic for the first time for a routine visit. He walks with the help of leg braces and a walker, and his speech is slurred and limited to short phrases. He has never been hospitalized, and he does not have swallowing problems. He began walking at the age of 2.5 years, and he is unable to take off his clothes and use the toilet without help. On examination, you find that the boy has only minimally increased tone in the upper extremities but good fine motor coordination; he has significantly increased tone and deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities. How would you categorize this child's CP?

options.label: E
options.text: Not visible in the provided source page

questions.initialExplanation:
Spastic diplegia predominantly affects both legs, with comparatively less upper-limb involvement. The child's need for braces and a walker supports the moderate diplegic classification in the source.

**Source note:** The screenshot of PDF page 1 is cut off at option D; option E is not visible and is not invented.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The child’s clinical presentation indicates involvement of both lower extremities with significant spasticity and increased deep tendon reflexes. This presentation is consistent with spastic diplegia, a subtype of CP characterized by predominantly lower limb involvement. The child’s ability to walk with the assistance of leg braces and a walker further supports the diagnosis of spastic diplegia. The absence of significant upper extremity involvement, along with good fine motor coordination in the upper limbs, suggests that the child’s motor impairment is primarily confined to the lower body. Therefore, based on the pattern of motor impairment described, the most appropriate classification of this child’s CP is moderate, diplegic.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric neurologist by her parents, who are concerned about her recent episodes of sudden, brief, involuntary jerking movements in her arms and shoulders, predominantly occurring in the early morning. These episodes began a few months ago and have been increasing in frequency. The child is developmentally normal for her age, with no history of febrile convulsions or family history of epilepsy. The neurologist notes the lack of accompanying neurological deficits and suspects a diagnosis of benign myoclonic epilepsy of infancy. Benign myoclonic epilepsies are often best treated with?
questions.initialExplanation:
The source identifies valproate as the preferred treatment, especially when myoclonic seizures coexist with generalized tonic-clonic or absence seizures.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Benign myoclonic epilepsies are often best treated with valproate, particularly when patients have associated generalized tonic-clonic and absence seizures. Benzodiazepines, clonazepam, lamotrigine, and topiramate are alternatives for the treatment of benign myoclonic epilepsy.

questions.stem: On the second day of treatment for pneumococcal meningitis, a 10-month-old child who had been alert is noted to be lethargic. Serum electrolytes reveal: Na 120 meq/L; Cl 82 meq/L; K 3.1 meq/L; BUN 2 mg/dL. The most appropriate management of this problem would be which of the following?

options.label: B
options.text: Restriction of fluid intake to 70% of maintenance requirements

options.label: C
options.text: Restriction of sodium intake to about 10% of normal

options.label: D
options.text: Administration of a diuretic such as furosemide

options.label: E
options.text: Discontinue intravenous fluids and begin oral fluids as tolerated

questions.initialExplanation:
For SIADH related to meningitis, the source recommends fluid restriction while treating the underlying infection. Hypertonic saline is reserved for life-threatening hyponatremia.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Therapy of inappropriate ADH secretion consists primarily of fluid restriction and, of course, treatment of the underlying condition, in this case, bacterial meningitis. Attempts to correct the hyponatremia by administration of sodium usually result in more retention of water and further hypervolemia and edema. Intravenous administration of hypertonic saline would be indicated only if the hyponatremia were life-threatening. Maintenance amounts of sodium should be administered. Diuretics are not very effective in this condition.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father because of multiple episodes of staring and facial grimacing that have occurred over the past 3 weeks. She does not respond to her family members during these episodes. One week ago, her brother witnessed an episode in which she woke up while sleeping, stared, and made hand gestures. She does not remember any of these episodes but does recall having a vague muddy taste in her mouth prior to the onset of these symptoms. After the episode, she feels lethargic and is confused. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
A gustatory aura followed by staring, unresponsiveness, automatisms, amnesia, and postictal confusion is typical of a focal impaired-awareness seizure, formerly called a complex partial seizure.

---

## Source Review Notes

- The source contains all numbered questions 1-55, but the PDF page order is scrambled; the entries above are organized by printed question number.
- PDF page 54 shows only options A-C for Question 47. The following PDF page shows the answer panel for Question 50, not a clearly linked continuation of Question 47; the source alignment is ambiguous and is flagged above.
- PDF page 1 does not show option E for Question 52.
- Some option labels in the source are duplicated or malformed (for example, several choices appear prefixed with “A.”). The answer choices are assigned A-E according to their visible top-to-bottom order; their wording is preserved.
- The source contains answer-key / selected-response inconsistencies on some pages. Where an answer letter and explanatory answer text visibly disagree, the discrepancy is recorded rather than silently resolved.
questions.detailedExplanation: This patient’s presentation is most consistent with recurrent complex partial seizures (focal seizures with impaired awareness), which are caused by abnormal electrical activity arising within the temporal lobe. The muddy taste in her mouth (gustatory aura) marks the onset of the seizure. The ictal phase consists of her staring, nonresponsiveness to external stimuli, and automatisms such as facial grimacing and hand gestures. The postictal phase of the complex partial seizure is characterized by lethargy, temporary confusion, and amnesia.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old, fully immunized boy is brought to the emergency room with a 3-hour history of fever to 39.5°C (103.1°F) and sore throat. The child appears alert, but anxious and toxic. He has mild inspiratory stridor and is drooling. He is sitting on the examination table leaning forward with his neck extended. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Examine the throat and obtain a culture.

options.label: B
options.text: Obtain an AP and lateral neck radiograph and start an IV line.

options.label: C
options.text: Administer a dose of nebulized epinephrine.

options.label: D
options.text: Prepare to establish an airway in the operating room.

options.label: E
options.text: Admit the child and place him in a mist tent.

questions.initialExplanation:
Epiglottitis can rapidly block a child's airway. Drooling, stridor, a toxic appearance, and leaning forward are emergency warning signs. The priority is to secure the airway in a controlled setting; do not examine the throat or delay for imaging.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In the past, epiglottitis was most commonly caused by invasive *Haemophilus influenzae* type B. Due to the widespread use of the Hib vaccine, this condition is now more commonly caused by group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, *Moraxella catarrhalis*, or *S. pneumoniae*. The radiography shows the typical “thumb” sign of a swollen epiglottis. Epiglottitis is a life-threatening form of infection-produced upper airway obstruction. The course of the illness is brief and prodromal symptoms are lacking. The patient experiences a sudden onset of sore throat, high fever, and prostration that is out of proportion to the duration of the illness. Drooling and difficulty in swallowing, a muffled voice, and preference for a characteristic sitting posture with the neck hyperextended may be noted. Radiography of the neck, which may delay definitive treatment, is often avoided. Rather, preparations are made for immediate intubation by skilled personnel, and any attempt to visualize the epiglottis should be avoided. Morbidity and mortality are usually related to a delay in establishing an airway early in the disease.

questions.stem: A three-year-old unvaccinated patient presents with fever, sore throat, muffled sound and stridor. He looks toxic and restless. This patient should be arranged for immediate:
questions.initialExplanation:
The combination of fever, muffled voice, stridor, and toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis. Swelling can close the airway quickly, so endotracheal intubation is the immediate priority.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Given the clinical presentation of a three-year-old unvaccinated patient with fever, sore throat, muffled voice, stridor, toxic appearance, and restlessness, along with the suspicion of epiglottitis, the immediate priority is to secure the airway. Therefore, the most appropriate immediate intervention is endotracheal intubation. Epiglottitis is a medical emergency that can rapidly progress to airway obstruction due to swelling of the epiglottis and surrounding structures. Endotracheal intubation is necessary to secure the airway and prevent complete obstruction, which can lead to respiratory failure and death.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the emergency department by his parents with a sudden onset of respiratory distress. The parents report that the child has been febrile for the past 24 hours, with a temperature reaching 39.4°C. The child appears toxic and ill, with noticeable drooling of saliva. On examination, there is stridor and the child leans forward to breathe, avoiding lying flat. The following suggest a diagnosis of epiglottitis rather than croup, EXCEPT:
questions.initialExplanation:
A barking cough is typical of croup, not epiglottitis. Epiglottitis more often causes sudden severe illness, drooling, difficulty swallowing, and a toxic appearance.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In croup, a viral infection affecting the larynx and trachea, a characteristic symptom is a “seal-like” or “barking” cough, often described as a harsh, metallic sound. Epiglottitis, on the other hand, is a bacterial infection that leads to inflammation of the epiglottis, causing a sudden onset of respiratory distress. The child may appear toxic and ill, leaning forward to maintain an open airway and exhibiting drooling due to difficulty swallowing. While a fever (option C) is present in both conditions, the absence of a severe barking cough is more indicative of epiglottitis.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presented to the ED with increased difficulty in breathing and stridor. The resident doctor started the child on nebulized racemic epinephrine, but despite the therapy, the child becomes more toxic-appearing and is drooling. The parents subsequently report the child has received no immunizations. Her respiratory rate is now 70 breaths per minute and she appears sleepy. At this point the best intervention is which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Blind intubation with a laryngeal mask airway.

options.label: B
options.text: Humidified oxygen and observation with the patient in a position of comfort.

options.label: C
options.text: Rapid sequence intubation in the emergency department.

options.label: D
options.text: Anesthesia assistance for intubation in the operating room with surgical availability.

questions.initialExplanation:
This child has signs of impending airway obstruction from epiglottitis. The safest plan is controlled intubation in the operating room with anesthesia and surgical backup immediately available.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: These findings are concerning for epiglottitis, a potentially life-threatening condition, especially when the patient is not immunized. Epiglottitis can rapidly progress to airway obstruction, and the patient may require intubation for airway protection. Performing intubation in the operating room with anesthesia assistance and surgical availability provides a controlled environment with immediate access to resources needed in case of complications, such as potential need for a surgical airway (tracheostomy). Blind intubation with a laryngeal mask airway is generally not recommended in the setting of epiglottitis due to the risk of further aggravating airway obstruction. Rapid sequence intubation in the emergency department is an option but may be less controlled compared to the operating room setting. Prompt administration of intravenous cefotaxime is essential but should not delay securing the airway in a patient with severe respiratory distress.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old unimmunized boy presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of labored breathing, drooling, and fever. On examination, he is toxic-appearing and drooling, and stridor is present on lung auscultation. Of the following, what organism is most likely responsible for his presentation?
questions.initialExplanation:
Hib was the classic cause of epiglottitis before routine vaccination made the disease much less common. In an unimmunized child with sudden fever, drooling, and stridor, Hib is the most likely organism in this question.

---

## Bacterial Tracheitis
questions.detailedExplanation: The symptoms of the patient in the vignette are consistent with acute epiglottitis. Epiglottitis is a medical emergency. Children with epiglottitis are at risk for airway obstruction due to swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures. Epiglottitis is caused most commonly by *H. influenzae* type b (Hib), though routine vaccination against Hib has markedly reduced the incidence. *Streptococcus pneumoniae* can cause epiglottitis and would be the most likely bacterial etiology in an immunized immunocompetent patient. Patients with epiglottitis have a sudden onset and rapid progression of symptoms including high fever, muffled voice, drooling, and anorexia. In order to receive better air entry, patients often sit leaning forward with their jaw thrust forward and mouth open, better known as the “sniffing position.” Lateral neck radiographs reveal the thumb print sign, due to a large and bulging epiglottis and swelling of the epiglottic folds. Diagnosis is confirmed with direct visualization of the epiglottis, which should only be done in the operating room with an anesthesiologist and surgeon prepared for intubation or tracheostomy if required. Children with epiglottitis require endotracheal intubation to maintain airway patency as well as antibiotic therapy. *Staphylococcus aureus* and several subtypes of *Streptococcus* have been implicated in epiglottitis, but Hib remains the most likely cause in an unvaccinated child.

questions.stem: A fully immunized 2-year-old presents to the emergency room with several days of low-grade fever, barking cough, and noisy breathing. Over the past few hours he has developed a fever of 40°C (104°F) and looks toxic. He has inspiratory and expiratory stridor. The family has not noticed drooling, and he seems to be drinking without pain. Direct laryngoscopy reveals a normal epiglottis. The management of this disease process includes which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: Observation in a cool mist tent.

questions.initialExplanation:
High fever, toxic appearance, and biphasic stridor after a viral illness suggest bacterial tracheitis rather than uncomplicated croup. The airway may become blocked by thick secretions, so airway protection and IV antibiotics are required.

---

## Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis)
questions.detailedExplanation: Bacterial tracheitis is an uncommon, but severe and life-threatening sequela of a viral laryngotracheobronchitis. The typical story is that presented in the case, with several days of viral upper respiratory symptoms, followed by an acute elevation of temperature and an increase in respiratory distress. Inspiratory stridor is typical in croup; the biphasic stridor and high fever in this patient should be a clue to consider alternative diagnoses. Children may also present acutely and without the initial viral symptoms. The differential must include epiglottitis; the lack of drooling and dysphagia (and the rarity of epiglottitis) help make this a case of tracheitis. Management for tracheitis includes establishing an airway with endotracheal intubation and IV antibiotics. Special attention is focused on preservation of the airway, as even intubated children with tracheitis can have secretions thick and copious enough to occlude the airway. Oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up for a patient with respiratory distress and toxic appearance is never appropriate. Inhaled epinephrine and oral steroids, as well as observation in a cool mist tent, suggest a diagnosis of croup, a disease that presents without high fever but with stridor a few days after an upper respiratory infection. In the case presentation, the fever and toxic appearance differentiate this condition from viral croup. Inhaled steroids suggest asthma, a diagnosis unlikely in a patient with high fever as outlined.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old male presented with a barking cough and stridor at night, preceded by mild fever and rhinorrhea two days earlier. He looks generally well. For this patient, you send an X-ray of the neck and chest, which shows:
questions.initialExplanation:
Croup causes swelling below the vocal cords. This produces the steeple sign on an AP neck radiograph and commonly causes a barking cough and inspiratory stridor.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The chest X-ray findings described, particularly the presence of a barking cough and stridor at night, preceded by fever and rhinorrhea, suggest the possibility of croup, a common viral upper respiratory tract infection in young children. The characteristic finding on neck X-ray for croup is the steeple sign. The “steeple sign” refers to the characteristic narrowing of the upper airway, resembling a steeple, seen on the neck X-ray due to subglottic narrowing caused by inflammation and swelling of the larynx and trachea, which is typical of croup.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old female presents to the emergency department with fever up to 102°F, a barky cough, and stridor. The examination shows an RR of 60 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 95% while breathing room air, marked stridor, moderate substernal retractions, and equal aeration without wheezes or rhonchi. As the patient is being evaluated, initial therapy for this patient should begin with which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: Humidified air only in a position of comfort.

options.label: E
options.text: Stat portable AP and lateral neck films.

questions.initialExplanation:
Marked stridor and retractions at rest indicate moderate-to-severe croup. Nebulized racemic epinephrine rapidly reduces airway swelling; dexamethasone is also given, and the child must be observed for recurrence of symptoms.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Nebulized epinephrine is the immediate treatment of choice for moderate-to-severe croup. Croup is considered moderate-to-severe if the patient has dyspnea and tachycardia at rest, severe stridor with significant retraction, and agitation. Careful monitoring of the heart rate is important because epinephrine can worsen tachycardia. In addition to epinephrine, oral/parenteral glucocorticoids (usually dexamethasone) are indicated. After administration of these agents, patients should continue to be monitored for improvement for 3–4 hours. If symptoms improve, patients can be discharged home; otherwise, patients should be admitted for airway monitoring and further treatment.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with cough and difficulty breathing. According to his parents, he has had a cough and cold symptoms for 2 days, which have gradually worsened. On the morning of presentation, they noticed that he was wheezing and his cough was severe, prompting an emergency department visit for evaluation. On examination, his respiratory rate is 45 breaths/min with no retractions or nasal flaring. On auscultation, there is a harsh noise on inspiration, heard best over the neck. Of the following, what is his most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute bronchospasm due to a viral illness.

questions.initialExplanation:
A harsh inspiratory sound heard over the neck is stridor, which points to upper-airway obstruction. A preceding cold and barking cough in a well-appearing child support croup.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The patient in the case has laryngotracheobronchitis, or croup. The harsh noise heard on physical examination is consistent with stridor. Stridor is heard best near the upper airways and is usually caused by obstruction of the extrathoracic airway. Wheezing is a high-pitched noise produced by partial obstruction of the lower airways and is heard best during exhalation. Croup, foreign body aspiration, and epiglottitis can all cause stridor; however, the patient in the vignette has associated cough and cold symptoms that point to croup as the most likely diagnosis. Epiglottitis is an acute inflammation of the epiglottis resulting from a bacterial infection with *Haemophilus influenzae* or *Staphylococcus aureus*. Patients present with severe symptoms of airway obstruction, such as drooling, sitting forward, or gasping for air. Epiglottitis is a pediatric emergency. While pneumonia and acute bronchospasm are associated with wheezing, neither is expected to produce stridor.

questions.stem: You are awakened in the night by your 2-year-old son, who has developed noisy breathing on inspiration, marked retractions of the chest wall, flaring of the nostrils, and a barking cough. He has had a mild upper respiratory infection (URI) for 2 days. Which of the following therapies is indicated?

options.label: A
options.text: Short-acting bronchodilators and a 5-day course of steroids.

options.label: C
options.text: Observation for hypoxia and dehydration alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Inhaled epinephrine and a dose of steroids.

questions.initialExplanation:
Croup is an upper-airway illness that causes inspiratory stridor and a barking cough. For a child with significant retractions and noisy breathing, give nebulized epinephrine and corticosteroids.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The signs of illness described are those involving the airway above the point at which the trachea enters the neck and leaves the thorax, resulting in inspiratory stridor such as in croup. The extrathoracic airway tends to collapse on inspiration, producing the characteristic findings this patient demonstrates; therapy usually is with a single dose of steroids. Agents causing croup include parainfluenza types 1 and 3, influenza A and B, RSV, and occasionally other viruses. Treatment is usually supportive, but racemic epinephrine and corticosteroids reduce the length of time in the emergency room and hospitalizations. Intrathoracic airway diseases, such as asthma (bronchodilators and short course of steroids) or bronchiolitis (supportive therapy including observation for hypoxia or dehydration alone), produce breathing difficulty on expiration, with expiratory wheezing, prolonged expiration, and signs of air trapping due to the increased narrowing during expiration as the airways are exposed to the same intrathoracic pressure changes as the alveoli. Acute airway foreign body (rigid bronchoscopy) should result in differential air movement between the two lungs. The typical case of epiglottitis (intubation and antibiotics) presents acutely and the child is toxic in appearance; it is now a rare disease with the widespread use of vaccines.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is brought to the pediatric emergency department by concerned parents. The child presented with difficulty breathing. On examination, the child appears anxious and has respiratory distress, with retractions noted during inhalation. Oxygen saturation is within normal limits. Regarding characteristics of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), each of the following may be included, EXCEPT:

options.label: C
options.text: Stridor upon activity or agitation or even at rest.

options.label: E
options.text: Hyperresonant chest due to excessive air trapping.

questions.initialExplanation:
Croup affects the upper airway, so barking cough, hoarseness, and stridor are typical. Hyperresonance suggests lower-airway air trapping and is not a characteristic finding of croup.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), the characteristic features include a barking cough, hoarseness of voice, and stridor upon activity or agitation, or even at rest. Respiratory distress and cyanosis may occur in severe cases due to airway obstruction. However, the chest is typically not hyper-resonant because croup predominantly involves the upper airways, and excessive air trapping in the lower airways is not a prominent feature. Hyper-resonance is more associated with conditions affecting the lower airways, such as asthma or bronchiolitis.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother because of a dry, harsh cough for 2 days that worsens at night. She has also had mild rhinorrhea and fever. Her older brother has asthma and had a cold last week. Immunizations are up-to-date. She appears to be in mild distress. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.5°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 99/56 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Examination shows clear rhinorrhea and a dry, hoarse cough. There is mild inspiratory stridor upon agitation that resolves with rest. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in treatment?
questions.initialExplanation:
This is mild croup: the child is stable, oxygenating well, and has stridor only when agitated. Supportive care and dexamethasone are appropriate; emergency intubation is not indicated.

---

## Asthma
questions.detailedExplanation: The history of an upper respiratory tract infection followed by a dry, hoarse cough and inspiratory stridor is indicative of croup. The girl is alert and has an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air, a stridor that resolves with rest, and no subcostal retractions, indicating she has mild croup. Since the etiology of croup is viral in nature, symptomatic relief is indicated. Cool mist helps reduce nasal passage irritation and dexamethasone reduces airway swelling.

questions.stem: One of your asthmatic patients arrives for a checkup. The mother reports that the child seems to need albuterol daily, especially when exercising, and she has coughing fits that awaken her from sleep about twice a week. Her grandmother had recommended a Chihuahua as a “cure” for her asthma, but her mother has seen no difference since the arrival of the pet. Appropriate treatment measures would include which of the following?

options.label: B
options.text: Daily leukotriene modifier with short-acting β-agonist.

options.label: D
options.text: Medium-dose, inhaled corticosteroids with short-acting β-agonists.

options.label: E
options.text: High-dose, inhaled corticosteroids with theophylline and short-acting β-agonists.

questions.initialExplanation:
Daily symptoms and nighttime waking more than once a week indicate persistent asthma that is not controlled with rescue albuterol alone. A controller medicine is needed; the source recommends medium-dose inhaled corticosteroids with a short-acting β-agonist for relief.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Asthma may be classified by severity based on the frequency of symptoms. Patients with mild intermittent asthma have symptoms less than two times a week and have less than two nighttime episodes a month. These patients do not require daily medication and only short-acting β-agonists are needed. The second classification is mild persistent asthma; these children have symptoms more than two times a week, and have 3 to 4 nights a month with symptoms. These patients may be managed with a number of anti-inflammatory choices, including low-dose inhaled corticosteroids, cromolyn, or a leukotriene inhibitor, and use short-acting β-agonists for rescue. Our patient has moderate persistent asthma; she has daily symptoms and difficulty at night more than once a week. Her treatment should consist of medium-dose corticosteroids, or a combination of low-dose corticosteroids and a long-acting β-agonist; alternatives include a leukotriene modifier or sustained-release theophylline. Patients with severe persistent asthma have continual symptoms and frequent nighttime symptoms. This group requires daily high-dose glucocorticoids as well as long-acting β-agonists; they may require oral steroids as well.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old male presents to the office with wheezing and increased work of breathing for the fifth time in the past year. On examination, his respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation is 98% while breathing room air. He is talking in complete sentences and there is expiratory wheezing with a prolonged expiratory phase. What is the first treatment he should receive?
questions.initialExplanation:
The child has an acute asthma exacerbation but is stable enough to speak in full sentences and has normal oxygen saturation. The first treatment is an inhaled short-acting β-agonist such as nebulized albuterol.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: This approach involves using medications such as albuterol, a short-acting beta-agonist, to relieve bronchoconstriction and improve airflow in the lungs. In asthma exacerbations, beta-agonists help by relaxing the smooth muscles of the airways. The provided clinical presentation is indicative of an asthma exacerbation, and the first step in managing such cases is to administer a short-acting beta-agonist via nebulization. This helps relieve acute bronchoconstriction and improves respiratory symptoms. If the child’s response is inadequate, additional treatments such as systemic corticosteroids may be considered.

questions.stem: A mother brings her 14-year-old son to the clinic. He has a past medical history significant for asthma and reports that he has been taking albuterol as needed. He describes having asthma exacerbations approximately twice per week, with one of these episodes often occurring during the day and the other at night. He does not use his inhaler outside of these episodes and does not feel that he is having difficulty with normal physical activity. Of the following, what is the best classification of his asthma?
questions.initialExplanation:
Asthma symptoms occurring more than twice a week are not intermittent. The source classifies this pattern as mild persistent asthma, using symptom frequency, nighttime waking, rescue-inhaler use, activity limitation, and lung function.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: For children older than 12 years of age, the National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) has categorized asthma severity as either intermittent (sometimes called mild intermittent) or persistent disease. Those with persistent disease can then be subdivided based on the level of severity into mild, moderate, or severe. The categorization depends upon several major factors including (1) the frequency of daytime symptoms, (2) the frequency of nighttime awakenings, (3) the frequency of rescue inhaler use for symptoms, (4) the level of interference with normal daily activities, and (5) the forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity of the lungs, percent predicted. Based on the presence of nightly awakenings more than twice per month, the patient in the vignette meets criteria for mild persistent disease. See the source table for the specific classification of asthma severity.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic with a history of recurrent episodes of wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. The parents note that these symptoms often occur in response to triggers such as cold air and exposure to allergens. On examination, the child appears well between episodes but has audible wheezing and decreased air entry during episodes. Spirometry reveals reversible airflow obstruction consistent with asthma. Which is the most common radiographic abnormality in a child with asthma?
questions.initialExplanation:
Asthma narrows the airways and makes it difficult to breathe air out. This causes air trapping and enlarged lung volumes, seen as generalized hyperinflation on chest X-ray.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In a child with asthma, the most common roentgenographic abnormality is generalized hyperinflation. This is a result of air trapping during expiration, leading to increased lung volumes. The chest X-ray may show a flattened diaphragm and increased anteroposterior diameter, reflecting the chronic nature of the condition and the presence of obstructive lung disease. The other options, such as pneumomediastinum, bronchiectasis, right middle lobe atelectasis, and lower lobe infiltrates, are less characteristic of the typical radiographic findings associated with asthma.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presented to the ED with increasing shortness of breath and tachypnea. He was diagnosed with an acute asthma exacerbation and received adequate management in the ED. Further history reveals that the patient has been using inhaled albuterol three times per week to control wheezing. He awakens each night with coughing, but seems better in the morning. In addition to albuterol and a short course of oral steroids, what is the best additional medicine he should receive to decrease the risk of future exacerbations?

options.label: A
options.text: Epinephrine auto-injector (Epi-Pen) to be used as needed.

options.label: B
options.text: Salmeterol to be used in divided doses daily.

options.label: C
options.text: Fluticasone to be used in divided doses daily.

options.label: D
options.text: Theophylline to be used in divided doses daily.

options.label: E
options.text: Cetirizine to be used in divided doses daily.

questions.initialExplanation:
Frequent albuterol use and nightly symptoms show that the asthma needs better long-term control. A daily inhaled corticosteroid such as fluticasone reduces airway inflammation and lowers the risk of future attacks.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The patient’s symptoms, including nighttime coughing and improvement with albuterol, suggest inadequate control of persistent asthma. Fluticasone, an inhaled corticosteroid, is recommended for daily use as a controller medication in asthma management. It helps reduce airway inflammation and prevent symptoms when used regularly. Salmeterol is a long-acting beta-agonist and is often combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, but using it alone is not recommended. Theophylline has a narrower therapeutic window and may have more side effects. Cetirizine is an antihistamine and is not typically used as a primary controller in asthma. The use of an epinephrine auto-injector is not indicated for routine asthma management.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presented with recurrent attacks of wheezing and night coughing. He was diagnosed as a case of moderate persistent asthma. He should fit the following, EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: Nighttime symptoms 5 times and more per month.

questions.initialExplanation:
Daily high-dose oral corticosteroids are not a routine maintenance treatment for moderate persistent asthma. Inhaled controller therapy is preferred because it treats airway inflammation with fewer systemic adverse effects.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: High-dose oral corticosteroids are not typically used as a daily treatment for moderate persistent asthma due to their significant side effects and potential for long-term harm.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with a known history of asthma is rushed to the emergency department in severe respiratory distress. The patient reports increasing shortness of breath over the past 24 hours, with minimal relief from the prescribed rescue inhaler. On examination, the patient appears agitated, with rapid and labored breathing. Auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds and prolonged expiratory phase. The following are features of life-threatening asthma, EXCEPT:
questions.initialExplanation:
