A silent chest, cyanosis, hypotension, and confusion are danger signs during a severe asthma attack. Night cough suggests poor chronic control, but it is not itself a feature of an acute life-threatening attack.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Indications of a severe exacerbation include breathlessness, retractions, accessory muscle use, tachypnea, cyanosis, mental status changes, a silent chest with poor air exchange, and severe airflow limitation (PEF or FEV1 value below 50% of personal best or predicted values). However, night cough is typically associated with poorly controlled asthma but is not a feature of an acute life-threatening asthma exacerbation. Life-threatening asthma episodes are characterized by a sudden and severe decline in respiratory function, often requiring immediate intervention with bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and, in severe cases, ventilatory support.

questions.stem: A known case of asthma presents with shortness of breath and cyanosis. The most ominous sign for respiratory failure is:
questions.initialExplanation:
During an asthma attack, patients usually breathe fast and have a low CO2 level. A normal CO2 level can mean that the patient is tiring and can no longer ventilate effectively, so respiratory failure may be near.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: In the context of a severe asthma attack, a normal or rising CO2 level is particularly concerning because it indicates that the patient is no longer able to adequately ventilate and blow off CO2, signifying impending respiratory failure. Initially, patients with asthma exacerbations typically hyperventilate, leading to low CO2 levels (respiratory alkalosis). As respiratory muscles fatigue and the airway obstruction worsens, CO2 retention occurs, and a “normal” CO2 level in this setting reflects a transition from hyperventilation to hypoventilation, which can rapidly progress to respiratory acidosis and failure. Cyanosis indicates significant hypoxemia and is very serious, but the CO2 level gives more direct information about ventilatory status and impending failure.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl presents with well-controlled, moderately persistent asthma. Her therapies consist of occasional use of short-acting β-agonists, daily inhaled steroids, and a leukotriene inhibitor. She presents with white patches on her buccal mucosa. You recommend which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: Discontinuation of all her asthma medications.

options.label: E
options.text: Rinse her mouth after use of her inhaled medications.

questions.initialExplanation:
Inhaled corticosteroids can leave medication in the mouth and allow Candida to grow, causing white patches (oral thrush). Rinsing the mouth after each use helps prevent this problem.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The patient in the question has well-controlled, moderately persistent asthma; this suggests that she is likely on inhaled steroids. Failure to rinse her mouth after administration of this medication can result in localized candida infection (thrush). Discontinuation of her asthma medications is contraindicated. While it is possible she has an immune dysfunction, simply rinsing her mouth is more likely to be both diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother secondary to wheezing. He is new to the practice and his past medical history reveals frequent emergency department visits for the same complaint. His mother states that he always improves after the breathing treatment in the ED and frequently is discharged on an oral medication. She reports that he has woken up coughing four times in the past month. Upon examination, his respiratory rate is 35 breaths/min; he does not have retractions, but does have diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezing on auscultation. After initiating treatment with inhaled albuterol and oral corticosteroids in the office, of the following, what is the next best step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Referral to a pulmonologist for uncontrolled asthma.

options.label: B
options.text: Advise the mother to give him a daily dose of albuterol.

options.label: C
options.text: Follow up with the child in 1 week to assess for improvement.

options.label: D
options.text: Begin daily treatment with an inhaled corticosteroid.

options.label: E
options.text: Not visible in the supplied PDF page.

questions.initialExplanation:
Repeated emergency visits and frequent nighttime cough indicate poorly controlled asthma. After treating the acute attack, start a daily inhaled corticosteroid to prevent future exacerbations and provide education about triggers, correct inhaler use, and an asthma action plan.

---


## Pneumonia
questions.detailedExplanation: The history and presentation of the patient in the vignette are consistent with poorly controlled asthma. One of the most important interventions for children with uncontrolled asthma is appropriate teaching regarding the diagnosis, which should include an explanation of symptoms associated with asthma, proper use of medications, as well as completion of an asthma action plan. Discussion should include possible triggers such as smoking, pets, perfumes, and carpet, as well as recognizing respiratory distress. An acute asthma exacerbation is managed with the use of inhaled albuterol and a brief course of oral corticosteroids. Patients with poorly controlled asthma should additionally be prescribed daily inhaled corticosteroid therapy to prevent future exacerbations. The patient in the vignette needs proper therapy and following up in 1 week would not correct his poorly controlled asthma symptoms. β2-agonists such as albuterol should not be used prophylactically. Pulmonology referral should be delayed until the patient fails appropriate management. If compliance to the appropriate therapy is established but the patient continues to be symptomatic, a referral may be warranted at that time. Addition of a long-acting β2-agonist could be considered if the patient in the vignette fails primary inhaled corticosteroid therapy.

questions.stem: A five-year-old girl shows failure to respond to treatment for bacterial pneumonia. Her new chest X-ray shows a hyperlucent, lens-shaped pleural lesion. The most common microorganism causing this complication is:
questions.initialExplanation:
A pneumatocele is a thin-walled, air-filled space that can develop after pneumonia. It is classically associated with *Staphylococcus aureus* infection in children.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The description of a hyperlucent, lens-shaped pleural lesion on chest X-ray in a child with failure to respond to treatment for bacterial pneumonia suggests the complication of a pneumatocele. The most common microorganism causing this complication is *Staphylococcus aureus*. Staphylococcus aureus is a common pathogen associated with the development of pneumatoceles, particularly in severe or complicated cases of pneumonia. Pneumatoceles are thin-walled, air-filled cystic lesions within the lung parenchyma that can occur as a complication of bacterial pneumonia, especially when caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with sudden high fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. During the past 24 hours, the child has become lethargic and irritable. Examination shows decreased breath sounds, an increased respiratory rate, and pleuritic chest pain on coughing. Chest X-ray reveals consolidation in the left lower lobe. Features of bacterial pneumonia include all of the following, EXCEPT:
questions.initialExplanation:
Bacterial pneumonia often begins suddenly and causes high fever, cough, and breathing difficulty. A low-grade fever is less typical and may suggest a viral infection instead.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Bacterial pneumonia commonly has a sudden onset with high-grade fever, cough, and respiratory distress. Symptoms may progress rapidly. Lobar consolidation, a large pleural effusion, and high fever favor a bacterial cause. Abdominal pain can occur, particularly with lower-lobe pneumonia in children. Nuchal rigidity may also be prominent in some cases, including right upper-lobe pneumonia. Bacterial pneumonia is generally associated with high-grade fever, whereas a low-grade fever is more suggestive of a viral infection.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old child is admitted with severe pneumonia requiring supplemental oxygen. In severe pediatric pneumonia, what additional intervention may be considered in addition to antibiotic therapy?
questions.initialExplanation:
CPAP supports a child who is struggling to breathe by delivering continuous positive pressure. This helps keep the lungs open and improves oxygenation in severe pneumonia.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) can be useful in severe pneumonia to maintain adequate oxygenation and ventilation, reduce the work of breathing, and help prevent progression to respiratory failure. CPAP provides a steady positive pressure that helps keep the airways and alveoli open, improves oxygenation, and supports the child's breathing. It may be considered when supplemental oxygen alone is insufficient and the child needs additional respiratory support.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had increasing breathing difficulty for three days. He has a mild cough and wheezing. His parents notice that he seems to breathe faster, especially while playing. His respiratory rate is increased, but he has no fever. What is the MOST consistent clinical manifestation of pneumonia?
questions.initialExplanation:
Tachypnea means breathing faster than normal. In children, it is an important and consistent clue to pneumonia, even when fever or cough is absent.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Tachypnea, or rapid breathing, is the most consistent sign of pneumonia in children and is often the first and sometimes the only sign, particularly in young children. Other symptoms, such as fever and cough, are also common but may not be present in every case.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child was diagnosed with pneumonia three times last year. The symptoms resolved after each episode, and the chest X-rays returned to normal. Which of the following best defines recurrent pneumonia?

options.label: A
options.text: Two or more episodes in one year with radiographic clearing between episodes.

options.label: B
options.text: Two or more episodes without radiographic clearing between episodes.

options.label: C
options.text: Three or more episodes with radiographic clearing between episodes.

options.label: D
options.text: Three or more episodes without radiographic clearing between episodes.

options.label: E
options.text: Four or more episodes in one year.

questions.initialExplanation:
Recurrent pneumonia means that separate episodes occur and the chest X-ray clears between them. If the same opacity remains, the problem is persistent rather than recurrent pneumonia.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Recurrent pneumonia is defined by two or more episodes of pneumonia in a single year or three or more episodes ever, with each episode being separated by a complete resolution of radiographic findings. This definition accounts for both the recurrence of the infections and the transient nature of the pulmonary findings. Radiographic clearing between episodes distinguishes recurrent pneumonia from persistent pneumonia, in which the abnormality does not resolve.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has persistent cough, headache, fever, malaise, and hoarseness for six days. He has no coryza and produces frothy white sputum after an initially nonproductive cough. Examination reveals fine crackles over the right chest, and the chest X-ray shows right lower-lobe interstitial infiltrates. What is the preferred therapy?
questions.initialExplanation:
Atypical pneumonia in a school-aged child or adolescent may be caused by *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*. Azithromycin is a macrolide that covers this organism.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The symptoms and radiographic findings suggest atypical pneumonia. Azithromycin, a macrolide antibiotic, is effective against atypical organisms such as *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* and is commonly used for community-acquired pneumonia caused by these organisms in children. Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, and ampicillin are used for typical bacterial pneumonia, but they may not provide adequate coverage for atypical pathogens. Symptomatic treatment provides supportive care but does not replace appropriate antimicrobial therapy when atypical bacterial pneumonia is suspected.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old patient presents with productive cough and fever for five days. Chest X-ray shows right lower-lobe consolidation with pleural effusion. Sputum Gram stain reveals gram-positive cocci in pairs. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.initialExplanation:
*Streptococcus pneumoniae* is a gram-positive diplococcus, meaning that it commonly appears as paired cocci on Gram stain. This finding strongly supports pneumococcal pneumonia.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Common pathogens that cause lobar bacterial pneumonia include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*. *Escherichia coli* can cause aspiration-related lobar pneumonia. *Streptococcus pneumoniae* appears as gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains. *Moraxella catarrhalis* is a gram-negative diplococcus; *Staphylococcus aureus* appears as gram-positive cocci in clusters; *Haemophilus influenzae* appears as gram-negative coccobacilli; and *E. coli* is a gram-negative bacillus. The finding of gram-positive cocci in pairs therefore supports pneumococcal pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with fever and cough for seven days. She has no history of travel, pets, or sick contacts and is otherwise healthy. Examination reveals diffuse crackles, and chest X-ray shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates without focal consolidation. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.initialExplanation:
In adolescents, a gradual illness with persistent cough and diffuse interstitial infiltrates suggests atypical pneumonia. *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is a common cause.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*. The symptoms and radiographic findings described for the patient in the vignette are consistent with an atypical pneumonia. In this age group, the most common etiology is *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*. Symptoms usually appear gradually and are similar to those of a viral upper respiratory tract infection. *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* should be suspected in a patient with malaise, protracted cough, fever, headache, and chills. Diagnosis is made on clinical symptoms, and a chest radiograph can be useful to exclude lobar pneumonias. *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Staphylococcus aureus* cause focal consolidations in the lungs, as opposed to diffuse interstitial findings. *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* should be suspected with pneumonia that fails to respond to conventional antibiotics or with cavitary lesions. *Pneumocystis jirovecii* (formerly *Pneumocystis carinii*) is an opportunistic organism in immunocompromised patients, often those with HIV; it may cause nonspecific malaise, cough, and fever with diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray.

questions.stem: Pleurisy, or inflammation of the pleura, is often accompanied by an effusion. Of the following, the MOST common cause of pleural effusion in children is:
questions.initialExplanation:
A pleural effusion is fluid that collects in the space around the lungs. In children, bacterial pneumonia is a common cause of a parapneumonic effusion because infection and inflammation can extend to the pleura.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The source page marks the selected answer as correct but does not provide a detailed written explanation.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has had cough and fever for two days, with temperatures up to 39°C despite over-the-counter antipyretics. The child has become more short of breath and appears ill, with respiratory distress, nasal flaring, crackles, and decreased breath sounds over the right lower lobe. What is the best treatment plan?

options.label: C
options.text: Six months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

questions.initialExplanation:
A child with severe suspected bacterial pneumonia and respiratory distress needs hospital assessment and empiric intravenous antibiotics. Ceftriaxone is a broad-spectrum option for common bacterial causes.

---

## Bronchiolitis and Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical presentation appears consistent with bacterial pneumonia, and the child likely requires hospitalization due to the severity of symptoms, including respiratory distress and high fever that is not responding to over-the-counter antipyretics. Intravenous ceftriaxone is an appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotic for severe bacterial pneumonia and provides coverage against common pathogens, including *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. While intravenous clarithromycin can be effective against atypical organisms, it is not typically the first-line treatment for severe bacterial pneumonia requiring hospitalization. A prolonged multidrug regimen for tuberculosis is not indicated by the information provided. A chest tube is used for conditions such as a significant pleural collection or pneumothorax, neither of which is established in this vignette.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with cough, rapid breathing, and difficulty taking a bottle. The infant has had nasal congestion and cough for two days, with worsening symptoms. The respiratory rate is 50/min, oxygen saturation is 92% on room air, and heart rate is 140/min. Examination shows subcostal retractions and mild wheezing. A β2-agonist treatment produces no improvement. What is the next best management step?
questions.initialExplanation:
Bronchiolitis is usually a viral infection of the small airways in infants. Treatment is mainly supportive: provide oxygen when saturation is low and clear nasal secretions. Routine bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics are not recommended when there is no other indication.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The infection is most consistent with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis. RSV can cause mild to severe lower respiratory tract disease, and infants and neonates are at risk of respiratory failure and death. Treatment is primarily supportive and includes supplemental oxygen when required and frequent nasopharyngeal suctioning to clear secretions. Pharmacologic agents generally provide little or no benefit in routine bronchiolitis. A one-hour nebulized β2-agonist treatment may be considered only in selected patients with a previous response or a history suggesting asthma. Racemic epinephrine and corticosteroids have not been shown to provide routine benefit. Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is a concurrent bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A premature 2-month-old infant presents with nasal flaring, tachypnea, and chest retractions. Which viral infection is most strongly associated with this presentation in young infants?
questions.initialExplanation:
RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis in infants. Premature babies are at increased risk of severe disease, which may cause fast breathing, nasal flaring, and chest retractions.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, particularly in premature infants. It commonly produces lower respiratory tract symptoms such as nasal flaring, tachypnea, and retractions, which indicate increased work of breathing. Prematurity increases the risk of severe RSV disease.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant presents with tachypnea, fever, mild intercostal and subcostal retractions, dry cough, and wheezing. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, peribronchial thickening, and increased interstitial markings. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.initialExplanation:
Infant bronchiolitis is usually viral. The main treatment is supportive care, including oxygen for hypoxemia and fluids to prevent dehydration when feeding is difficult.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The presentation is consistent with bronchiolitis, a common viral lower respiratory tract infection in infants, most often caused by RSV. Management is supportive. Oxygen should be provided when needed to correct hypoxemia, and adequate fluid intake should be maintained, particularly when respiratory symptoms interfere with feeding. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for an uncomplicated viral illness. Corticosteroids and nebulized epinephrine are not routine treatments for bronchiolitis.

questions.stem: A previously well 1-year-old child develops runny nose, sneezing, and cough over two days. Family members have similar symptoms. The cough worsens, and the child develops moderate respiratory distress with nasal flaring, a hyperexpanded chest, and audible wheezing without rales. Chest X-ray shows patchy infiltrates and flattened diaphragms. What is the most appropriate next action?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor oxygenation and fluid status alone.

options.label: B
options.text: Give inhaled epinephrine and a single dose of a steroid.

options.label: C
options.text: Give short-acting bronchodilators and a short course of oral steroids.

options.label: D
options.text: Perform emergency intubation and give antibiotics.

questions.initialExplanation:
This is most consistent with viral bronchiolitis. The important steps are to observe breathing and oxygen levels and maintain hydration. Routine steroids and bronchodilators are not recommended for typical bronchiolitis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical picture and chest radiograph are compatible with bronchiolitis. Management is supportive, with monitoring of oxygenation and hydration. Bronchodilators and corticosteroids are treatments more commonly used for asthma and are less likely to help a child with a first episode of viral wheezing and no history of wheeze or atopy. A trial of a β-agonist may have limited benefit in selected cases, but it is not routine therapy. Croup and epiglottitis have different characteristic upper-airway findings. Pneumothorax would be more likely with unilateral findings or evidence of lung collapse. RSV is a common cause of bronchiolitis, which is usually self-limited and managed with supportive care.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has had a runny nose and cough for two to three days, with fever up to 39.2°C. The respiratory rate is 50/min, and the infant uses abdominal muscles to breathe. Examination reveals mild wheezing and coarse breath sounds throughout the chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Bronchiolitis is a viral infection of the small airways, especially common in infants. It begins like a cold and then causes cough, wheezing, and increased work of breathing. Treatment is usually supportive.

---

## Cystic Fibrosis
questions.detailedExplanation: Bronchiolitis is the most common cause of lower respiratory tract infection in children under one year of age. RSV is often the causative organism. Viral invasion of the lower airways causes increased mucus production, leading to bronchiolar obstruction, atelectasis, air trapping, and decreased ventilation. Symptoms range from mild to severe and may be fatal. A few days of cold-like symptoms are often followed by worsening cough and increased work of breathing. Examination may show wheezing, rales, retractions, and crackles. Chest X-ray findings are variable and may include hyperinflation with atelectasis, commonly in the right upper lobe. Treatment is supportive. Bronchitis involves inflammation of the bronchi rather than the bronchioles and is often viral and self-limited over 7–10 days. Acute pharyngitis causes sore throat and cold-like symptoms. Pneumonia may present similarly but more often has focal findings or consolidation. Bacterial tracheitis involves the larynx, trachea, and bronchi and may cause croup-like stridor, barking cough, and fever, with poor response to routine croup treatment; it requires antibiotics. Bronchoscopy may show an adherent mucopurulent membrane, and *Staphylococcus aureus* is a common cause.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent lung infections, chronic cough with sputum production, and poor growth. What is the most common cause of clinically significant bronchiectasis in the developed world?
questions.initialExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis causes thick, sticky secretions that are difficult to clear from the lungs. This leads to repeated infections and, over time, permanent airway damage called bronchiectasis.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic condition that leads to the production of thick, sticky mucus. This mucus can clog the airways and lead to recurrent respiratory infections and chronic inflammation. Over time, repeated infection and inflammation can cause bronchiectasis, which is permanent enlargement and destruction of the airways.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant has poor weight gain, persistent cough, and a history of pneumonia. The infant has also passed very large, foul-smelling stools for several months. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate?

options.label: D
options.text: Not visible in the supplied PDF image.

questions.initialExplanation:
The combination of recurrent respiratory disease, poor growth, and bulky foul-smelling stools suggests cystic fibrosis. A sweat chloride test is a key diagnostic test; a value above 60 mEq/L supports the diagnosis. Option D is not visible in the supplied page image, so it has not been reconstructed.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem disease caused by an abnormally functioning cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein. Abnormal secretions are produced as a result of decreased permeability to chloride ions in the secretory epithelium of a number of organs. Progressive lung failure is caused by accumulation of viscous secretions that obstruct the airway and lead to infection, bronchiectasis, and inflammatory changes. Survival has improved markedly during recent decades as a result of prompt recognition and aggressive treatment; the median age at death has increased from less than 10 years to more than 30 years. Therapeutic approaches include inhalation therapy, chest physical therapy, aggressive antibiotics, bronchodilators, oxygen, and nutritional support. Heart-lung transplantation has prolonged life and improved quality of life for terminal patients. Treatments discussed for the basic defect include amiloride, purified human plasma alpha-1 antitrypsin, recombinant DNAase, and gene therapy. Amiloride inhibits sodium and, with it, water reabsorption, improving airway hydration. Alpha-1 antitrypsin counters neutrophil elastase. DNAase acts on DNA released by dead leukocytes to reduce sputum viscosity. Gene therapy aims to alter the genetic material. Lung cancer does not appear to be associated with CF. Sweat chloride testing shows little overlap with control values: a result above 60 mEq/L is diagnostic, below 40 mEq/L is normal, and 40–60 mEq/L is intermediate. Genetic studies test for common CFTR mutations. Newborn screening may use immunoreactive trypsinogen followed by confirmatory testing. Other conditions can elevate sweat chloride, including adrenal insufficiency, ectodermal dysplasia, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, and malnutrition.

questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis can present with all of the following, EXCEPT:
questions.initialExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis can affect the lungs, sinuses, pancreas, and biliary tract. Rectal polyposis is not a typical feature; rectal prolapse is a separate complication that may occur.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Rectal polyposis is not a typical feature of cystic fibrosis. Rectal prolapse, however, can occur in patients with CF, partly because of chronic coughing and the passage of bulky stools. Cystic fibrosis is a multisystem disease and may involve the respiratory tract, paranasal sinuses, pancreas, and biliary system. Salt depletion can occur because of increased salt loss in sweat. Pansinusitis, pancreatitis, and cholelithiasis may also occur as manifestations or complications of the disease.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old patient with cystic fibrosis has increased cough and sputum production, with a decline in FEV1. Which pathogen isolated from a lower-airway sputum culture strongly suggests cystic fibrosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
*S. aureus* is an important early airway colonizer in children with cystic fibrosis. Chronic respiratory symptoms and characteristic cultures should prompt evaluation for CF.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Isolation of *Staphylococcus aureus* is common in cystic fibrosis, particularly in younger patients. It is among the earliest organisms to colonize the airways of patients with CF and can support the diagnosis when classic clinical symptoms are present, together with appropriate genetic testing. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, especially the mucoid form, becomes increasingly indicative in older patients with CF, but *S. aureus* is more strongly associated with early airway disease.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child has poor weight gain, frequent bulky greasy stools, and a persistent productive cough. The child has had two previous hospital admissions for respiratory infections, and a sibling has cystic fibrosis. What is the most common presenting feature of cystic fibrosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis affects several organs, but chronic cough and recurrent respiratory infections are often the first and most common presenting problems. Poor growth and greasy stools may provide additional clues.

---

## Bronchiectasis
questions.detailedExplanation: Although cystic fibrosis is a multisystem disease, persistent respiratory symptoms, such as chronic cough, recurrent wheezing, recurrent pneumonia, or bronchitis, are often the most common initial findings. Failure to thrive and abnormal stools are also common manifestations, but they may not be as immediately evident. Meconium ileus is a presentation in some newborns, rather than the most common presenting feature across all patients. Hepatobiliary disease may develop as another complication.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl has been diagnosed with bronchiectasis and presents for routine follow-up. What is the most common complaint in patients with this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Cough with production of copious purulent sputum.

questions.initialExplanation:
Bronchiectasis is permanent widening and damage of the airways. Mucus collects in the damaged airways and becomes infected, causing a long-term cough with large amounts of purulent sputum.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The hallmark of bronchiectasis is a chronic cough with production of a large amount of sputum, which is often purulent. This occurs because chronic infection and inflammation lead to permanent dilation and damage of the airways. The chronic productive cough is typically the most consistent and common complaint. Hemoptysis, fever, anorexia, and poor weight gain may occur, but they are not as characteristic or as common as the chronic cough with copious sputum.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has chronic cough and recurrent respiratory infections, with frequent pneumonia since infancy. Examination reveals coarse crackles, and imaging shows dilated, thickened bronchi in the lower lobes. What is the most likely cause of the bronchiectasis?
questions.initialExplanation:
In children, cystic fibrosis is an important cause of bronchiectasis. Thick mucus is difficult to clear, leading to repeated infections, chronic inflammation, and permanent airway dilation.

---

## Pneumothorax
questions.detailedExplanation: Bronchiectasis in children is often associated with underlying conditions that predispose to chronic respiratory infections and airway inflammation. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common cause of bronchiectasis in children. CF is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by dysfunction of the CFTR protein, leading to thick, sticky mucus in the airways. This mucus predisposes patients to recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis. Patients with CF often have chronic cough, recurrent pneumonia, and failure to thrive. Asthma, although common, is not typically associated with bronchiectasis unless it is severe and poorly controlled. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to *Aspergillus* antigens in the airways that can cause bronchial inflammation and mucus plugging, but it is less common in children than in adults. Immunodeficiency predisposes patients to recurrent infections, but it is less commonly associated with bronchiectasis in children than CF.

questions.stem: A newborn infant is suspected of having a tension pneumothorax. Which combination of clinical signs is most consistent with this condition?
questions.initialExplanation:
Air trapped in the pleural space can collapse the lung and impair breathing. In a tension pneumothorax, pressure can also reduce blood return to the heart, leading to cardiovascular instability. This is an emergency.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Infants with a symptomatic pneumothorax may present with tachypnea, cyanosis, and increased work of breathing. Apnea and irritability may also occur early. Examination may show an asymmetric chest and decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side. A tension pneumothorax can progress to cardiovascular compromise and shock; hypotension and bradycardia may occur as the condition worsens. The cardiac apex may be shifted away from the affected side. Prompt recognition and treatment are essential.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with known asthma presents with an acute attack and respiratory distress. One side of the chest has markedly decreased breath sounds and a tympanitic percussion note. The trachea and heart are shifted toward the unaffected side. What is the most likely complication?
questions.initialExplanation:
Unilateral absent or reduced breath sounds, a hyperresonant chest, and mediastinal shift suggest pneumothorax. With tension physiology, pressure pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side and can rapidly become life-threatening.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: The clinical scenario suggests a pneumothorax, specifically a possible tension pneumothorax. Key findings include markedly decreased breath sounds on one side, a tympanitic percussion note due to air in the pleural space, and tracheal and cardiac shift toward the unaffected side. A pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space, causing the lung to collapse. In a tension pneumothorax, air accumulates under pressure, compresses the opposite lung, and displaces the trachea and heart away from the affected side. This can cause severe respiratory distress and cardiovascular compromise. The other options do not explain this combination of characteristic findings.

questions.stem: A 1-year-old child is hospitalized with pneumonia, and blood culture grows *Staphylococcus aureus*. Within 20 hours, the child acutely deteriorates, with increased work of breathing, increasing oxygen requirements, and hypotension. Which item should be ordered immediately?

options.label: A
options.text: A second chest X-ray to evaluate for a pneumatocele.

options.label: B
options.text: A large-bore needle and chest-tube kit for aspiration of a probable tension pneumothorax.

options.label: C
options.text: A change in antibiotics to include gentamicin.

options.label: E
options.text: A thoracentesis kit to drain a probable pleural effusion.

questions.initialExplanation:
Sudden respiratory and circulatory deterioration in a child with pneumonia raises concern for tension pneumothorax. Immediate pleural decompression is required; do not delay emergency treatment for a routine repeat X-ray.

---

## Retropharyngeal Abscess
questions.detailedExplanation: The sudden deterioration, worsening hypoxia, increased work of breathing, and hypotension suggest a tension pneumothorax. This can complicate pneumonia, including pneumonia caused by *Staphylococcus aureus*, when alveolar rupture allows air to enter the pleural space. A tension pneumothorax can be rapidly fatal if not recognized and treated. Immediate relief is required by needle or catheter decompression, followed by definitive chest drainage. The source explanation describes insertion of a needle or catheter into the second or third intercostal space in the midclavicular line in a supine patient. Waiting for repeat imaging or changing antibiotics alone would delay treatment of the immediate life-threatening problem.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy has had low-grade fever, upper respiratory symptoms, and sore throat for three days. He then develops sudden high fever, dysphagia, difficulty handling secretions, and worsening throat pain. Examination reveals a fluctuant swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall, and a lateral neck radiograph shows widening of the prevertebral space. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?

options.label: B
options.text: A trial of oral penicillin V.

options.label: C
options.text: Surgical consultation for incision and drainage under general anesthesia.

questions.initialExplanation:
A retropharyngeal abscess is a deep collection of pus behind the throat. A fluctuant swelling with fever and difficulty swallowing needs urgent specialist management and drainage, with careful airway planning.

---

## Other Pediatric Respiratory Conditions
questions.detailedExplanation: A retropharyngeal abscess is a suppurative infection of the lymph nodes located between the posterior pharyngeal wall and the prevertebral fascia. Common organisms include *Staphylococcus aureus*, group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, and oral anaerobes. The history may include pharyngitis followed by abrupt fever, sore throat, refusal to eat, drooling, or noisy breathing. A bulge of the posterior pharyngeal wall is an important diagnostic finding, and a lateral neck radiograph may show increased prevertebral soft-tissue thickness. When a fluctuant mass is present, incision and drainage are indicated, with appropriate preparation to protect the airway. The other options would delay definitive treatment of a potentially life-threatening infection.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl was playing in a garage while her father was using a weed-whacker. The child was found gagging and vomiting, and the smell of gasoline was noted. Her symptoms initially improved, but she later developed cough, tachypnea, and subcostal retractions. What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Perform pulse oximetry and obtain an arterial blood gas.

questions.initialExplanation:
Gasoline aspiration can injure the lungs. When a child develops cough or breathing difficulty after hydrocarbon exposure, assess oxygenation and respiratory status first. Do not induce vomiting, because this can increase aspiration.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Hydrocarbons with low viscosity and high volatility, such as gasoline, kerosene, and furniture polish, can cause significant respiratory symptoms. Aspiration may lead to dyspnea, cyanosis, and respiratory failure. Management is mainly symptomatic and may require intubation and mechanical ventilation in severe cases. Emetics are contraindicated because they can worsen aspiration. Nasogastric lavage is generally reserved for a large-volume ingestion or when the hydrocarbon is mixed with another toxin. Activated charcoal has no useful role for a typical hydrocarbon ingestion, and there is no intravenous gasoline-binding agent. The immediate priority in a symptomatic child is to assess respiratory involvement and oxygenation.

questions.stem: A healthy 18-month-old child suddenly begins coughing while in a separate room. The coughing then improves, but the child develops increased drooling and refuses food by mouth. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: B
options.text: A foreign body in the airway.

options.label: E
options.text: A foreign body in the esophagus.

questions.initialExplanation:
Sudden choking followed by drooling and refusal to swallow suggests an esophageal foreign body. Persistent swallowing difficulty is an important clue that the object may be in the esophagus rather than the airway.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Objects such as small toys, coins, and pieces of food can cause esophageal obstruction. Many objects become lodged below the cricopharyngeal muscle or near the level of the aortic arch. Initial symptoms may include coughing, drooling, or choking. Later, the child may develop pain and refuse food; liquids may be tolerated better than solid food. Diagnosis is based on the history and radiographs, particularly when the object is radiopaque. The usual treatment is removal by esophagoscopy. Severe gastroesophageal reflux does not usually cause this abrupt presentation and is more often associated with ongoing symptoms such as asthma, pneumonia, or failure to thrive. An airway foreign body may cause acute cough that later improves when the object settles in the airway, but persistent drooling and refusal to swallow suggest esophageal obstruction. Croup usually causes a barking cough after upper respiratory symptoms. Epiglottitis is associated with high fever, a toxic appearance, and stridor.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant has had noisy breathing since birth. The sound is wet and snoring-like, particularly during feeding or when lying on the back. There are no feeding or swallowing problems, cyanosis, or choking episodes. The infant is thriving, has no respiratory distress, and has an oxygen saturation of 98%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation:
Laryngomalacia occurs when soft tissue above the vocal cords temporarily collapses inward during breathing in. This causes noisy breathing that is often worse when feeding or lying down; many otherwise healthy infants improve as they grow.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of noisy breathing in infants. It is caused by dynamic collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration, producing stridor or a wet, snoring, or crowing sound. It often presents during the first weeks or months of life and may be more noticeable during feeding, when lying down, or when the infant is agitated. Infants are otherwise often well and continue to thrive, as in this case.

questions.stem: A previously healthy, active 18-month-old child presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and foul-smelling nasal discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: A foreign body in the nose.

questions.initialExplanation:
A toddler with one-sided nasal blockage and foul-smelling discharge should be assessed for a nasal foreign body. The object can cause local infection and a persistent unpleasant smell.

---
questions.detailedExplanation: Young children commonly place small objects in their noses. A nasal foreign body may initially cause local irritation, followed by prolonged obstruction, pain, and purulent, foul-smelling, or blood-stained discharge. Unilateral nasal discharge with obstruction should prompt examination for a foreign body. Nasal polyps can cause obstruction but are unusual in a child this young and may be associated with cystic fibrosis. Frontal sinusitis is less likely to present in this way, and the frontal sinuses are poorly developed in very young children. A deviated septum does not explain the typical acute unilateral foul discharge. Choanal atresia usually presents in the newborn period with respiratory distress at rest that improves when the infant cries.
